abstract: We have used analog VLSI technology to model a class of small oscillating biological neural circuits known as central pattern generators (CPG). These circuits generate rhythmic patterns of activity which drive locomotor behaviour in the animal. We have designed, fabricated, and tested a model neuron circuit which relies on many of the same mechanisms as a biological central pattern generator neuron, such as delays and internal feedback. We show that this neuron can be used to build several small circuits based on known biological CPG circuits, and that these circuits produce patterns of output which are very similar to the observed biological patterns.
originalAbstract: We have used analog VLSI technology to model a class of small oscillating biological neural circuits known as central pattern generators (CPG). These circuits generate rhythmic patterns of activity which drive locomotor behaviour in the animal. We have designed, fabricated, and tested a model neuron circuit which relies on many of the same mechanisms as a biological central pattern generator neuron, such as delays and internal feedback. We show that this neuron can be used to build several small circuits based on known biological CPG circuits, and that these circuits produce patterns of output which are very similar to the observed biological patterns.

paragraphs: This paper uses analog VLSI circuitry to model central pattern generators, small biological networks that produce rhythms for locomotion. The focus is on reproducing the ongoing patterns generated by interacting neurons. Such a model must capture how activity develops over time and how circuit interactions sustain a rhythm.

The researchers design, fabricate, and test a neuron circuit that uses mechanisms also found in biological pattern-generator neurons, including delays and internal feedback. These mechanisms make timing and recurrent influence part of the circuit’s operation. The resulting neuron is then used as a building block for several small network configurations.

Those configurations are based on known biological central pattern generators, and their outputs closely resemble the observed biological activity patterns. The result connects the design of individual electronic neurons to the rhythms produced by assembled networks. The contribution is therefore a tested hardware modeling approach: biologically motivated temporal mechanisms at the neuron level can support recognizable biological patterns when the circuits are connected into small networks.
summary.tldr: Fabricated analog neuron circuits use delays and feedback to reproduce activity patterns resembling biological locomotion rhythm generators.

title: Modeling Small Oscillating Biological Networks in Analog VLSI

paragraphs: The paper applies neural networks to impulse noise in color television signals. Its motivation is that established consumer technologies still contain signal-processing problems that learned systems might address. Improving an existing video operation offers a concrete application for neural computation within a technology already used in everyday products.

The authors propose a modular neural network and compare it with a conventional median filter. Training and analysis take place on conventional computers, while real-time simulations run on the massively parallel Princeton Engine. This separates learning and analysis from the evaluation of whether the processing approach can operate at the pace required by video.

Both quantitative analysis and real-time simulations support the neural system’s technical superiority over the median filter in the reported work. The abstract also identifies hardware complexity and cost as subjects of ongoing investigation. The findings establish a technical advantage for the proposed processing approach while treating economical hardware implementation as a further step toward its use in consumer electronics.
summary.tldr: A modular neural network outperforms a median filter for television impulse noise in analysis and real-time simulations.

title: Applications of Neural Networks in Video Signal Processing

abstract: The neocognitron is a neural network for pattern recognition and feature extraction. An analog CCD parallel processing architecture developed at Lincoln Laboratory is particularly well suited to the computational re(cid:173) quirements of shared-weight networks such as the neocognitron, and imple(cid:173) mentation of the neocognitron using the CCD architecture was simulated. A modification to the neocognitron training procedure, which improves network performance under the limited arithmetic precision that would be imposed by the CCD architecture, is presented.

An analog CCD parallel processing architecture developed at Lincoln Laboratory is particularly well suited to the computational re(cid:173) quirements of shared-weight networks such as the neocognitron, and imple(cid:173) mentation of the neocognitron using the CCD architecture was simulated. A modification to the neocognitron training procedure, which improves network performance under the limited arithmetic precision that would be imposed by the CCD architecture, is presented.

paragraphs: The paper examines how to implement the neocognitron, a network for pattern recognition and feature extraction, on an analog CCD parallel processing architecture. The architecture is described as particularly well matched to shared-weight networks. Sharing weights means that the same learned parameters participate in multiple parts of the computation, making that reuse an important implementation consideration.

The authors simulate a neocognitron implementation on the CCD architecture. Their investigation considers the interaction between a recognition network and the arithmetic available in the proposed hardware. In particular, the architecture would impose limited numerical precision, so the network must perform its computations with restricted accuracy in the values it represents.

The paper introduces a modification to the training procedure that improves performance under this precision constraint. The result shows how adapting learning to the intended computing platform can help preserve network performance. Its contribution combines an architectural match for shared-weight computation with a training change aimed at a specific limitation of the simulated hardware implementation.
summary.tldr: Modified neocognitron training improves performance under the limited arithmetic precision of a simulated analog CCD architecture.

title: Simulation of the Neocognitron on a CCD Parallel Processing Architecture

abstract: We present a new connectionist planning method [TML90]. By interaction with an unknown environment, a world model is progressively construc(cid:173) ted using gradient descent. For deriving optimal actions with respect to future reinforcement, planning is applied in two steps: an experience net(cid:173) work proposes a plan which is subsequently optimized by gradient descent with a chain of world models, so that an optimal reinforcement may be obtained when it is actually run. The appropriateness of this method is demonstrated by a robotics application and a pole balancing task.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a connectionist planning method for an initially unknown environment. As the system interacts with that environment, it progressively learns a world model using gradient descent. The model provides a learned basis for considering the consequences of actions, linking experience in the environment with subsequent planning.

Planning proceeds in two stages. An experience network first proposes a plan. The system then refines that proposal by gradient descent through a chain of world models, seeking actions that produce favorable future reinforcement. The initial proposal and its optimization have distinct roles: one supplies a candidate course of action, while the other adjusts it using predicted consequences.

The authors demonstrate the method on a robotics application and a pole-balancing task. These examples support the use of a learned world model as part of the planning process. The approach joins model learning, plan proposal, and plan refinement in one system, allowing experience to shape both its account of the environment and the actions selected for future reward.
summary.tldr: A planner learns an environment model, proposes plans with an experience network, and refines them through predicted future reinforcement.

title: Planning with an Adaptive World Model

abstract: We propose a paradigm for modeling speech production based on neural networks. We focus on characteristics of the musculoskeletal system. Using real physiological data - articulator movements and EMG from muscle activity(cid:173) a neural network learns the forward dynamics relating motor commands to muscles and the ensuing articulator behavior. After learning, simulated perturbations, were used to asses properties of the acquired model, such as natural frequency, damping, and interarticulator couplings. Finally, a cascade neural network is used to generate continuous motor commands from a sequence of discrete articulatory targets.

After learning, simulated perturbations, were used to asses properties of the acquired model, such as natural frequency, damping, and interarticulator couplings. paragraphs: Speech production depends on how muscle commands move articulators, so a useful model needs to capture the musculoskeletal dynamics underlying sound production. This paper learns those forward dynamics from physiological measurements. It uses articulator motion and electromyography rather than relying only on acoustic observations.

A neural network maps motor commands and muscle activity to the resulting articulator behavior. After training, simulated perturbations probe properties of the learned system, including natural frequency, damping, and couplings between articulators. These tests examine whether the model captures meaningful dynamic relationships rather than merely reproducing recorded trajectories.

A cascade network then generates continuous motor commands from sequences of discrete articulatory targets. The contribution connects a learned physiological dynamics model with a mechanism for organizing movement commands over time. It offers a neural-network framework for studying both how speech movements unfold and how a sequence of intended articulations can be translated into continuous control.
summary.tldr: Physiological movement and EMG data train neural forward dynamics for speech, then support continuous commands from discrete articulatory targets.

title: Forward Dynamics Modeling of Speech Motor Control Using Physiological Data

abstract: An incremental network model is introduced which is able to learn the important topological relations in a given set of input vectors by means of a simple Hebb-like learning rule. In contrast to previous approaches like the "neural gas" method of Martinetz and Schulten (1991, 1994), this model has no parameters which change over time and is able to continue learning, adding units and connections, until a performance criterion has been met. Applications of the model include vector quantization, clustering, and interpolation.
originalAbstract: An incremental network model is introduced which is able to learn the important topological relations in a given set of input vectors by means of a simple Hebb-like learning rule. In contrast to previous approaches like the "neural gas" method of Martinetz and Schulten (1991, 1994), this model has no parameters which change over time and is able to continue learning, adding units and connections, until a performance criterion has been met. Applications of the model include vector quantization, clustering, and interpolation.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a network that grows while learning the structure of a collection of input vectors. Its goal is to capture important topological relationships: how different parts of the input data relate to one another. Learning therefore concerns both the units used to represent the data and the connections that express relationships among those units.

The model uses a simple Hebb-like learning rule and can add units and connections as learning proceeds. Unlike the earlier neural gas approach described in the abstract, it does not require parameters that change according to a time schedule. It can continue adapting until a chosen performance criterion has been satisfied, connecting the duration of learning to that criterion.

This combination matters because representation size and connectivity can develop during learning rather than being fixed throughout the process. The abstract identifies vector quantization, clustering, and interpolation as applications. Across these uses, the shared contribution is an incremental representation that learns relationships in the data while expanding its own structure.
summary.tldr: Growing neural gas learns relationships among inputs by adding units and connections until a performance criterion is met.

title: A Growing Neural Gas Network Learns Topologies

abstract: A biologically motivated model of cortical self-organization is proposed. Context is combined with bottom-up information via a maximum likelihood cost function. Clusters of one or more units are modulated by a common contextual gating Signal; they thereby organize themselves into mutually supportive predictors of abstract contextual features. The model was tested in its ability to discover viewpoint-invariant classes on a set of real image sequences of centered, gradually rotating faces. It performed considerably better than supervised back-propagation at generalizing to novel views from a small number of training examples.
originalAbstract: A biologically motivated model of cortical self-organization is proposed. Context is combined with bottom-up information via a maximum likelihood cost function. Clusters of one or more units are modulated by a common contextual gating Signal; they thereby organize themselves into mutually supportive predictors of abstract contextual features. The model was tested in its ability to discover viewpoint-invariant classes on a set of real image sequences of centered, gradually rotating faces. It performed considerably better than supervised back-propagation at generalizing to novel views from a small number of training examples.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a biologically motivated model for how useful representations can organize themselves. Its central idea is to combine immediate, bottom-up information with context, allowing the model to learn features that remain meaningful as observations change. The combination is expressed through a maximum-likelihood objective.

Groups containing one or more units share a contextual gating signal that modulates their activity. Through learning, the units become mutually supportive predictors of abstract contextual features. Shared modulation gives context an organizing role: it influences how groups of units develop their representations, rather than leaving each unit to respond only to the current bottom-up input.

The authors test whether the model can discover classes that stay consistent across viewpoints using real image sequences of centered faces rotating gradually. With few training examples, it generalizes to unseen views considerably better than supervised backpropagation. The result supports the value of contextual organization for this setting, where changing images contain persistent class information and the training sequences expose that continuity.
summary.tldr: Contextually gated groups learn representations that generalize across unseen face views from few training examples.

title: Learning Temporally Persistent Hierarchical Representations

abstract: We consider neural network models for stochastic nonlinear dynamical systems where measurements of the variable of interest are only avail(cid:173) able at irregular intervals i.e. most realizations are missing. Difficulties arise since the solutions for prediction and maximum likelihood learn(cid:173) ing with missing data lead to complex integrals, which even for simple cases cannot be solved analytically. In this paper we propose a spe(cid:173) cific combination of a nonlinear recurrent neural predictive model and a linear error model which leads to tractable prediction and maximum likelihood adaptation rules. In particular, the recurrent neural network can be trained using the real-time recurrent learning rule and the linear error model can be trained by an EM adaptation rule, implemented us(cid:173) ing forward-backward Kalman filter equations. The model is applied to predict the glucose/insulin metabolism of a diabetic patient where blood glucose measurements are only available a few times a day at irregular intervals. The new model shows considerable improvement with respect to both recurrent neural networks trained with teacher forcing or in a free running mode and various linear models.

paragraphs: Predicting a changing system becomes difficult when measurements arrive only occasionally and at irregular intervals. For nonlinear systems with randomness, accounting for the unobserved values can require integrals that have no analytical solution. The paper addresses this obstacle in both prediction and maximum-likelihood learning.

The proposed model combines a nonlinear recurrent neural predictor with a linear model of its errors. This particular combination makes the prediction and adaptation rules tractable. The recurrent component is trained with real-time recurrent learning, while the error component uses expectation-maximization implemented through forward-backward Kalman filtering equations. The two components therefore handle different parts of the modeling problem.

The authors apply the approach to a diabetic patient's glucose and insulin metabolism, with blood glucose measured only a few times daily at irregular times. They report considerable improvement over recurrent networks trained through teacher forcing or free-running prediction, as well as several linear models. The result supports combining nonlinear prediction with structured error modeling when observations are sparse and unevenly spaced.
summary.tldr: Combining a recurrent predictor with a linear error model makes learning from irregularly missing measurements tractable.

title: A Solution for Missing Data in Recurrent Neural Networks with an Application to Blood Glucose Prediction

abstract: We have developed a neural network architecture that implements a the(cid:173) ory of attention, learning, and trans-cortical communication based on adaptive synchronization of 5-15 Hz and 30-80 Hz oscillations between cortical areas. Here we present a specific higher order cortical model of attentional networks, rhythmic expectancy, and the interaction of hi~her­ order and primar¥, cortical levels of processing. It accounts for the' mis(cid:173) match negativity' of the auditory ERP and the results of psychological experiments of Jones showing that auditory stream segregation depends on the rhythmic structure of inputs. The timing mechanisms of the model allow us to explain how relative timing information such as the relative order of events between streams is lost when streams are formed. The model suggests how the theories of auditory perception and attention of Jones and Bregman may be reconciled.

paragraphs: This paper presents a neural-network model linking attention and auditory perception through synchronized oscillations between cortical areas. The broader architecture uses adaptive synchronization in the 5–15 Hz and 30–80 Hz ranges. Here the focus is rhythmic expectation and interaction between higher-order cortical processing and primary processing.

The model accounts for mismatch negativity in auditory event-related potentials and for psychological findings that the rhythmic structure of sounds affects how they separate into perceptual streams. Rhythm therefore plays a role in organizing what is heard, connecting the timing of incoming events with the attentional processes represented in the network.

Its timing mechanisms also explain how forming separate streams can lose information about the relative order of events across those streams. This connects successful grouping with a specific loss of timing information. The authors suggest that the model can reconcile the auditory-perception and attention theories of Jones and Bregman, providing a shared account of rhythmic organization, attention, and cross-stream temporal judgments.
summary.tldr: A synchronized neural-network model links rhythmic expectation to auditory stream formation and the loss of timing information between streams.

title: Synchronized Auditory and Cognitive 40 Hz Attentional Streams, and the Impact of Rhythmic Expectation on Auditory Scene Analysis

abstract: This paper reveals a previously ignored connection between two important fields: regularization and independent component anal(cid:173) ysis (ICA). We show that at least one representative of a broad class of algorithms (regularizers that reduce network complexity) extracts independent features as a by-product. This algorithm is Flat Minimum Search (FMS), a recent general method for finding low-complexity networks with high generalization capability. FMS works by minimizing both training error and required weight pre(cid:173) cision. According to our theoretical analysis the hidden layer of an FMS-trained autoassociator attempts at coding each input by a sparse code with as few simple features as possible. In experi(cid:173) ments the method extracts optimal codes for difficult versions of the "noisy bars" benchmark problem by separating the underlying sources, whereas ICA and PCA fail. Real world images are coded with fewer bits per pixel than by ICA or PCA.

paragraphs: This paper links network regularization with independent component analysis by showing that a particular complexity-reduction method can extract independent features as a by-product. The method is Flat Minimum Search, which minimizes training error together with the precision needed to specify network weights. The claim concerns this demonstrated representative of a broader class of regularizers.

The theoretical analysis examines an autoassociator trained with Flat Minimum Search. It indicates that the hidden layer attempts to represent each input through a sparse code using as few simple features as possible. This connects pressure for a low-complexity network with the emergence of a compact representation of the input's underlying sources.

In experiments, the method finds optimal codes on difficult versions of the noisy-bars problem by separating sources, while ICA and PCA fail on those cases. For real-world images, it uses fewer bits per pixel than ICA or PCA. These findings show that the studied regularization procedure can support both source separation and efficient coding, without establishing that all complexity-reducing methods do so.
summary.tldr: Flat Minimum Search can produce sparse, source-separating representations as a by-product of reducing network complexity.

title: Source Separation as a By-Product of Regularization

abstract: Transduction is an inference principle that takes a training sam(cid:173) ple and aims at estimating the values of a function at given points contained in the so-called working sample as opposed to the whole of input space for induction. Transduction provides a confidence measure on single predictions rather than classifiers - a feature particularly important for risk-sensitive applications. The possibly infinite number of functions is reduced to a finite number of equiv(cid:173) alence classes on the working sample. A rigorous Bayesian analysis reveals that for standard classification loss we cannot benefit from considering more than one test point at a time. The probability of the label of a given test point is determined as the posterior measure of the corresponding subset of hypothesis space. We con(cid:173) sider the PAC setting of binary classification by linear discriminant functions (perceptrons) in kernel space such that the probability of labels is determined by the volume ratio in version space. We suggest to sample this region by an ergodic billiard. Experimen(cid:173) tal results on real world data indicate that Bayesian Transduction compares favourably to the well-known Support Vector Machine, in particular if the posterior probability of labellings is used as a confidence measure to exclude test points of low confidence.

paragraphs: Transduction aims to predict values at a specified set of test points rather than learn a function for the entire input space. This paper develops a Bayesian treatment that attaches confidence to individual predictions. Functions that agree on the working sample can be grouped together, reducing a potentially infinite collection to finitely many equivalence classes.

The analysis shows that, under standard classification loss, considering several test points together provides no benefit over considering them individually. A point's label probability is the posterior probability assigned to the hypotheses that give it that label. For binary classification with linear discriminants in kernel space, the authors express these probabilities through volume ratios in version space and propose an ergodic billiard for sampling that region.

Experiments on real-world data indicate favorable performance relative to support vector machines, especially when posterior confidence is used to exclude uncertain test points. That qualification matters: some of the reported advantage concerns predictions retained after low-confidence cases are removed. The framework makes prediction-specific uncertainty central to the inference procedure.
summary.tldr: Bayesian transduction assigns posterior confidence to individual test labels and compares favorably with SVMs, particularly when uncertain predictions are excluded.

title: Bayesian Transduction

abstract: In this paper we show that on-line algorithms for classiﬁcation and re- gression can be naturally used to obtain hypotheses with good data- dependent tail bounds on their risk. Our results are proven without re- quiring complicated concentration-of-measure arguments and they hold for arbitrary on-line learning algorithms. Furthermore, when applied to concrete on-line algorithms, our results yield tail bounds that in many cases are comparable or better than the best known bounds.
originalAbstract: In this paper we show that on-line algorithms for classiﬁcation and re- gression can be naturally used to obtain hypotheses with good data- dependent tail bounds on their risk. Our results are proven without re- quiring complicated concentration-of-measure arguments and they hold for arbitrary on-line learning algorithms. Furthermore, when applied to concrete on-line algorithms, our results yield tail bounds that in many cases are comparable or better than the best known bounds.

paragraphs: The paper connects online learning with guarantees about predictive risk. Online algorithms update as examples arrive, while a generalization guarantee concerns how well a resulting predictor performs beyond the observations used in learning. The authors show how online classification and regression algorithms can yield hypotheses with data-dependent tail bounds on that risk.

A tail bound controls the probability of an unfavorable risk outcome, and a data-dependent bound incorporates information from the observed learning data. The framework applies to arbitrary online learning algorithms. The authors also establish the results without requiring complicated concentration-of-measure arguments, providing a comparatively direct route to the guarantees.

When specialized to concrete online algorithms, the framework gives bounds that are comparable to or better than the best known bounds in many cases. This is a qualified comparison, rather than an improvement claimed for every algorithm. The result matters because it supplies a general bridge from sequential learning procedures to probabilistic statements about their resulting predictors' performance.
summary.tldr: A general framework turns online learning algorithms into predictors with data-dependent risk bounds that are competitive in many cases.

title: On the Generalization Ability of On-Line Learning Algorithms

abstract: We propose a model that can learn parts-based representations of high- dimensional data. Our key assumption is that the dimensions of the data can be separated into several disjoint subsets, or factors, which take on values independently of each other. We assume each factor has a small number of discrete states, and model it using a vector quantizer. The selected states of each factor represent the multiple causes of the input. Given a set of training examples, our model learns the association of data dimensions with factors, as well as the states of each VQ. Inference and learning are carried out efﬁciently via variational algorithms. We present applications of this model to problems in image decomposition, collaborative ﬁltering, and text classiﬁcation.

Our key assumption is that the dimensions of the data can be separated into several disjoint subsets, or factors, which take on values independently of each other. paragraphs: This paper proposes a model that learns a parts-based representation of high-dimensional data. Its key assumption is that the dimensions can be divided into disjoint groups, called factors, whose values vary independently. Each factor is assumed to have only a small number of discrete states, providing a compact description of its possible configurations.

The model represents each factor with a vector quantizer. An input is explained by the selected states of several factors, which act as its multiple causes. Learning determines both which dimensions belong to each factor and which states each factor can take. The decomposition and the representations of its parts are therefore learned together from training examples.

Variational algorithms make inference and learning efficient within this formulation. The authors present applications to image decomposition, collaborative filtering, and text classification. These examples illustrate how the same factor-based model can be used across different data types. Its interpretation rests on the stated independent, disjoint-factor structure, which defines how the learned parts combine to represent an input.
summary.tldr: Multiple cause vector quantization learns independent groups of dimensions and discrete states that jointly provide a parts-based representation.

title: Multiple Cause Vector Quantization

abstract: The Bradley-Terry model for paired comparison has been popular in many areas. We propose a generalized version in which paired individual comparisons are extended to paired team comparisons. We introduce a simple algorithm with convergence proofs to solve the model and obtain individual skill. A useful application to multi-class probability estimates using error-correcting codes is demonstrated.
originalAbstract: The Bradley-Terry model for paired comparison has been popular in many areas. We propose a generalized version in which paired individual comparisons are extended to paired team comparisons. We introduce a simple algorithm with convergence proofs to solve the model and obtain individual skill. A useful application to multi-class probability estimates using error-correcting codes is demonstrated.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to estimate individual skill when the observed comparisons are between teams. It starts from the Bradley–Terry model, which handles paired comparisons between individuals, and generalizes that setting to paired groups. The central change is in what gets compared: outcomes concern collections of participants, while the quantities of interest remain individual abilities.

This creates a distinction between the level at which evidence is observed and the level at which the model must explain it. A team comparison supplies evidence about a group outcome; the generalized model provides a way to connect that evidence to individual skill estimates. The authors introduce a simple algorithm for solving the model and provide proofs of its convergence.

The paper also demonstrates an application to estimating probabilities for multiple classes using error-correcting codes. This connects the group-comparison formulation to a classification problem beyond direct skill assessment. Together, the contributions are a broader comparison model, a procedure with convergence support, and a demonstrated use of that model for multiclass probability estimation.
summary.tldr: A generalized Bradley–Terry model estimates individual skill from team comparisons and supports multiclass probability estimation.

title: A Generalized Bradley-Terry Model: From Group Competition to Individual Skill

abstract: We extend a previously developed Bayesian framework for perception to account for sensory adaptation. We ﬁrst note that the perceptual ef- fects of adaptation seems inconsistent with an adjustment of the inter- nally represented prior distribution. Instead, we postulate that adaptation increases the signal-to-noise ratio of the measurements by adapting the operational range of the measurement stage to the input range. We show that this changes the likelihood function in such a way that the Bayesian estimator model can account for reported perceptual behavior. In particu- lar, we compare the model’s predictions to human motion discrimination data and demonstrate that the model accounts for the commonly observed perceptual adaptation effects of repulsion and enhanced discriminability.

We show that this changes the likelihood function in such a way that the Bayesian estimator model can account for reported perceptual behavior. paragraphs: The paper extends a Bayesian model of perception to explain sensory adaptation. It begins from the observation that adaptation's perceptual effects appear inconsistent with simply changing the internally represented prior distribution. The authors therefore investigate a different component of the perceptual process: how sensory measurements are produced.

They propose that adaptation adjusts the measurement stage's operating range to match the input range, increasing the signal-to-noise ratio. This changes the likelihood function, which describes how measurements relate to the stimulus in the Bayesian model. The proposed mechanism connects changes in sensory measurement with changes in the perceptual estimates that follow.

The authors compare the resulting predictions with human motion discrimination data. The model accounts for two commonly observed adaptation effects: perceptual repulsion and improved discriminability. The findings show how both effects can be accommodated within the extended Bayesian framework through a change in measurement quality. The contribution is a proposed measurement-level explanation of adaptation whose predictions agree with the reported perceptual behavior considered in the paper.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian perception model explains reported adaptation effects by proposing changes to sensory measurement range and signal-to-noise ratio.

title: Sensory Adaptation within a Bayesian Framework for Perception

abstract: This paper introduces Gaussian Process Dynamical Models (GPDM) for nonlinear time series analysis. A GPDM comprises a low-dimensional latent space with associated dynamics, and a map from the latent space to an observation space. We marginalize out the model parameters in closed-form, using Gaussian Process (GP) priors for both the dynamics and the observation mappings. This results in a nonparametric model for dynamical systems that accounts for uncertainty in the model. We demonstrate the approach on human motion capture data in which each pose is 62-dimensional. Despite the use of small data sets, the GPDM learns an effective representation of the nonlinear dynamics in these spaces. Webpage: http://www.dgp.toronto.edu/

This results in a nonparametric model for dynamical systems that accounts for uncertainty in the model. We demonstrate the approach on human motion capture data in which each pose is 62-dimensional. paragraphs: Gaussian Process Dynamical Models are introduced as a way to analyze nonlinear time series. The model describes observations through a lower-dimensional latent space, whose states evolve over time. A separate mapping connects those latent states to the observed measurements, so the representation includes both temporal behavior and how that behavior appears in the data.

The authors place Gaussian process priors on the dynamics and on the mapping to observations. They then marginalize the model parameters in closed form. The resulting nonparametric model accounts for uncertainty in the model while retaining this division between the hidden dynamics and their observable expression.

The approach is demonstrated on human motion capture data, with each pose described by 62 dimensions. Despite using small datasets, it learns an effective representation of the nonlinear dynamics in those spaces. This finding supports the usefulness of combining a compact latent representation with uncertainty-aware modeling in the demonstrated setting. The central contribution is a single framework for representing high-dimensional observations and learning their underlying temporal evolution.
summary.tldr: Gaussian Process Dynamical Models combine low-dimensional latent dynamics and observation mappings to model nonlinear time series while accounting for model uncertainty.

title: Gaussian Process Dynamical Models

abstract: We demonstrate the ﬁrst fully hardware implementation of retinotopic self-organization, from photon transduction to neural map formation. A silicon retina transduces patterned illumination into correlated spike trains that drive a population of silicon growth cones to automatically wire a topographic mapping by migrating toward sources of a diffusible guidance cue that is released by postsynaptic spikes. We varied the pat- tern of illumination to steer growth cones projected by different retinal ganglion cell types to self-organize segregated or coordinated retinotopic maps.
originalAbstract: We demonstrate the ﬁrst fully hardware implementation of retinotopic self-organization, from photon transduction to neural map formation. We varied the pat- tern of illumination to steer growth cones projected by different retinal ganglion cell types to self-organize segregated or coordinated retinotopic maps.

paragraphs: This paper demonstrates a hardware system that builds an organized retinal map from visual input. The authors describe it as the first fully hardware implementation covering the entire process from photon transduction to retinotopic self-organization. The map is formed automatically through interactions among silicon components driven by patterned illumination.

A silicon retina converts the light patterns into correlated spike trains. These signals drive silicon growth cones, which migrate toward sources of a diffusible guidance cue released by postsynaptic spikes. Their movement wires a topographic mapping, connecting the activity generated by visual input to the physical organization of the resulting neural map.

By changing the illumination pattern, the researchers steer growth cones associated with different retinal ganglion-cell types toward either segregated or coordinated retinotopic maps. This shows that the organization produced by the hardware depends on the structure of its input. The contribution is an integrated demonstration of sensory-driven map formation, with illumination influencing how different populations organize their projections.
summary.tldr: A silicon retina and silicon growth cones form topographic maps automatically, with illumination patterns steering their organization.

title: Silicon growth cones map silicon retina

abstract: We consider a general form of transductive learning on graphs with Laplacian regularization, and derive margin-based generalization bounds using appropriate geometric properties of the graph. We use this analysis to obtain a better understanding of the role of normalization of the graph Laplacian matrix as well as the effect of dimension reduction. The results suggest a limitation of the standard degree-based normalization. We propose a remedy from our analysis and demonstrate empirically that the remedy leads to improved classification performance.

We use this analysis to obtain a better understanding of the role of normalization of the graph Laplacian matrix as well as the effect of dimension reduction. The results suggest a limitation of the standard degree-based normalization. We propose a remedy from our analysis and demonstrate empirically that the remedy leads to improved classification performance.

paragraphs: The paper examines transductive learning on graphs with Laplacian regularization. In this setting, graph structure helps guide predictions for the objects under consideration. The authors study a general form of the learning problem and derive margin-based generalization bounds that depend on appropriate geometric properties of the graph.

They use those bounds to understand two modeling choices: how the graph Laplacian is normalized and how reducing dimension affects learning. Normalization changes the matrix used by the regularizer, so its role matters to the behavior of the resulting classifier. The analysis suggests a limitation of the standard normalization based on node degrees.

The authors then propose a remedy motivated by that analysis and show empirically that it improves classification performance. The paper connects a theoretical investigation of graph geometry to a practical adjustment in the learning method. Its findings give a reason to examine the normalization choice carefully, while establishing an empirical benefit for the proposed remedy in the reported evaluation.
summary.tldr: Graph-based generalization bounds expose a limitation of degree normalization and motivate a remedy that improves classification empirically.

title: Learning on Graph with Laplacian Regularization

abstract: Recently, we have introduced a novel approach to dynamic programming and re- inforcement learning that is based on maintaining explicit representations of sta- tionary distributions instead of value functions. In this paper, we investigate the convergence properties of these dual algorithms both theoretically and empirically, and show how they can be scaled up by incorporating function approximation.
originalAbstract: Recently, we have introduced a novel approach to dynamic programming and re- inforcement learning that is based on maintaining explicit representations of sta- tionary distributions instead of value functions. In this paper, we investigate the convergence properties of these dual algorithms both theoretically and empirically, and show how they can be scaled up by incorporating function approximation.

paragraphs: The paper examines an alternative representation for dynamic programming and reinforcement learning. The authors’ previously introduced approach explicitly maintains stationary distributions in place of value functions. This changes the central object tracked by the algorithm: its representation concerns stationary behavior rather than a function assigning values.

Here, the authors focus on the convergence properties of these dual algorithms. They investigate those properties through both theoretical analysis and empirical study. Convergence is a central question for such a representational change because introducing a different quantity to maintain also raises the question of how the resulting iterative learning procedure behaves.

The paper additionally shows how function approximation can be incorporated to scale up the approach. This connects the investigation of convergence with the practical issue of using the representation in larger problems. The stated contribution is therefore a study of the behavior and scalability of an existing dual approach, combining mathematical and empirical examination with an approximation-based extension. Its significance lies in developing stationary-distribution methods as an alternative foundation for these learning and planning algorithms.
summary.tldr: The paper studies convergence and function-approximation-based scaling for dynamic programming algorithms that maintain stationary distributions instead of value functions.

title: Stable Dual Dynamic Programming

abstract: Semantic memory refers to our knowledge of facts and relationships between con- cepts. A successful semantic memory depends on inferring relationships between items that are not explicitly taught. Recent mathematical modeling of episodic memory argues that episodic recall relies on retrieval of a gradually-changing rep- resentation of temporal context. We show that retrieved context enables the de- velopment of a global memory space that reﬂects relationships between all items that have been previously learned. When newly-learned information is integrated into this structure, it is placed in some relationship to all other items, even if that relationship has not been explicitly learned. We demonstrate this effect for global semantic structures shaped topologically as a ring, and as a two-dimensional sheet. We also examined the utility of this learning algorithm for learning a more realistic semantic space by training it on a large pool of synonym pairs. Retrieved context enabled the model to “infer” relationships between synonym pairs that had not yet been presented.

This paper connects that ability to a mechanism from models of episodic memory: retrieving a representation of temporal context that changes gradually over time. The question is whether retrieved context can help organize broader knowledge.

The authors show that this mechanism supports the formation of a global memory space reflecting relationships among previously learned items. When new information enters that space, it takes on relationships to other items even when those connections have not been explicitly learned. They demonstrate this effect for structures with ring and two-dimensional sheet topologies.

The model is also trained on a large collection of synonym pairs to examine a more realistic semantic setting. Retrieved context enables it to infer relationships between pairs that have not yet been presented. The contribution links a temporal-context mechanism associated with remembering episodes to the emergence of semantic structure, showing how individual learning experiences can become part of a more interconnected representation.
summary.tldr: Retrieved temporal context helps a memory model build global semantic structure and infer relationships that were not explicitly taught.

title: Retrieved context and the discovery of semantic structure

abstract: We describe a new content publishing system that selects articles to serve to a user, choosing from an editorially programmed pool that is frequently refreshed. It is now deployed on a major Internet portal, and selects articles to serve to hundreds of millions of user visits per day, significantly increasing the number of user clicks over the original manual approach, in which editors periodically selected articles to display. Some of the challenges we face include a dynamic content pool, short article lifetimes, non-stationary click-through rates, and extremely high traffic volumes. The fundamental problem we must solve is to quickly identify which items are popular(perhaps within different user segments), and to exploit them while they remain current. We must also explore the underlying pool constantly to identify promising alternatives, quickly discarding poor performers. Our approach is based on tracking per article performance in near real time through online models. We describe the characteristics and constraints of our application setting, discuss our design choices, and show the importance and effectiveness of coupling online models with a simple randomization procedure. We discuss the challenges encountered in a production online content-publishing environment and highlight issues that deserve careful attention. Our analysis of this application also suggests a number of future research avenues.

The setting makes prediction unusually time-sensitive: articles have short useful lifetimes, click rates change, and traffic is extremely high. The system must discover which articles attract interest quickly enough to use that information while the articles remain current.

The approach tracks individual articles' performance through online models updated in near real time. These models are coupled with a simple randomization procedure. The combination supports both serving articles already judged promising and continuing to test alternatives, so the system can discover emerging successes and discard weak performers as the available content changes.

The system serves hundreds of millions of user visits per day on a major Internet portal and significantly increases clicks compared with the previous manual selection approach. The paper also discusses design choices and production constraints. Its practical finding is that continually updated models and ongoing exploration can work together effectively in a large, rapidly changing content-publishing environment.
summary.tldr: A deployed article-selection system combines online performance models with randomization to significantly increase clicks over manual selection.

title: Online Models for Content Optimization

abstract: Bayesian inference provides a unifying framework for addressing problems in machine learning, artificial intelligence, and robotics, as well as the problems facing the human mind. Unfortunately, exact Bayesian inference is intractable in all but the simplest models. Therefore minds and machines have to approximate Bayesian inference. Approximate inference algorithms can achieve a wide range of time-accuracy tradeoffs, but what is the optimal tradeoff? We investigate time-accuracy tradeoffs using the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm as a metaphor for the mind's inference algorithm(s). We find that reasonably accurate decisions are possible long before the Markov chain has converged to the posterior distribution, i.e. during the period known as burn-in. Therefore the strategy that is optimal subject to the mind's bounded processing speed and opportunity costs may perform so few iterations that the resulting samples are biased towards the initial value. The resulting cognitive process model provides a rational basis for the anchoring-and-adjustment heuristic. The model's quantitative predictions are tested against published data on anchoring in numerical estimation tasks. Our theoretical and empirical results suggest that the anchoring bias is consistent with approximate Bayesian inference.

paragraphs: The paper asks how much computation an approximate Bayesian decision maker should perform before acting. Exact inference is generally intractable in complex models, so additional computation trades time for accuracy. The authors use Metropolis–Hastings sampling as a metaphor for mental inference to study that tradeoff.

They find that decisions can become reasonably accurate before the sampling chain has converged to the posterior distribution. During this initial period, called burn-in, samples still depend on the starting value. With limited processing speed and costs for spending more time, an optimal strategy may stop after relatively few iterations. Its estimates can therefore remain pulled toward their initial value.

This mechanism provides a rational account of anchoring and adjustment: an initial estimate continues to influence the final judgment because further computation may not justify its cost. The authors test quantitative predictions against published numerical-estimation data. Their theoretical and empirical results suggest that anchoring is consistent with approximate Bayesian inference, using the sampling model as an explanatory account of the behavior.
summary.tldr: Anchoring may reflect a rational decision to stop approximate Bayesian computation before its dependence on the initial estimate disappears.

title: Burn-in, bias, and the rationality of anchoring

abstract: For data assumed to come from a finite mixture with an unknown number of components, it has become common to use Dirichlet process mixtures (DPMs) not only for density estimation, but also for inferences about the number of components. The typical approach is to use the posterior distribution on the number of components occurring so far --- that is, the posterior on the number of clusters in the observed data. However, it turns out that this posterior is not consistent --- it does not converge to the true number of components. In this note, we give an elementary demonstration of this inconsistency in what is perhaps the simplest possible setting: a DPM with normal components of unit variance, applied to data from a mixture" with one standard normal component. Further, we find that this example exhibits severe inconsistency: instead of going to 1, the posterior probability that there is one cluster goes to 0."

paragraphs: A mixture model describes a population using several component distributions. When the number of components is unknown, researchers sometimes fit a Dirichlet process mixture and use its posterior number of occupied clusters to estimate that number. This paper examines whether that practice gives the correct answer as more observations become available.

The authors provide an elementary counterexample in an especially simple setting. The fitted model has normal components with unit variance, while the observations actually come from a single standard normal distribution. The true component count is therefore one. Nevertheless, the posterior distribution over the number of clusters does not concentrate on that answer.

The failure is particularly strong: the posterior probability of exactly one cluster approaches zero rather than one. More data therefore do not repair this inference in the example. The result concerns using occupied clusters to infer the underlying component count; it distinguishes that objective from the separate task of estimating a probability density.
summary.tldr: A simple Gaussian example shows that a Dirichlet process mixture's posterior cluster count can become increasingly inconsistent with the true component count.

title: A simple example of Dirichlet process mixture inconsistency for the number of components

abstract: We introduce a new multi-task framework, in which $K$ online learners are sharing a single annotator with limited bandwidth. On each round, each of the $K$ learners receives an input, and makes a prediction about the label of that input. Then, a shared (stochastic) mechanism decides which of the $K$ inputs will be annotated. The learner that receives the feedback (label) may update its prediction rule, and we proceed to the next round. We develop an online algorithm for multi-task binary classification that learns in this setting, and bound its performance in the worst-case setting. Additionally, we show that our algorithm can be used to solve two bandits problems: contextual bandits, and dueling bandits with context, both allowed to decouple exploration and exploitation. Empirical study with OCR data, vowel prediction (VJ project) and document classification, shows that our algorithm outperforms other algorithms, one of which uses uniform allocation, and essentially makes more (accuracy) for the same labour of the annotator.

paragraphs: The paper studies multiple online learners that must share one annotator with limited capacity. On each round, every learner receives an input and predicts its label. A shared stochastic mechanism then selects which input receives an annotation, and the learner receiving that label can update its prediction rule.

The key problem is therefore how to allocate feedback across tasks as learning proceeds. The authors develop an algorithm for binary classification in this setting and bound its performance under worst-case conditions. They also show how it can solve contextual bandit problems and contextual dueling-bandit problems in settings where exploration and exploitation may be decoupled.

Empirical evaluations cover optical character recognition, vowel prediction, and document classification. The proposed algorithm outperforms comparison algorithms, including one that distributes annotations uniformly. These results indicate that choosing where feedback goes can improve accuracy for the same annotation labor. The framework makes the allocation of a shared labeling resource an explicit part of the learning problem.
summary.tldr: An online algorithm allocates a shared annotator across multiple tasks, improving reported accuracy for the same labeling effort.

title: Learning Multiple Tasks in Parallel with a Shared Annotator

abstract: Events in an online social network can be categorized roughly into endogenous events, where users just respond to the actions of their neighbors within the network, or exogenous events, where users take actions due to drives external to the network. How much external drive should be provided to each user, such that the network activity can be steered towards a target state? In this paper, we model social events using multivariate Hawkes processes, which can capture both endogenous and exogenous event intensities, and derive a time dependent linear relation between the intensity of exogenous events and the overall network activity. Exploiting this connection, we develop a convex optimization framework for determining the required level of external drive in order for the network to reach a desired activity level. We experimented with event data gathered from Twitter, and show that our method can steer the activity of the network more accurately than alternatives.

paragraphs: Social network activity can arise from users responding to their neighbors or from influences outside the network. This paper asks how much external drive to direct toward each user to move overall activity toward a desired level. Answering that question requires accounting for the activity that external influences can trigger through social responses.

The authors model events with multivariate Hawkes processes, which represent both external activity and activity generated through interactions within the network. They derive a time-dependent linear relationship between external event intensity and total network activity. This relationship connects an adjustable input to its modeled effects across the network over time.

Using that connection, the paper develops a convex optimization framework for selecting the external drive needed to reach an activity target. Experiments using event data from Twitter show more accurate steering than the alternatives tested. The contribution turns a model of interacting social events into a planning method, using the relationship between direct stimulation and induced responses to choose how external influence is allocated.
summary.tldr: A Hawkes-process model and convex optimization allocate external drive to steer social network activity toward a target.

title: Shaping Social Activity by Incentivizing Users

abstract: We consider the problem of learning models of options for real-time abstract planning, in the setting where reward functions can be specified at any time and their expected returns must be efficiently computed. We introduce a new model for an option that is independent of any reward function, called the {\it universal option model (UOM)}. We prove that the UOM of an option can construct a traditional option model given a reward function, and the option-conditional return is computed directly by a single dot-product of the UOM with the reward function. We extend the UOM to linear function approximation, and we show it gives the TD solution of option returns and value functions of policies over options. We provide a stochastic approximation algorithm for incrementally learning UOMs from data and prove its consistency. We demonstrate our method in two domains. The first domain is document recommendation, where each user query defines a new reward function and a document's relevance is the expected return of a simulated random-walk through the document's references. The second domain is a real-time strategy game, where the controller must select the best game unit to accomplish dynamically-specified tasks. Our experiments show that UOMs are substantially more efficient in evaluating option returns and policies than previously known methods.

paragraphs: The paper addresses abstract planning when reward functions can change at any time. An option represents an extended course of action whose expected return must be evaluated for the current task. The authors introduce a universal option model that is independent of the reward function, allowing the learned model to be reused as rewards change.

They prove that a universal option model can construct a traditional option model once rewards are specified. An option's conditional expected return can be computed directly with a single dot product. They extend the framework to linear function approximation, establish its connection to temporal-difference solutions, and provide an incremental learning algorithm with a consistency proof.

Applications include document recommendation, where each query defines rewards for a simulated walk through references, and a real-time strategy game with dynamically specified tasks. Experiments report substantially more efficient evaluation of option returns and policies than previously known methods. The contribution separates learning reusable option models from evaluating particular rewards, supporting rapid reassessment when planning objectives change.
summary.tldr: Universal option models reuse reward-independent information to evaluate changing planning objectives efficiently, including through a single dot product.

title: Universal Option Models

abstract: The asynchronous parallel implementations of stochastic gradient (SG) have been broadly used in solving deep neural network and received many successes in practice recently. However, existing theories cannot explain their convergence and speedup properties, mainly due to the nonconvexity of most deep learning formulations and the asynchronous parallel mechanism. To fill the gaps in theory and provide theoretical supports, this paper studies two asynchronous parallel implementations of SG: one is on the computer network and the other is on the shared memory system. We establish an ergodic convergence rate $O(1/\sqrt{K})$ for both algorithms and prove that the linear speedup is achievable if the number of workers is bounded by $\sqrt{K}$ ($K$ is the total number of iterations). Our results generalize and improve existing analysis for convex minimization.

To fill the gaps in theory and provide theoretical supports, this paper studies two asynchronous parallel implementations of SG: one is on the computer network and the other is on the shared memory system. We establish an ergodic convergence rate $O(1/\sqrt{K})$ for both algorithms and prove that the linear speedup is achievable if the number of workers is bounded by $\sqrt{K}$ ($K$ is the total number of iterations). paragraphs: Asynchronous stochastic gradient methods allow multiple workers to contribute to optimization without proceeding in synchronized rounds. Such implementations had achieved practical success in deep learning, but existing theory did not adequately explain their convergence or speedup for nonconvex objectives. This paper addresses that theoretical gap.

The authors analyze two implementations: one operating across a computer network and another using shared memory. For both, they establish an ergodic convergence rate of O(1/√K), where K is the total number of iterations. The ergodic qualification concerns an aggregate convergence measure across iterations, rather than asserting the same progress for every individual update.

They also show that linear speedup is achievable when the number of workers is bounded by √K. This makes the parallelism claim conditional on the relationship between worker count and iteration count. The results extend and improve earlier convex analyses, providing theoretical support for asynchronous computation in the nonconvex setting that motivates deep learning applications.
summary.tldr: Two asynchronous stochastic gradient implementations receive nonconvex convergence guarantees and conditional linear-speedup results.

title: Asynchronous Parallel Stochastic Gradient for Nonconvex Optimization

abstract: We consider the problem of variational inference in probabilistic models with both log-submodular and log-supermodular higher-order potentials. These models can represent arbitrary distributions over binary variables, and thus generalize the commonly used pairwise Markov random fields and models with log-supermodular potentials only, for which efficient approximate inference algorithms are known. While inference in the considered models is #P-hard in general, we present efficient approximate algorithms exploiting recent advances in the field of discrete optimization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in a large set of experiments, where our model allows reasoning about preferences over sets of items with complements and substitutes.

paragraphs: This paper studies probabilistic models over binary variables with a mixture of log-submodular and log-supermodular higher-order potentials. These components allow interactions among groups of variables. Together, they can represent arbitrary binary distributions, making the model family broader than pairwise Markov random fields or models restricted to log-supermodular potentials.

That expressive power makes inference difficult: the general problem is #P-hard. The authors develop efficient approximate inference algorithms using advances in discrete optimization. The approach seeks to make reasoning with this richer model family practical through approximation, while retaining its ability to describe varied interactions.

The experiments focus on preferences over sets of items that can include both complements and substitutes. Complements capture items whose joint presence is attractive, while substitutes capture alternatives within a selection. A model that supports both can express different relationships within the same preference problem. A large collection of experiments demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach, supporting the use of mixed potentials when preferences depend on how items combine.
summary.tldr: Discrete-optimization-based approximate inference makes expressive binary models with both complementary and substitutable item relationships practical.

title: Variational Inference in Mixed Probabilistic Submodular Models

abstract: We study the problem of using causal models to improve the rate at which good interventions can be learned online in a stochastic environment. Our formalism combines multi-arm bandits and causal inference to model a novel type of bandit feedback that is not exploited by existing approaches. We propose a new algorithm that exploits the causal feedback and prove a bound on its simple regret that is strictly better (in all quantities) than algorithms that do not use the additional causal information.
originalAbstract: We study the problem of using causal models to improve the rate at which good interventions can be learned online in a stochastic environment. Our formalism combines multi-arm bandits and causal inference to model a novel type of bandit feedback that is not exploited by existing approaches. We propose a new algorithm that exploits the causal feedback and prove a bound on its simple regret that is strictly better (in all quantities) than algorithms that do not use the additional causal information.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a learner can discover good interventions through repeated interaction with a stochastic environment. Its central question is whether a causal model can help the learner make better use of what it observes. The goal is to improve the rate at which useful interventions are identified, making causal information part of the learning problem.

The proposed formalism combines multi-arm bandits with causal inference. In a bandit problem, the learner must gather information while choosing actions; here, the feedback additionally has causal structure. The authors identify a form of feedback that existing approaches do not exploit and design an algorithm specifically to use that extra information.

The theoretical result concerns simple regret, which measures the quality of the intervention recommended after learning. The authors prove a bound that improves in every quantity over the bounds for algorithms that do not use the additional causal information in their setting. The contribution therefore gives a formal advantage for exploiting causal feedback, rather than merely suggesting that causal knowledge might help intervention selection.
summary.tldr: A bandit algorithm exploits causal feedback to obtain a strictly better simple-regret bound than approaches that ignore that additional information.

title: Causal Bandits: Learning Good Interventions via Causal Inference

abstract: Practical applications of machine learning often involve successive training iterations with changes to features and training examples. Ideally, changes in the output of any new model should only be improvements (wins) over the previous iteration, but in practice the predictions may change neutrally for many examples, resulting in extra net-zero wins and losses, referred to as unnecessary churn. These changes in the predictions are problematic for usability for some applications, and make it harder and more expensive to measure if a change is statistically significant positive. In this paper, we formulate the problem and present a stabilization operator to regularize a classifier towards a previous classifier. We use a Markov chain Monte Carlo stabilization operator to produce a model with more consistent predictions without adversely affecting accuracy. We investigate the properties of the proposal with theoretical analysis. Experiments on benchmark datasets for different classification algorithms demonstrate the method and the resulting reduction in churn.

paragraphs: Updating a classifier with new features or training examples can change many individual predictions without improving overall accuracy. Some changes become wins while others become offsetting losses. The paper calls these unnecessary changes prediction churn and explains why they matter: they can disrupt usability and make it harder or more expensive to establish whether an update is statistically beneficial.

The authors formulate churn reduction as a learning problem and introduce a stabilization operator that regularizes a classifier toward its predecessor. Their proposed operator uses Markov chain Monte Carlo. The aim is to produce more consistent predictions across model versions while preserving accuracy, tying the new model's behavior to an already deployed reference.

The paper investigates the proposal theoretically and evaluates it across benchmark datasets and different classification algorithms. The experiments demonstrate reduced churn, and the abstract reports more consistent predictions without an adverse effect on accuracy. This addresses a practical distinction between aggregate performance and continuity: two models can have similar accuracy while making substantially different decisions on individual examples.
summary.tldr: A Markov chain Monte Carlo stabilization operator reduces unnecessary prediction changes between classifier versions without harming accuracy in the reported results.

title: Launch and Iterate: Reducing Prediction Churn

abstract: Several applications of Reinforcement Learning suffer from instability due to high variance. This is especially prevalent in high dimensional domains. Regularization is a commonly used technique in machine learning to reduce variance, at the cost of introducing some bias. Most existing regularization techniques focus on spatial (perceptual) regularization. Yet in reinforcement learning, due to the nature of the Bellman equation, there is an opportunity to also exploit temporal regularization based on smoothness in value estimates over trajectories. This paper explores a class of methods for temporal regularization. We formally characterize the bias induced by this technique using Markov chain concepts. We illustrate the various characteristics of temporal regularization via a sequence of simple discrete and continuous MDPs, and show that the technique provides improvement even in high-dimensional Atari games.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning estimates can have high variance, producing unstable learning, especially in high-dimensional settings. Regularization can reduce that variability while introducing bias. This paper studies a temporal form of regularization that uses smoothness in value estimates along trajectories, adding a source of structure beyond regularization based on perceptual similarity.

The opportunity comes from the Bellman equation, which relates values across successive stages of experience. The authors explore a class of methods that exploit this temporal relationship. They also use Markov-chain concepts to formally characterize the bias the regularization introduces, making the statistical tradeoff part of the analysis.

A sequence of discrete and continuous Markov decision processes illustrates the methods' characteristics, and experiments show improvement in high-dimensional Atari games. These findings support temporal smoothness as a useful regularization principle in the settings examined. The approach aims to stabilize value learning by using trajectory structure, with its induced bias explicitly acknowledged and analyzed rather than assuming smoothing is cost-free.
summary.tldr: Temporal regularization smooths value estimates along trajectories, with analyzed bias and demonstrated reinforcement-learning improvements.

title: Temporal Regularization for Markov Decision Process

abstract: We consider testing and learning problems on causal Bayesian networks as defined by Pearl (Pearl, 2009). Given a causal Bayesian network M on a graph with n discrete variables and bounded in-degree and bounded ``confounded components'', we show that O(log n) interventions on an unknown causal Bayesian network X on the same graph, and O(n/epsilon^2) samples per intervention, suffice to efficiently distinguish whether X=M or whether there exists some intervention under which X and M are farther than epsilon in total variation distance. We also obtain sample/time/intervention efficient algorithms for: (i) testing the identity of two unknown causal Bayesian networks on the same graph; and (ii) learning a causal Bayesian network on a given graph. Although our algorithms are non-adaptive, we show that adaptivity does not help in general: Omega(log n) interventions are necessary for testing the identity of two unknown causal Bayesian networks on the same graph, even adaptively. Our algorithms are enabled by a new subadditivity inequality for the squared Hellinger distance between two causal Bayesian networks.

paragraphs: The paper studies how interventions can test and learn causal Bayesian networks. Its setting uses discrete variables on a given graph, with bounded numbers of incoming edges and bounded confounded components. The testing question asks whether an unknown network matches a reference or differs substantially under at least one possible intervention.

For a graph with n variables, the authors show that O(log n) interventions and O(n/epsilon²) samples per intervention suffice for this distinction, where epsilon specifies the total-variation separation to detect. They also develop efficient methods for comparing two unknown networks on the same graph and for learning a network whose graph is supplied.

The interventions can be chosen non-adaptively, without using earlier outcomes to select later experiments. A lower bound shows that comparing two unknown networks can still require Omega(log n) interventions even with adaptive choices. A new inequality for squared Hellinger distance enables the algorithms. Together, these results identify efficient intervention strategies and a matching general barrier on the intervention count for the two-unknown-network testing problem.
summary.tldr: Under stated graph restrictions, causal networks can be tested efficiently with logarithmically many interventions, and adaptivity cannot generally improve that order.

title: Learning and Testing Causal Models with Interventions

abstract: We consider the problem of answering queries about formulas of first-order logic based on background knowledge partially represented explicitly as other formulas, and partially represented as examples independently drawn from a fixed probability distribution. PAC semantics, introduced by Valiant, is one rigorous, general proposal for learning to reason in formal languages: although weaker than classical entailment, it allows for a powerful model theoretic framework for answering queries while requiring minimal assumptions about the form of the distribution in question. To date, however, the most significant limitation of that approach, and more generally most machine learning approaches with robustness guarantees, is that the logical language is ultimately essentially propositional, with finitely many atoms. Indeed, the theoretical findings on the learning of relational theories in such generality have been resoundingly negative. This is despite the fact that first-order logic is widely argued to be most appropriate for representing human knowledge. In this work, we present a new theoretical approach to robustly learning to reason in first-order logic, and consider universally quantified clauses over a countably infinite domain. Our results exploit symmetries exhibited by constants in the language, and generalize the notion of implicit learnability to show how queries can be computed against (implicitly) learned first-order background knowledge.
