paragraphs: This paper asks how a system can answer logical queries when some background knowledge is written as formulas and some is available only through examples. The examples are independently drawn from a fixed distribution. The goal is to combine formal reasoning with learning while retaining a rigorous account of what the answers mean.

The approach builds on PAC semantics, which supports a probabilistic form of reasoning weaker than classical entailment while requiring few assumptions about the distribution. Earlier robust approaches were largely restricted to essentially propositional languages with finitely many atoms. The paper develops a theoretical approach for universally quantified first-order clauses over a countably infinite domain.

The key ingredient is symmetry among constants in the logical language. Exploiting those symmetries lets the authors extend implicit learnability and compute queries against background knowledge learned implicitly from examples. The contribution is a route beyond the finite propositional setting for the specified class of formulas, linking relational reasoning to sample-based knowledge without requiring all learned knowledge to be represented explicitly.
summary.tldr: A symmetry-based theoretical approach extends implicit learning and query answering to first-order clauses over a countably infinite domain.

title: Implicitly learning to reason in first-order logic

abstract: Actor-critic methods, a type of model-free Reinforcement Learning, have been successfully applied to challenging tasks in continuous control, often achieving state-of-the art performance. However, wide-scale adoption of these methods in real-world domains is made difficult by their poor sample efficiency. We address this problem both theoretically and empirically. On the theoretical side, we identify two phenomena preventing efficient exploration in existing state-of-the-art algorithms such as Soft Actor Critic. First, combining a greedy actor update with a pessimistic estimate of the critic leads to the avoidance of actions that the agent does not know about, a phenomenon we call pessimistic underexploration. Second, current algorithms are directionally uninformed, sampling actions with equal probability in opposite directions from the current mean. This is wasteful, since we typically need actions taken along certain directions much more than others. To address both of these phenomena, we introduce a new algorithm, Optimistic Actor Critic, which approximates a lower and upper confidence bound on the state-action value function. This allows us to apply the principle of optimism in the face of uncertainty to perform directed exploration using the upper bound while still using the lower bound to avoid overestimation. We evaluate OAC in several challenging continuous control tasks, achieving state-of the art sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Actor-critic reinforcement learning methods can handle difficult continuous-control tasks, but learning may require many interactions. This paper identifies two obstacles to efficient exploration. First, a greedy actor paired with a pessimistic value estimate can avoid unfamiliar actions. Second, sampling equally in opposite directions around the current action mean can spend interactions on directions that are less useful.

Optimistic Actor Critic addresses both obstacles by approximating upper and lower confidence bounds on action values. The upper bound guides exploration toward actions that could be valuable despite uncertainty. The lower bound retains a cautious estimate to avoid overestimation. Assigning these bounds different roles lets the method direct exploration while maintaining protection against overly favorable value estimates.

The paper supports this design with theoretical analysis and evaluations on challenging continuous-control tasks. Those evaluations achieve state-of-the-art sample efficiency. The central finding is that uncertainty can help determine where to explore, rather than merely making value estimates more conservative, and that this distinction improves the use of collected experience in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Optimistic Actor Critic uses upper value bounds for directed exploration and lower bounds to avoid overestimation, improving sample efficiency.

title: Better Exploration with Optimistic Actor Critic

abstract: Diverse image captioning models aim to learn one-to-many mappings that are innate to cross-domain datasets, such as of images and texts. Current methods for this task are based on generative latent variable models, eg. VAEs with structured latent spaces. Yet, the amount of multimodality captured by prior work is limited to that of the paired training data -- the true diversity of the underlying generative process is not fully captured. To address this limitation, we leverage the contextual descriptions in the dataset that explain similar contexts in different visual scenes. To this end, we introduce a novel factorization of the latent space, termed context-object split, to model diversity in contextual descriptions across images and texts within the dataset. Our framework not only enables diverse captioning through context-based pseudo supervision, but extends this to images with novel objects and without paired captions in the training data. We evaluate our COS-CVAE approach on the standard COCO dataset and on the held-out COCO dataset consisting of images with novel objects, showing significant gains in accuracy and diversity.

paragraphs: An image can support several valid descriptions, so diverse captioning requires learning multiple possible text outputs for one visual input. This paper argues that earlier latent-variable approaches capture only the diversity present in their paired training examples. Descriptions attached to other images may contain useful contextual variation that those approaches do not fully exploit.

The proposed COS-CVAE separates its latent space into context and object components. This factorization lets the model use descriptions of similar contexts across different visual scenes. Context-based pseudo supervision provides an additional source of guidance for producing varied captions, drawing on relationships across the dataset rather than only each image's own paired descriptions.

The framework also extends to images containing novel objects and lacking paired captions in training. Evaluation uses both standard COCO and a held-out COCO dataset containing novel objects. The authors report significant gains in accuracy and diversity, indicating that the added contextual variation improves the range of captions without merely trading away their accuracy.
summary.tldr: Separating context and object information lets a captioning model reuse contextual descriptions and improve caption accuracy and diversity.

title: Diverse Image Captioning with Context-Object Split Latent Spaces

abstract: We tackle the Multi-task Batch Reinforcement Learning problem. Given multiple datasets collected from different tasks, we train a multi-task policy to perform well in unseen tasks sampled from the same distribution. The task identities of the unseen tasks are not provided. To perform well, the policy must infer the task identity from collected transitions by modelling its dependency on states, actions and rewards. Because the different datasets may have state-action distributions with large divergence, the task inference module can learn to ignore the rewards and spuriously correlate \textit{only} state-action pairs to the task identity, leading to poor test time performance. To robustify task inference, we propose a novel application of the triplet loss. To mine hard negative examples, we relabel the transitions from the training tasks by approximating their reward functions. When we allow further training on the unseen tasks, using the trained policy as an initialization leads to significantly faster convergence compared to randomly initialized policies (up to 80% improvement and across 5 different Mujoco task distributions). We name our method \textbf{MBML} (\textbf{M}ulti-task \textbf{B}atch RL with \textbf{M}etric \textbf{L}earning).

paragraphs: This paper trains a policy from datasets collected on multiple tasks so it can handle unseen tasks drawn from the same distribution. Because the new task’s identity is not supplied, the policy must infer it from transitions involving states, actions, and rewards. Task inference is therefore a central part of deciding how to act.

The authors identify a shortcut that can undermine this inference. When training datasets have very different state-action distributions, the model may associate those patterns with task identity and ignore rewards. MBML addresses this problem through metric learning with a triplet loss. To construct difficult negative examples, it approximates training-task reward functions and uses them to relabel transitions.

The method aims to make task inference more robust to misleading differences between datasets. The authors also evaluate a setting that permits further training on unseen tasks. There, initializing from the learned policy produces significantly faster convergence than random initialization, with improvements of up to 80% across five MuJoCo task distributions. That finding concerns adaptation with additional training.
summary.tldr: MBML uses metric learning and reward relabeling to strengthen task inference and accelerate subsequent learning on unseen tasks.

title: Multi-task Batch Reinforcement Learning with Metric Learning

abstract: When designing new molecules with particular properties, it is not only important what to make but crucially how to make it. These instructions form a synthesis directed acyclic graph (DAG), describing how a large vocabulary of simple building blocks can be recursively combined through chemical reactions to create more complicated molecules of interest. In contrast, many current deep generative models for molecules ignore synthesizability. We therefore propose a deep generative model that better represents the real world process, by directly outputting molecule synthesis DAGs. We argue that this provides sensible inductive biases, ensuring that our model searches over the same chemical space that chemists would also have access to, as well as interpretability. We show that our approach is able to model chemical space well, producing a wide range of diverse molecules, and allows for unconstrained optimization of an inherently constrained problem: maximize certain chemical properties such that discovered molecules are synthesizable.

paragraphs: Molecule design involves finding a structure with useful properties and determining how to produce it. The paper addresses these goals together by generating synthesis instructions directly. Those instructions take the form of a directed acyclic graph, describing how simple building blocks are combined through chemical reactions into more complicated molecules.

The proposed deep generative model therefore searches over construction processes. The authors argue that this representation supplies useful inductive biases: it directs the model toward chemical possibilities accessible through the building blocks and reactions, while making the route to a proposed molecule interpretable. The synthesis graph connects a generated structure to the steps intended to create it.

The reported results show that the model represents chemical space well and produces diverse molecules. The approach also allows optimization of chemical properties within a representation that incorporates synthesizability. Its significance is that a constraint normally imposed alongside molecule search becomes part of what the model generates, so searching for desirable properties simultaneously yields a proposed synthesis route.
summary.tldr: Generating synthesis graphs lets a molecular design model search for desirable properties while incorporating how each molecule can be made.

title: Barking up the right tree: an approach to search over molecule synthesis DAGs

abstract: One of the basic primitives in the class of submodular optimization problems is the submodular maximization under a cardinality constraint. Here we are given a ground set $V$ that is endowed with a monotone submodular function $f: 2^V \rightarrow \REAL^+$ and a parameter $0 < k \le n$ and the goal is to return an optimal set $S \subseteq V$ of at most $k$ elements, i.e., $f(S)$ is maximum among all subsets of $V$ of size at most $k$. This basic primitive has many applications in machine learning as well as combinatorial optimization. Example applications are agglomerative clustering, exemplar-based clustering, categorical feature compression, document and corpus summarization, recommender systems, search result diversification, data subset selection, minimum spanning tree, max flow, global minimum cut, maximum matching, traveling salesman problem, max clique, max cut, set cover and knapsack, among the others. In this paper, we propose the first dynamic algorithm for this problem. Given a stream of inserts and deletes of elements of an underlying ground set $V$, we develop a dynamic algorithm that with high probability, maintains a $(\frac{1}{2} - \epsilon)$-approximation of a cardinality-constrained monotone submodular maximization for any sequence of $z$ updates (inserts and deletes) in time $O(k^2z\epsilon^{-3}\cdot \log^5 n)$, where $n$ is the maximum size of $V$ at any time. That is, the amortized update time of our algorithm is $O(k^2\epsilon^{-3}\cdot \log^5 n)$.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to maintain a valuable subset when available items keep changing. The objective is monotone and submodular: adding items does not decrease value, and additional items have diminishing returns. A cardinality constraint limits the chosen subset to at most k elements. This selection problem appears in applications such as summarization, recommendation, and data subset selection.

The authors introduce a dynamic algorithm that handles both insertions and deletions from the available ground set. With high probability, it maintains a solution worth at least a fraction one-half minus epsilon of the current optimum over a sequence of updates. The guarantee is approximate, allowing efficient maintenance without requiring an exact optimal subset after each change.

For z updates, the total running time is O(k²z epsilon⁻³ log⁵ n), where n is the largest ground-set size encountered. Consequently, the average cost per update is O(k² epsilon⁻³ log⁵ n). The result provides a formal combination of solution quality and update efficiency, with only a polylogarithmic dependence on the ground-set size.
summary.tldr: A dynamic algorithm maintains a near-half-optimal submodular selection with high probability as items are inserted and deleted.

title: Dynamic Submodular Maximization

abstract: We study RL in the tabular MDP setting where the agent receives additional observations per step in the form of transitions samples. Such additional observations can be provided in many tasks by auxiliary sensors or by leveraging prior knowledge about the environment (e.g., when certain actions yield similar outcome). We formalize this setting using a feedback graph over state-action pairs and show that model-based algorithms can incorporate additional observations for more sample-efficient learning. We give a regret bound that predominantly depends on the size of the maximum acyclic subgraph of the feedback graph, in contrast with a polynomial dependency on the number of states and actions in the absence of side observations. Finally, we highlight fundamental challenges for leveraging a small dominating set of the feedback graph, as compared to the well-studied bandit setting, and propose a new algorithm that can use such a dominating set to learn a near-optimal policy faster.
originalAbstract: We study RL in the tabular MDP setting where the agent receives additional observations per step in the form of transitions samples. Such additional observations can be provided in many tasks by auxiliary sensors or by leveraging prior knowledge about the environment (e.g., when certain actions yield similar outcome). We formalize this setting using a feedback graph over state-action pairs and show that model-based algorithms can incorporate additional observations for more sample-efficient learning. We give a regret bound that predominantly depends on the size of the maximum acyclic subgraph of the feedback graph, in contrast with a polynomial dependency on the number of states and actions in the absence of side observations. Finally, we highlight fundamental challenges for leveraging a small dominating set of the feedback graph, as compared to the well-studied bandit setting, and propose a new algorithm that can use such a dominating set to learn a near-optimal policy faster.

paragraphs: An agent may receive information beyond the transition caused by its chosen action. Auxiliary sensors or prior knowledge can provide additional transition samples, including information about actions with similar outcomes. This paper studies how such side observations can improve learning in tabular Markov decision processes.

The authors represent observation relationships with a feedback graph over state-action pairs. Model-based algorithms then incorporate the extra samples into learning. Their regret bound depends predominantly on the size of a maximum acyclic subgraph, shifting the main complexity measure toward the structure of available feedback rather than the usual polynomial dependence on state and action counts.

The paper also examines whether a small dominating set in the graph can help an agent gather useful information efficiently. It identifies fundamental challenges that distinguish this setting from bandit problems, then proposes an algorithm that can exploit such a set to learn a near-optimal policy faster. The results show how both the availability and arrangement of side observations matter.
summary.tldr: Feedback graphs let model-based reinforcement learning exploit extra transition observations, with guarantees tied to the graph’s structure.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Feedback Graphs

abstract: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) has emerged as a powerful Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method to sample from complex continuous distributions. However, a fundamental limitation of HMC is that it can not be applied to distributions with mixed discrete and continuous variables. In this paper, we propose mixed HMC (M-HMC) as a general framework to address this limitation. M-HMC is a novel family of MCMC algorithms that evolves the discrete and continuous variables in tandem, allowing more frequent updates of discrete variables while maintaining HMC's ability to suppress random-walk behavior. We establish M-HMC's theoretical properties, and present an efficient implementation with Laplace momentum that introduces minimal overhead compared to existing HMC methods. The superior performances of M-HMC over existing methods are demonstrated with numerical experiments on Gaussian mixture models (GMMs), variable selection in Bayesian logistic regression (BLR), and correlated topic models (CTMs).

Such mixed distributions require a way to update the two kinds of quantities together. This paper introduces mixed Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, or M-HMC, as a general framework for that purpose.

This permits more frequent changes to discrete variables while preserving HMC's ability to suppress random-walk behavior, where sampling progresses through less directed wandering. The authors establish theoretical properties of the framework and describe an efficient implementation using Laplace momentum that adds minimal overhead relative to existing HMC methods.

Numerical experiments examine Gaussian mixture models, variable selection in Bayesian logistic regression, and correlated topic models. M-HMC outperforms existing methods in those experiments. The contribution combines a broader sampling framework with an implementation intended to retain computational efficiency, and the reported evaluations demonstrate its usefulness across several models that involve both discrete choices and continuous quantities.
summary.tldr: M-HMC jointly updates discrete and continuous variables while retaining HMC's resistance to random-walk sampling behavior.

title: Mixed Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Mixed Discrete and Continuous Variables

abstract: We propose contrastive coding to learn shared, dense image representations, referred to as CoMIRs (Contrastive Multimodal Image Representations). CoMIRs enable the registration of multimodal images where existing registration methods often fail due to a lack of sufficiently similar image structures. CoMIRs reduce the multimodal registration problem to a monomodal one, in which general intensity-based, as well as feature-based, registration algorithms can be applied. The method involves training one neural network per modality on aligned images, using a contrastive loss based on noise-contrastive estimation (InfoNCE). Unlike other contrastive coding methods, used for, e.g., classification, our approach generates image-like representations that contain the information shared between modalities. We introduce a novel, hyperparameter-free modification to InfoNCE, to enforce rotational equivariance of the learnt representations, a property essential to the registration task. We assess the extent of achieved rotational equivariance and the stability of the representations with respect to weight initialization, training set, and hyperparameter settings, on a remote sensing dataset of RGB and near-infrared images. We evaluate the learnt representations through registration of a biomedical dataset of bright-field and second-harmonic generation microscopy images; two modalities with very little apparent correlation. The proposed approach based on CoMIRs significantly outperforms registration of representations created by GAN-based image-to-image translation, as well as a state-of-the-art, application-specific method which takes additional knowledge about the data into account. Code is available at: https://github.com/MIDA-group/CoMIR.

CoMIR learns dense, image-like representations that retain information shared across modalities. Aligning these representations turns the original multimodal registration problem into one that can use ordinary intensity-based or feature-based registration algorithms.

Training requires aligned images and a separate neural network for each modality. A contrastive objective based on InfoNCE teaches the networks to produce shared representations. The authors modify that objective without adding hyperparameters to enforce rotational equivariance: the representation should respond consistently when an image rotates, a property needed for registration.

It then evaluates registration on bright-field and second-harmonic generation microscopy images, which have little apparent correlation. These results support learning shared spatial information as a useful route to multimodal alignment.
summary.tldr: CoMIR learns shared image representations that let conventional registration algorithms align visually different imaging modalities.

title: CoMIR: Contrastive Multimodal Image Representation for Registration

abstract: Many real-world problems are compositional – solving them requires completing interdependent sub-tasks, either in series or in parallel, that can be represented as a dependency graph. Deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents often struggle to learn such complex tasks due to the long time horizons and sparse rewards. To address this problem, we present Compositional Design of Environments (CoDE), which trains a Generator agent to automatically build a series of compositional tasks tailored to the RL agent’s current skill level. This automatic curriculum not only enables the agent to learn more complex tasks than it could have otherwise, but also selects tasks where the agent’s performance is weak, enhancing its robustness and ability to generalize zero-shot to unseen tasks at test-time. We analyze why current environment generation techniques are insufficient for the problem of generating compositional tasks, and propose a new algorithm that addresses these issues. Our results assess learning and generalization across multiple compositional tasks, including the real-world problem of learning to navigate and interact with web pages. We learn to generate environments composed of multiple pages or rooms, and train RL agents capable of completing wide-range of complex tasks in those environments. We contribute two new benchmark frameworks for generating compositional tasks, compositional MiniGrid and gMiniWoB for web navigation. CoDE yields 4x higher success rate than the strongest baseline, and demonstrates strong performance of real websites learned on 3500 primitive tasks.

This is intended to build competence on increasingly complex combinations while improving robustness and transfer to unseen tasks without additional test-time learning. The authors examine shortcomings of existing environment-generation techniques for compositional tasks and introduce an algorithm designed to address them.

The evaluation covers multiple compositional settings, including navigation and interaction across web pages and environments containing multiple rooms. The paper contributes compositional MiniGrid and gMiniWoB as benchmark frameworks. It reports a success rate four times that of the strongest baseline and strong performance on real websites after learning from 3,500 primitive tasks. These findings support adaptive environment generation as a way to teach combinations of skills.
summary.tldr: CoDE generates an adaptive curriculum of compositional environments to improve complex-task learning and zero-shot generalization.

title: Environment Generation for Zero-Shot Compositional Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. A range of defense methods have been proposed to train adversarially robust DNNs, among which adversarial training has demonstrated promising results. However, despite preliminary understandings developed for adversarial training, it is still not clear, from the architectural perspective, what configurations can lead to more robust DNNs. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation on the impact of network width and depth on the robustness of adversarially trained DNNs. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) more parameters (higher model capacity) does not necessarily help adversarial robustness; 2) reducing capacity at the last stage (the last group of blocks) of the network can actually improve adversarial robustness; and 3) under the same parameter budget, there exists an optimal architectural configuration for adversarial robustness. We also provide a theoretical analysis explaning why such network configuration can help robustness. These architectural insights can help design adversarially robust DNNs.

paragraphs: Adversarial training is a promising way to make neural networks more resistant to adversarial attacks. Yet the training procedure leaves an architectural question: how should the network's width and depth be arranged? This paper investigates those choices, focusing on how architecture affects robustness in adversarially trained networks.

The study reports three main observations. Increasing the total parameter count does not necessarily improve robustness. Reducing capacity in the final group of network blocks can actually help. And when the total parameter budget is fixed, the allocation of that capacity admits an optimal architectural configuration for robustness in the studied setting. These findings make the placement of parameters a central consideration.

The authors also provide theoretical analysis explaining why such a configuration can improve robustness. Together, the analysis and observations suggest that robust architecture design should consider where capacity is used, alongside how much capacity is available. The findings concern adversarially trained networks and support deliberate choices about width and depth when designing them.
summary.tldr: In adversarially trained networks, how capacity is distributed across width, depth, and stages can matter more than simply adding parameters.

title: Exploring Architectural Ingredients of Adversarially Robust Deep Neural Networks

abstract: We study multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) in a stochastic network of agents. The objective is to find localized policies that maximize the (discounted) global reward. In general, scalability is a challenge in this setting because the size of the global state/action space can be exponential in the number of agents. Scalable algorithms are only known in cases where dependencies are static, fixed and local, e.g., between neighbors in a fixed, time-invariant underlying graph. In this work, we propose a Scalable Actor Critic framework that applies in settings where the dependencies can be non-local and stochastic, and provide a finite-time error bound that shows how the convergence rate depends on the speed of information spread in the network. Additionally, as a byproduct of our analysis, we obtain novel finite-time convergence results for a general stochastic approximation scheme and for temporal difference learning with state aggregation, which apply beyond the setting of MARL in networked systems.

paragraphs: In a network of learning agents, the collective state and action space can grow exponentially with the number of participants. This makes optimizing their shared performance difficult. The paper seeks localized policies that maximize discounted global reward, while allowing dependencies between agents to be stochastic and to extend beyond fixed local neighbors.

Earlier scalable approaches described in the abstract rely on static, local dependencies in an unchanging graph. The proposed Scalable Actor Critic framework broadens that setting. Its analysis connects learning behavior to the speed at which information spreads through the network, making network dynamics an explicit part of the convergence guarantee.

The authors provide a finite-time error bound showing how that information spread affects the convergence rate. This gives a quantitative account of learning under changing and potentially non-local interactions. Their analysis also yields finite-time convergence results for a general stochastic approximation scheme and for temporal difference learning with state aggregation. Those additional results apply beyond the particular multi-agent setting, extending the theoretical contribution to other learning procedures.
summary.tldr: A scalable actor-critic framework handles stochastic, potentially non-local agent dependencies and relates convergence to information spread through the network.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning in Stochastic Networked Systems

abstract: In reinforcement learning, a promising direction to avoid online trial-and-error costs is learning from an offline dataset. Current offline reinforcement learning methods commonly learn in the policy space constrained to in-support regions by the offline dataset, in order to ensure the robustness of the outcome policies. Such constraints, however, also limit the potential of the outcome policies. In this paper, to release the potential of offline policy learning, we investigate the decision-making problems in out-of-support regions directly and propose offline Model-based Adaptable Policy LEarning (MAPLE). By this approach, instead of learning in in-support regions, we learn an adaptable policy that can adapt its behavior in out-of-support regions when deployed. We conduct experiments on MuJoCo controlling tasks with offline datasets. The results show that the proposed method can make robust decisions in out-of-support regions and achieve better performance than SOTA algorithms.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains a decision-making policy from an existing dataset, avoiding the costs of collecting experience through online trial and error. Many approaches restrict policies to behavior supported by that dataset to improve robustness. This paper examines the accompanying tradeoff: those restrictions can also limit what a learned policy is able to achieve.

The proposed method, Model-based Adaptable Policy Learning, or MAPLE, directly addresses decisions outside the dataset's support. It learns a policy designed to adapt its behavior in those regions when deployed. The central change is therefore in the policy's intended capability: learning includes preparation for deployment situations that are not adequately represented by the offline examples.

Experiments use offline datasets for MuJoCo control tasks. The authors report robust decisions in out-of-support regions and better performance than the state-of-the-art algorithms considered. These results support adaptable policy learning as a way to explore the performance potential constrained by conventional offline restrictions. The evidence concerns the evaluated control settings, rather than a universal guarantee of reliable decisions everywhere beyond the training data.
summary.tldr: MAPLE learns offline policies that adapt beyond dataset-supported regions and improves performance in reported MuJoCo control experiments.

title: Offline Model-based Adaptable Policy Learning

abstract: There is an increasing need for effective active learning algorithms that are compatible with deep neural networks. This paper motivates and revisits a classic, Fisher-based active selection objective, and proposes BAIT, a practical, tractable, and high-performing algorithm that makes it viable for use with neural models. BAIT draws inspiration from the theoretical analysis of maximum likelihood estimators (MLE) for parametric models. It selects batches of samples by optimizing a bound on the MLE error in terms of the Fisher information, which we show can be implemented efficiently at scale by exploiting linear-algebraic structure especially amenable to execution on modern hardware. Our experiments demonstrate that BAIT outperforms the previous state of the art on both classification and regression problems, and is flexible enough to be used with a variety of model architectures.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which examples to obtain labels for, making the selection rule an important part of learning. This paper revisits an objective based on Fisher information and develops BAIT to make it practical for neural networks. Its motivation comes from theoretical analysis of maximum likelihood estimators in parametric models.

BAIT selects batches by optimizing a bound on estimation error expressed through Fisher information. This connects the selection of examples to a statistical objective about the resulting estimator. The paper's computational contribution is to exploit linear-algebraic structure so that this objective can be handled efficiently at scale using operations suited to modern hardware.

Experiments show BAIT outperforming the previous state of the art on both classification and regression problems, and the method works with a variety of model architectures. The findings support the usefulness of making a classical information-based selection principle computationally tractable for neural learning. The reported advantage is empirical across the evaluated problems, alongside the theoretical motivation for the selection objective.
summary.tldr: BAIT makes Fisher-information-based batch selection practical for neural active learning and improves classification and regression results in experiments.

title: Gone Fishing: Neural Active Learning with Fisher Embeddings

abstract: Differentiable programs have recently attracted much interest due to their interpretability, compositionality, and their efficiency to leverage differentiable training. However, synthesizing differentiable programs requires optimizing over a combinatorial, rapidly exploded space of program architectures. Despite the development of effective pruning heuristics, previous works essentially enumerate the discrete search space of program architectures, which is inefficient. We propose to encode program architecture search as learning the probability distribution over all possible program derivations induced by a context-free grammar. This allows the search algorithm to efficiently prune away unlikely program derivations to synthesize optimal program architectures. To this end, an efficient gradient-descent based method is developed to conduct program architecture search in a continuous relaxation of the discrete space of grammar rules. Experiment results on four sequence classification tasks demonstrate that our program synthesizer excels in discovering program architectures that lead to differentiable programs with higher F1 scores, while being more efficient than state-of-the-art program synthesis methods.

Their structure can support interpretation and composition, but finding a suitable architecture requires searching a rapidly growing collection of discrete possibilities. This paper addresses the cost of that search, which earlier approaches largely handled through enumeration aided by pruning heuristics.

The authors represent architecture search as learning a probability distribution over program derivations generated by a context-free grammar. They then relax the discrete choices among grammar rules into a continuous search space and apply gradient descent. Learning which derivations are unlikely allows the method to prune them, directing search toward more promising program architectures.

Experiments on four sequence classification tasks show that the resulting synthesizer finds architectures whose differentiable programs achieve higher F1 scores while using search more efficiently than the compared state-of-the-art synthesis methods. The central contribution is to make the architecture choices themselves amenable to continuous optimization. The reported results demonstrate the value of this formulation on the evaluated tasks, alongside the interpretability and compositional motivation for using programs.
summary.tldr: A grammar-based continuous search method finds differentiable program architectures more efficiently and with higher F1 scores on four sequence classification tasks.

title: Differentiable Synthesis of Program Architectures

abstract: Various non-trivial spaces are becoming popular for embedding structured data such as graphs, texts, or images. Following spherical and hyperbolic spaces, more general product spaces have been proposed. However, searching for the best configuration of a product space is a resource-intensive procedure, which reduces the practical applicability of the idea. We generalize the concept of product space and introduce an overlapping space that does not have the configuration search problem. The main idea is to allow subsets of coordinates to be shared between spaces of different types (Euclidean, hyperbolic, spherical). As a result, we often need fewer coordinates to store the objects. Additionally, we propose an optimization algorithm that automatically learns the optimal configuration. Our experiments confirm that overlapping spaces outperform the competitors in graph embedding tasks with different evaluation metrics. We also perform an empirical analysis in a realistic information retrieval setup, where we compare all spaces by incorporating them into DSSM. In this case, the proposed overlapping space consistently achieves nearly optimal results without any configuration tuning. This allows for reducing training time, which can be essential in large-scale applications.

paragraphs: Representing a graph geometrically can benefit from combining Euclidean, hyperbolic, and spherical spaces. Conventional product spaces require choosing how those spaces are configured, and searching for a good combination can be expensive. This paper proposes overlapping spaces to remove the need for that separate configuration search.

The main change is to let spaces of different types share subsets of coordinates. This often reduces the number of coordinates required to store objects. An optimization algorithm automatically learns the configuration, bringing the choice of geometric structure into the learning procedure rather than leaving it to an external tuning process.

Experiments show improvements over competing methods on graph-embedding tasks under multiple evaluation metrics. The practical benefit combines compact representations with reduced tuning effort; avoiding that search can lower training time, which the authors identify as especially relevant for large-scale applications.
summary.tldr: Overlapping geometric spaces share coordinates and learn their configuration automatically, improving compact graph representations without separate configuration tuning.

title: Overlapping Spaces for Compact Graph Representations

abstract: Multimodal meta-learning is a recent problem that extends conventional few-shot meta-learning by generalizing its setup to diverse multimodal task distributions. This setup makes a step towards mimicking how humans make use of a diverse set of prior skills to learn new skills. Previous work has achieved encouraging performance. In particular, in spite of the diversity of the multimodal tasks, previous work claims that a single meta-learner trained on a multimodal distribution can sometimes outperform multiple specialized meta-learners trained on individual unimodal distributions. The improvement is attributed to knowledge transfer between different modes of task distributions. However, there is no deep investigation to verify and understand the knowledge transfer between multimodal tasks. Our work makes two contributions to multimodal meta-learning. First, we propose a method to quantify knowledge transfer between tasks of different modes at a micro-level. Our quantitative, task-level analysis is inspired by the recent transference idea from multi-task learning. Second, inspired by hard parameter sharing in multi-task learning and a new interpretation of related work, we propose a new multimodal meta-learner that outperforms existing work by considerable margins. While the major focus is on multimodal meta-learning, our work also attempts to shed light on task interaction in conventional meta-learning. The code for this project is available at https://miladabd.github.io/KML.

Earlier work reported that a single learner trained across these modes can sometimes beat separate specialists, attributing the improvement to knowledge transfer. This paper investigates that explanation more directly by examining how individual tasks interact.

The authors introduce a task-level measure of transfer between different modes, drawing on the idea of transference from multi-task learning. It provides a way to quantify cross-task transfer at the level where the proposed explanation operates.

The paper also explores how this perspective might illuminate interactions in conventional meta-learning.
summary.tldr: Task-level transfer analysis and ideas from parameter sharing yield a stronger meta-learner for diverse task distributions.

title: Revisit Multimodal Meta-Learning through the Lens of Multi-Task Learning

abstract: As predictive models are deployed into the real world, they must increasingly contend with strategic behavior. A growing body of work on strategic classification treats this problem as a Stackelberg game: the decision-maker "leads" in the game by deploying a model, and the strategic agents "follow" by playing their best response to the deployed model. Importantly, in this framing, the burden of learning is placed solely on the decision-maker, while the agents’ best responses are implicitly treated as instantaneous. In this work, we argue that the order of play in strategic classification is fundamentally determined by the relative frequencies at which the decision-maker and the agents adapt to each other’s actions. In particular, by generalizing the standard model to allow both players to learn over time, we show that a decision-maker that makes updates faster than the agents can reverse the order of play, meaning that the agents lead and the decision-maker follows. We observe in standard learning settings that such a role reversal can be desirable for both the decision-maker and the strategic agents. Finally, we show that a decision-maker with the freedom to choose their update frequency can induce learning dynamics that converge to Stackelberg equilibria with either order of play.

abstract: Existing methods for unsupervised domain adaptation often rely on minimizing some statistical distance between the source and target samples in the latent space. To avoid the sampling variability, class imbalance, and data-privacy concerns that often plague these methods, we instead provide a memory and computation-efficient probabilistic framework to extract class prototypes and align the target features with them. We demonstrate the general applicability of our method on a wide range of scenarios, including single-source, multi-source, class-imbalance, and source-private domain adaptation. Requiring no additional model parameters and having a moderate increase in computation over the source model alone, the proposed method achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation transfers learning from labeled source data to target data without target labels. Many approaches compare source and target samples in a learned feature space and try to reduce their statistical differences. This paper instead organizes adaptation around class prototypes: representations that summarize individual classes and provide reference points for target features.

The proposed probabilistic framework extracts these prototypes and aligns target features with them. The motivation is to avoid difficulties associated with direct sample comparisons, including sampling variability, unequal class frequencies, and concerns about access to private source data. Prototypes make class summaries central to adaptation while keeping memory and computation requirements manageable.

The authors demonstrate the approach across single-source and multiple-source adaptation, class imbalance, and settings involving private source data. It introduces no additional model parameters and adds a moderate amount of computation beyond the source model. Its reported performance is competitive with leading methods, supporting prototypes as a practical basis for adaptation across these different settings.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic adaptation framework aligns target features with class prototypes, achieving competitive results with no additional model parameters.

title: A Prototype-Oriented Framework for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

abstract: In this paper, we aim to tackle the challenging few-shot segmentation task from a new perspective. Typical methods follow the paradigm to firstly learn prototypical features from support images and then match query features in pixel-level to obtain segmentation results. However, to obtain satisfactory segments, such a paradigm needs to couple the learning of the matching operations with heavy segmentation modules, limiting the flexibility of design and increasing the learning complexity. To alleviate this issue, we propose Mask Matching Transformer (MM-Former), a new paradigm for the few-shot segmentation task. Specifically, MM-Former first uses a class-agnostic segmenter to decompose the query image into multiple segment proposals. Then, a simple matching mechanism is applied to merge the related segment proposals into the final mask guided by the support images. The advantages of our MM-Former are two-fold. First, the MM-Former follows the paradigm of 'decompose first and then blend', allowing our method to benefit from the advanced potential objects segmenter to produce high-quality mask proposals for query images. Second, the mission of prototypical features is relaxed to learn coefficients to fuse correct ones within a proposal pool, making the MM-Former be well generalized to complex scenarios or cases. We conduct extensive experiments on the popular COCO-$20^i$ and Pascal-$5^i$ benchmarks. Competitive results well demonstrate the effectiveness and the generalization ability of our MM-Former. Code is available at https://github.com/Picsart-AI-Research/Mask-Matching-Transformer.

paragraphs: Few-shot segmentation uses a small set of support images to identify the relevant region in a query image. Typical approaches summarize support features and match them against individual query pixels. The paper argues that producing good masks this way tightly couples feature matching with substantial segmentation machinery, increasing learning complexity and restricting design flexibility.

MM-Former separates the process into two stages. A class-agnostic segmenter first divides the query image into candidate segment proposals. A simpler matching mechanism then uses the support images to select and combine relevant proposals into the final mask. The support representation learns blending coefficients over a proposal pool rather than handling the entire pixel-level segmentation problem.

This organization lets the system benefit from strong segmenters for generating candidate masks while assigning matching a more focused role. Experiments on COCO-20i and Pascal-5i produce competitive results supporting effectiveness and generalization. The contribution is a different allocation of work between proposing image regions and determining which regions correspond to the support examples.
summary.tldr: MM-Former performs few-shot segmentation by generating candidate masks first, then using support images to blend the relevant proposals.

title: Mask Matching Transformer for Few-Shot Segmentation

abstract: Recent advances in quantum computing and in particular, the introduction of quantum GANs, have led to increased interest in quantum zero-sum game theory, extending the scope of learning algorithms for classical games into the quantum realm. In this paper, we focus on learning in quantum zero-sum games under Matrix Multiplicative Weights Update (a generalization of the multiplicative weights update method) and its continuous analogue, Quantum Replicator Dynamics. When each player selects their state according to quantum replicator dynamics, we show that the system exhibits conservation laws in a quantum-information theoretic sense. Moreover, we show that the system exhibits Poincare recurrence, meaning that almost all orbits return arbitrarily close to their initial conditions infinitely often. Our analysis generalizes previous results in the case of classical games.

paragraphs: This paper examines learning dynamics in quantum zero-sum games, extending a line of analysis previously developed for classical games. Its motivation includes growing interest in quantum computing and quantum generative adversarial networks. The focus is on how players' selected quantum states evolve when their choices are governed by particular learning rules.

The authors study Matrix Multiplicative Weights Update and its continuous counterpart, Quantum Replicator Dynamics. For players following the continuous dynamics, they establish conservation laws expressed in quantum-information terms. These laws identify quantities that remain preserved as the players' states change, providing mathematical structure for understanding the resulting joint evolution.

The system also exhibits Poincare recurrence: almost all trajectories return arbitrarily close to their starting conditions infinitely many times. This describes repeated near-returns, without requiring every trajectory to repeat exactly or follow a fixed period. The results generalize earlier classical-game findings to the quantum setting and characterize persistent behavior of the learning dynamics, rather than presenting them simply as a route to a settled state.
summary.tldr: Quantum replicator dynamics in quantum zero-sum games obey conservation laws and exhibit recurrence for almost all trajectories.

title: Matrix Multiplicative Weights Updates in Quantum Zero-Sum Games: Conservation Laws & Recurrence

abstract: Most knowledge graphs (KGs) are incomplete, which motivates one important research topic on automatically complementing knowledge graphs. However, evaluation of knowledge graph completion (KGC) models often ignores the incompleteness---facts in the test set are ranked against all unknown triplets which may contain a large number of missing facts not included in the KG yet. Treating all unknown triplets as false is called the closed-world assumption. This closed-world assumption might negatively affect the fairness and consistency of the evaluation metrics. In this paper, we study KGC evaluation under a more realistic setting, namely the open-world assumption, where unknown triplets are considered to include many missing facts not included in the training or test sets. For the currently most used metrics such as mean reciprocal rank (MRR) and Hits@K, we point out that their behavior may be unexpected under the open-world assumption. Specifically, with not many missing facts, their numbers show a logarithmic trend with respect to the true strength of the model, and thus, the metric increase could be insignificant in terms of reflecting the true model improvement. Further, considering the variance, we show that the degradation in the reported numbers may result in incorrect comparisons between different models, where stronger models may have lower metric numbers. We validate the phenomenon both theoretically and experimentally. Finally, we suggest possible causes and solutions for this problem. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/GraphPKU/Open-World-KG .

paragraphs: Knowledge graphs contain recorded facts but usually omit many true ones. Evaluating a completion model often involves ranking a known test fact against unknown triples, effectively treating the unknown candidates as false. This paper investigates what happens when that evaluation encounters missing facts that are actually true.

Under an open-world assumption, unknown triples can include valid facts absent from both training and test data. The authors show that common measures such as mean reciprocal rank and Hits@K can then behave unexpectedly. Even with relatively few missing facts, the metrics can exhibit a logarithmic relationship with true model strength, compressing meaningful improvements into small numerical changes.

The problem also affects comparisons between models. When metric variance is considered, a stronger model can receive a lower reported score than a weaker one. The paper establishes these phenomena theoretically and experimentally and discusses possible causes and solutions. Its central implication is that benchmark rankings can reflect graph incompleteness as well as predictive ability, so small metric gains or reversed rankings may misrepresent actual progress.
summary.tldr: Missing true facts can compress knowledge-graph evaluation gains and even cause common metrics to rank stronger models below weaker ones.

title: Rethinking Knowledge Graph Evaluation Under the Open-World Assumption

abstract: Sign languages are visual languages using manual articulations and non-manual elements to convey information. For sign language recognition and translation, the majority of existing approaches directly encode RGB videos into hidden representations. RGB videos, however, are raw signals with substantial visual redundancy, leading the encoder to overlook the key information for sign language understanding. To mitigate this problem and better incorporate domain knowledge, such as handshape and body movement, we introduce a dual visual encoder containing two separate streams to model both the raw videos and the keypoint sequences generated by an off-the-shelf keypoint estimator. To make the two streams interact with each other, we explore a variety of techniques, including bidirectional lateral connection, sign pyramid network with auxiliary supervision, and frame-level self-distillation. The resulting model is called TwoStream-SLR, which is competent for sign language recognition (SLR). TwoStream-SLR is extended to a sign language translation (SLT) model, TwoStream-SLT, by simply attaching an extra translation network. Experimentally, our TwoStream-SLR and TwoStream-SLT achieve state-of-the-art performance on SLR and SLT tasks across a series of datasets including Phoenix-2014, Phoenix-2014T, and CSL-Daily.

A model trained directly on color video must find these signals among substantial visual redundancy, which can cause it to overlook important information. The paper introduces an encoder that combines the original video with a more structured description of movement.

The encoder has two streams: one processes raw video, and the other processes keypoint sequences from an existing keypoint estimator. The authors explore ways to make the streams interact, including bidirectional connections, a sign pyramid network with auxiliary supervision, and frame-level self-distillation. summary.tldr: Two interacting video and keypoint streams achieve reported state-of-the-art sign-language recognition and translation across several datasets.

title: Two-Stream Network for Sign Language Recognition and Translation

abstract: This paper focus on few-shot object detection~(FSOD) and instance segmentation~(FSIS), which requires a model to quickly adapt to novel classes with a few labeled instances. The existing methods severely suffer from bias classification because of the missing label issue which naturally exists in an instance-level few-shot scenario and is first formally proposed by us. Our analysis suggests that the standard classification head of most FSOD or FSIS models needs to be decoupled to mitigate the bias classification. Therefore, we propose an embarrassingly simple but effective method that decouples the standard classifier into two heads. Then, these two individual heads are capable of independently addressing clear positive samples and noisy negative samples which are caused by the missing label. In this way, the model can effectively learn novel classes while mitigating the effects of noisy negative samples. Without bells and whistles, our model without any additional computation cost and parameters consistently outperforms its baseline and state-of-the-art by a large margin on PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO benchmarks for FSOD and FSIS tasks.\footnote{\url{https://csgaobb.github.io/Projects/DCFS}.}

paragraphs: Few-shot detection and instance segmentation require models to recognize new object classes from only a few labeled instances. This paper identifies missing labels as a source of biased classification in that setting. When an object lacks a label, it can contribute a misleading negative training example, even though it should not be treated as evidence against recognizing the object.

The authors' analysis motivates splitting the usual classification head into two heads. These separately handle clear positive examples and noisy negatives arising from missing labels. The purpose is to let the model learn new classes while reducing interference from incorrect negative supervision. The proposed change reorganizes the classifier without adding parameters or computational cost, according to the abstract.

Experiments evaluate the method on PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO for both few-shot object detection and instance segmentation. The authors report consistent, large improvements over their baseline and leading methods. The contribution links a specific supervision problem to a simple architectural response: distinguishing reliable positive evidence from negative evidence that may be corrupted by incomplete annotation.
summary.tldr: Splitting the classifier into two heads reduces bias from missing labels and improves few-shot detection and instance segmentation without added computation or parameters.

title: Decoupling Classifier for Boosting Few-shot Object Detection and Instance Segmentation

abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are known for requiring extensive computational resources, and quantization is among the best and most common methods for compressing them. While aggressive quantization (i.e., less than 4-bits) performs well for classification, it may cause severe performance degradation in image-to-image tasks such as semantic segmentation and depth estimation. In this paper, we propose Wavelet Compressed Convolution (WCC)---a novel approach for high-resolution activation maps compression integrated with point-wise convolutions, which are the main computational cost of modern architectures. To this end, we use an efficient and hardware-friendly Haar-wavelet transform, known for its effectiveness in image compression, and define the convolution on the compressed activation map. We experiment with various tasks that benefit from high-resolution input. By combining WCC with light quantization, we achieve compression rates equivalent to 1-4bit activation quantization with relatively small and much more graceful degradation in performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/BGUCompSci/WaveletCompressedConvolution.

paragraphs: Compressing neural-network activations can reduce their resource demands, but image-to-image tasks are sensitive to aggressive quantization. Using fewer than four bits can work well for classification yet seriously degrade tasks such as semantic segmentation and depth estimation. This paper targets high-resolution activation maps with a compression method designed around that difficulty.

Wavelet Compressed Convolution, or WCC, applies an efficient, hardware-friendly Haar-wavelet transform and performs convolution on the compressed activation map. The method integrates compression with point-wise convolutions, which the abstract identifies as a major computational cost in modern architectures. Compression therefore becomes part of the convolutional operation itself.

Across experiments on tasks benefiting from high-resolution inputs, WCC combined with light quantization reaches compression rates equivalent to one- to four-bit activation quantization. The reported performance degradation is relatively small and more gradual. These findings support wavelet-based activation compression as a useful way to obtain substantial compression while better preserving performance on the evaluated image-to-image tasks.
summary.tldr: WCC combines Haar-wavelet activation compression with point-wise convolutions to achieve strong compression with gentler image-to-image performance degradation.

title: Wavelet Feature Maps Compression for Image-to-Image CNNs

abstract: Understanding to what extent neural networks memorize training data is an intriguing question with practical and theoretical implications. In this paper we show that in some cases a significant fraction of the training data can in fact be reconstructed from the parameters of a trained neural network classifier.We propose a novel reconstruction scheme that stems from recent theoretical results about the implicit bias in training neural networks with gradient-based methods.To the best of our knowledge, our results are the first to show that reconstructing a large portion of the actual training samples from a trained neural network classifier is generally possible.This has negative implications on privacy, as it can be used as an attack for revealing sensitive training data. We demonstrate our method for binary MLP classifiers on a few standard computer vision datasets.

We demonstrate our method for binary MLP classifiers on a few standard computer vision datasets.

paragraphs: Neural networks may retain information about individual training examples, raising questions about both learning behavior and privacy. This paper asks whether actual examples can be reconstructed directly from the parameters of a trained classifier, beyond merely determining whether a sample was used.

The authors develop a reconstruction scheme motivated by theoretical results about the implicit bias of gradient-based neural-network training. The reported result is that, in some cases, a significant fraction of the training data can be recovered from the fitted model.

Demonstrations use binary multilayer-perceptron classifiers on several standard computer-vision datasets. The abstract does not quantify the recovered fraction or establish the same vulnerability for every architecture and training procedure. Its privacy implication is concrete but scoped: releasing a trained model can expose more than aggregate patterns, and the demonstrated reconstruction attacks warrant attention to the particular training and model conditions.
summary.tldr: Some trained neural classifiers expose substantial portions of their training data through their parameters.

title: Reconstructing Training Data From Trained Neural Networks

abstract: Finding an optimal individualized treatment regimen is considered one of the most challenging precision medicine problems. Various patient characteristics influence the response to the treatment, and hence, there is no one-size-fits-all regimen. Moreover, the administration of an unsafe dose during the treatment can have adverse effects on health. Therefore, a treatment model must ensure patient \emph{safety} while \emph{efficiently} optimizing the course of therapy. We study a prevalent medical problem where the treatment aims to keep a physiological variable in a safe range and preferably close to a target level, which we refer to as \emph{leveling}. Such a task may be relevant in numerous other domains as well. We propose ESCADA, a novel and generic multi-armed bandit (MAB) algorithm tailored for the leveling task, to make safe, personalized, and context-aware dose recommendations. We derive high probability upper bounds on its cumulative regret and safety guarantees. Following ESCADA's design, we also describe its Thompson sampling-based counterpart. We discuss why the straightforward adaptations of the classical MAB algorithms such as GP-UCB may not be a good fit for the leveling task. Finally, we make \emph{in silico} experiments on the bolus-insulin dose allocation problem in type-1 diabetes mellitus disease and compare our algorithms against the famous GP-UCB algorithm, the rule-based dose calculators, and a clinician.

paragraphs: The paper studies treatment decisions where the objective is to keep a physiological measurement within a safe interval and preferably near a desired level. The authors call this leveling. It differs from simply seeking the largest possible response: the desired outcome is proximity to a target, and patient characteristics affect which dose achieves it.

ESCADA is a multi-armed bandit algorithm designed around this objective. It makes personalized dose recommendations using contextual information while accounting for safety as it learns. The authors derive high-probability bounds on cumulative regret and provide safety guarantees. They also describe a related Thompson sampling method and explain why straightforward adaptations of algorithms such as GP-UCB may fit leveling poorly.

The evaluation uses computer simulations of bolus-insulin allocation for type-1 diabetes. Comparisons include GP-UCB, rule-based dose calculators, and a clinician. These simulations place the method in a concrete dosing problem; the abstract does not report a comparative winner. The contribution combines a target-seeking formulation, algorithms tailored to it, and theoretical analysis of performance and safety.
summary.tldr: ESCADA frames personalized dosing as safely learning to keep a physiological variable near a target and provides bandit algorithms with theoretical guarantees.

title: ESCADA: Efficient Safety and Context Aware Dose Allocation for Precision Medicine

abstract: Formal XAI (explainable AI) is a growing area that focuses on computing explanations with mathematical guarantees for the decisions made by ML models. Inside formal XAI, one of the most studied cases is that of explaining the choices taken by decision trees, as they are traditionally deemed as one of the most interpretable classes of models. Recent work has focused on studying the computation of sufficient reasons, a kind of explanation in which given a decision tree $T$ and an instance $x$, one explains the decision $T(x)$ by providing a subset $y$ of the features of $x$ such that for any other instance $z$ compatible with $y$, it holds that $T(z) = T(x)$, intuitively meaning that the features in $y$ are already enough to fully justify the classification of $x$ by $T$. It has been argued, however, that sufficient reasons constitute a restrictive notion of explanation. For such a reason, the community has started to study their probabilistic counterpart, in which one requires that the probability of $T(z) = T(x)$ must be at least some value $\delta \in (0, 1]$, where $z$ is a random instance that is compatible with $y$. Our paper settles the computational complexity of $\delta$-sufficient-reasons over decision trees, showing that both (1) finding $\delta$-sufficient-reasons that are minimal in size, and (2) finding $\delta$-sufficient-reasons that are minimal inclusion-wise, do not admit polynomial-time algorithms (unless P = NP). This is in stark contrast with the deterministic case ($\delta = 1$) where inclusion-wise minimal sufficient-reasons are easy to compute. By doing this, we answer two open problems originally raised by Izza et al., and extend the hardness of explanations for Boolean circuits presented by W{\"a}ldchen et al. to the more restricted case of decision trees. On the positive side, we identify structural restrictions of decision trees that make the problem tractable, and show how SAT solvers might be able to tackle these problems in practical settings.
originalAbstract: Formal XAI (explainable AI) is a growing area that focuses on computing explanations with mathematical guarantees for the decisions made by ML models. Inside formal XAI, one of the most studied cases is that of explaining the choices taken by decision trees, as they are traditionally deemed as one of the most interpretable classes of models. Recent work has focused on studying the computation of sufficient reasons, a kind of explanation in which given a decision tree $T$ and an instance $x$, one explains the decision $T(x)$ by providing a subset $y$ of the features of $x$ such that for any other instance $z$ compatible with $y$, it holds that $T(z) = T(x)$, intuitively meaning that the features in $y$ are already enough to fully justify the classification of $x$ by $T$. It has been argued, however, that sufficient reasons constitute a restrictive notion of explanation. For such a reason, the community has started to study their probabilistic counterpart, in which one requires that the probability of $T(z) = T(x)$ must be at least some value $\delta \in (0, 1]$, where $z$ is a random instance that is compatible with $y$. Our paper settles the computational complexity of $\delta$-sufficient-reasons over decision trees, showing that both (1) finding $\delta$-sufficient-reasons that are minimal in size, and (2) finding $\delta$-sufficient-reasons that are minimal inclusion-wise, do not admit polynomial-time algorithms (unless P = NP). This is in stark contrast with the deterministic case ($\delta = 1$) where inclusion-wise minimal sufficient-reasons are easy to compute. By doing this, we answer two open problems originally raised by Izza et al., and extend the hardness of explanations for Boolean circuits presented by W{\"a}ldchen et al. to the more restricted case of decision trees. On the positive side, we identify structural restrictions of decision trees that make the problem tractable, and show how SAT solvers might be able to tackle these problems in practical settings.

paragraphs: A sufficient explanation for a decision-tree prediction fixes a subset of an example’s features that guarantees the same prediction for every compatible input. Probabilistic explanations relax that requirement: a random compatible input need only receive the same prediction with probability at least a chosen threshold.

The paper determines the computational difficulty of finding compact explanations of this kind. It distinguishes minimum-size explanations from inclusion-wise minimal ones, where no feature can be removed while preserving the required guarantee. In the general probabilistic problem, neither form admits a polynomial-time algorithm unless P equals NP. Thus, relaxing certainty does not automatically make explanation generation easier.

This contrasts with the deterministic case, where inclusion-wise minimal sufficient explanations are easy to compute. The hardness results settle two open problems and establish difficulty even for decision trees, despite their reputation for interpretability. The authors also identify structural restrictions that make the problem tractable and explain how SAT solvers might address practical instances. Those positive directions distinguish general worst-case hardness from the possibilities available for particular tree structures or solver-based approaches.
summary.tldr: Finding minimal probabilistic explanations for decision trees is generally computationally hard, although restricted structures admit tractable solutions.

title: On Computing Probabilistic Explanations for Decision Trees

abstract: Given a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the goal of Euclidean $(k,\ell)$-clustering is to find $k$ centers that minimize the sum of the $\ell$-th powers of the Euclidean distance of each point to the closest center. In practical situations, the clustering result must be stable against points missing in the input data so that we can make trustworthy and consistent decisions. To address this issue, we consider the average sensitivity of Euclidean $(k,\ell)$-clustering, which measures the stability of the output in total variation distance against deleting a random point from the input data. We first show that a popular algorithm \textsc{$k$-means++} and its variant called \textsc{$D^\ell$-sampling} have low average sensitivity. Next, we show that any approximation algorithm for Euclidean $(k,\ell)$-clustering can be transformed to an algorithm with low average sensitivity while almost preserving the approximation guarantee. As byproducts of our results, we provide several algorithms for consistent $(k,\ell)$-clustering and dynamic $(k,\ell)$-clustering in the random-order model, where the input points are randomly permuted and given in an online manner. The goal of the consistent setting is to maintain a good solution while minimizing the number of changes to the solution during the process, and that of the dynamic setting is to maintain a good solution while minimizing the (amortized) update time.

paragraphs: Clustering should remain useful when an input point is missing. This paper studies that requirement for Euclidean clustering, where the objective is to choose k centers minimizing a sum of powered distances to the nearest center. It measures stability through average sensitivity: how much the distribution of an algorithm's output changes, in total variation distance, when a randomly selected input point is deleted.

The authors show that k-means++ and its D-to-the-ell sampling variant have low average sensitivity. They also establish a broader transformation: any approximation algorithm for this clustering objective can be converted into one with low average sensitivity while nearly retaining its approximation guarantee. This links stability to solution quality without requiring a particular starting algorithm.

The analysis also yields algorithms for points arriving online in random order. In the consistent setting, the aim is to preserve a good clustering while changing the maintained solution infrequently. In the dynamic setting, the aim is to keep average update costs low. These results concern average deletion sensitivity and random-order arrivals, rather than an unrestricted guarantee against every possible disruption.
summary.tldr: The paper proves stability guarantees for Euclidean clustering and shows how to add low average sensitivity while nearly preserving approximation quality.

title: Average Sensitivity of Euclidean k-Clustering

abstract: Diffusion models have gained increasing attention for their impressive generation abilities but currently struggle with rendering accurate and coherent text. To address this issue, we introduce TextDiffuser, focusing on generating images with visually appealing text that is coherent with backgrounds. TextDiffuser consists of two stages: first, a Transformer model generates the layout of keywords extracted from text prompts, and then diffusion models generate images conditioned on the text prompt and the generated layout. Additionally, we contribute the first large-scale text images dataset with OCR annotations, MARIO-10M, containing 10 million image-text pairs with text recognition, detection, and character-level segmentation annotations. We further collect the MARIO-Eval benchmark to serve as a comprehensive tool for evaluating text rendering quality. Through experiments and user studies, we demonstrate that TextDiffuser is flexible and controllable to create high-quality text images using text prompts alone or together with text template images, and conduct text inpainting to reconstruct incomplete images with text. We will make the code, model and dataset publicly available.
