paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate compelling images while struggling to render accurate, coherent text inside them. TextDiffuser addresses that problem by explicitly planning where words should appear before generating the image. Its goal includes both readable text and a visual relationship between that text and its background.

The system has two stages. A Transformer generates a layout for keywords extracted from the prompt, and diffusion models then generate an image conditioned on both the prompt and that layout. The paper also introduces MARIO-10M, containing ten million image-text pairs with text recognition, detection, and character-level segmentation annotations, plus the MARIO-Eval benchmark for assessing text rendering.

Experiments and user studies demonstrate flexible, controllable generation using prompts alone or prompts together with text-template images. TextDiffuser also supports text inpainting to reconstruct incomplete images containing text. The contribution combines an explicit layout mechanism with data and evaluation resources, addressing text rendering as a structured part of image creation. The reported findings concern both output quality and the different ways users can control generation.
summary.tldr: TextDiffuser combines keyword-layout planning with diffusion generation to create controllable text-containing images and reconstruct incomplete ones.

title: TextDiffuser: Diffusion Models as Text Painters

abstract: Whittle index policy is a heuristic to the intractable restless multi-armed bandits (RMAB) problem. Although it is provably asymptotically optimal, finding Whittle indices remains difficult. In this paper, we present Neural-Q-Whittle, a Whittle index based Q-learning algorithm for RMAB with neural network function approximation, which is an example of nonlinear two-timescale stochastic approximation with Q-function values updated on a faster timescale and Whittle indices on a slower timescale. Despite the empirical success of deep Q-learning, the non-asymptotic convergence rate of Neural-Q-Whittle, which couples neural networks with two-timescale Q-learning largely remains unclear. This paper provides a finite-time analysis of Neural-Q-Whittle, where data are generated from a Markov chain, and Q-function is approximated by a ReLU neural network. Our analysis leverages a Lyapunov drift approach to capture the evolution of two coupled parameters, and the nonlinearity in value function approximation further requires us to characterize the approximation error. Combing these provide Neural-Q-Whittle with $\mathcal{O}(1/k^{2/3})$ convergence rate, where $k$ is the number of iterations.

paragraphs: The Whittle index policy offers a heuristic for the computationally difficult restless multi-armed bandit problem, but computing its indices is itself challenging. This paper presents Neural-Q-Whittle, which combines index learning with Q-learning and neural network function approximation. Its main focus is understanding how quickly this coupled learning procedure converges.

The algorithm operates on two timescales. Q-function estimates change on the faster timescale, while Whittle indices update more slowly. The analysis considers observations generated by a Markov chain and a Q-function represented by a ReLU neural network. These features require accounting for dependent data, interacting updates, and nonlinear approximation within the same argument.

The authors use a Lyapunov drift approach to track the evolution of the two coupled parameter sets and characterize the neural approximation error. Together, these steps yield an O(1/k^(2/3)) convergence rate after k iterations in the analyzed setting. The contribution supplies a finite-iteration characterization, making the learning dynamics more explicit than an eventual-convergence statement alone.
summary.tldr: Neural-Q-Whittle receives a finite-time convergence analysis for coupled neural Q-learning and Whittle-index updates with Markov-chain data.

title: Finite-Time Analysis of Whittle Index based Q-Learning for Restless Multi-Armed Bandits with Neural Network Function Approximation

abstract: Diffusion models are a new class of generative models, and have dramatically promoted image generation with unprecedented quality and diversity. Existing diffusion models mainly try to reconstruct input image from a corrupted one with a pixel-wise or feature-wise constraint along spatial axes. However, such point-based reconstruction may fail to make each predicted pixel/feature fully preserve its neighborhood context, impairing diffusion-based image synthesis. As a powerful source of automatic supervisory signal, context has been well studied for learning representations. Inspired by this, we for the first time propose ConPreDiff to improve diffusion-based image synthesis with context prediction. We explicitly reinforce each point to predict its neighborhood context (i.e., multi-stride pixels/features) with a context decoder at the end of diffusion denoising blocks in training stage, and remove the decoder for inference. In this way, each point can better reconstruct itself by preserving its semantic connections with neighborhood context. This new paradigm of ConPreDiff can generalize to arbitrary discrete and continuous diffusion backbones without introducing extra parameters in sampling procedure. Extensive experiments are conducted on unconditional image generation, text-to-image generation and image inpainting tasks. Our ConPreDiff consistently outperforms previous methods and achieves new SOTA text-to-image generation results on MS-COCO, with a zero-shot FID score of 6.21.

paragraphs: Diffusion image models learn to reconstruct images from corrupted versions, often supervising individual pixels or features. The paper argues that this can leave predicted points insufficiently connected to their surroundings. ConPreDiff adds a training task that explicitly asks each point to predict information about its neighborhood.

A context decoder is attached to the ends of diffusion denoising blocks during training. It predicts neighboring pixels or features at multiple strides, encouraging each location to preserve semantic relationships with nearby content. The decoder is removed for inference, so the additional training machinery introduces no extra parameters into the sampling procedure. The framework is designed to apply to both discrete and continuous diffusion backbones.

The authors report consistent improvements over previous methods, including a zero-shot FID of 6.21 on MS-COCO and a new state-of-the-art text-to-image result in their evaluation. The findings support neighborhood prediction as useful supervision that improves generation without retaining an additional decoder during sampling.
summary.tldr: ConPreDiff improves diffusion image generation with neighborhood prediction during training, then removes the added decoder for sampling.

title: Improving Diffusion-Based Image Synthesis with Context Prediction

abstract: With the advent of deep learning, progressively larger neural networks have been designed to solve complex tasks. We take advantage of these capacity-rich models to lower the cost of inference by exploiting computation in superposition. To reduce the computational burden per input, we propose Multiple-Input-Multiple-Output Neural Networks (MIMONets) capable of handling many inputs at once. MIMONets augment various deep neural network architectures with variable binding mechanisms to represent an arbitrary number of inputs in a compositional data structure via fixed-width distributed representations. Accordingly, MIMONets adapt nonlinear neural transformations to process the data structure holistically, leading to a speedup nearly proportional to the number of superposed input items in the data structure. After processing in superposition, an unbinding mechanism recovers each transformed input of interest. MIMONets also provide a dynamic trade-off between accuracy and throughput by an instantaneous on-demand switching between a set of accuracy-throughput operating points, yet within a single set of fixed parameters. We apply the concept of MIMONets to both CNN and Transformer architectures resulting in MIMOConv and MIMOFormer, respectively. Empirical evaluations show that MIMOConv achieves $\approx 2$–$4\times$ speedup at an accuracy delta within [+0.68, -3.18]% compared to WideResNet CNNs on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100. Similarly, MIMOFormer can handle $2$–$4$ inputs at once while maintaining a high average accuracy within a [-1.07, -3.43]% delta on the long range arena benchmark. Finally, we provide mathematical bounds on the interference between superposition channels in MIMOFormer. Our code is available at https://github.com/IBM/multiple-input-multiple-output-nets.

paragraphs: MIMONets aim to reduce inference cost by letting one neural computation process several inputs in superposition. Variable-binding mechanisms combine inputs into a fixed-width distributed representation. The network processes that combined structure, and an unbinding mechanism recovers the transformed inputs of interest afterward.

The authors adapt nonlinear transformations to operate on the combined representation and apply the approach to CNNs and Transformers, producing MIMOConv and MIMOFormer. A single set of parameters supports on-demand switching among accuracy-throughput operating points. This makes the number of simultaneously represented inputs a way to adjust throughput without switching to a separately parameterized model.

MIMOConv reports roughly two- to fourfold speedups against WideResNet CNNs on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, with accuracy changes ranging from +0.68% to -3.18%. MIMOFormer processes two to four inputs together, with average accuracy changes of -1.07% to -3.43% on Long Range Arena. Mathematical bounds characterize interference between its superposition channels, connecting the shared computation mechanism to the interaction among represented inputs.
summary.tldr: MIMONets process several inputs in superposition to trade accuracy for throughput using one fixed set of network parameters.

title: MIMONets: Multiple-Input-Multiple-Output Neural Networks Exploiting Computation in Superposition

abstract: Symmetries have been leveraged to improve the generalization of neural networks through different mechanisms from data augmentation to equivariant architectures. However, despite their potential, their integration into neural solvers for partial differential equations (PDEs) remains largely unexplored. We explore the integration of PDE symmetries, known as Lie point symmetries, in a major family of neural solvers known as physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). We propose a loss function that informs the network about Lie point symmetries in the same way that PINN models try to enforce the underlying PDE through a loss function. Intuitively, our symmetry loss ensures that the infinitesimal generators of the Lie group conserve the PDE solutions.. Effectively, this means that once the network learns a solution, it also learns the neighbouring solutions generated by Lie point symmetries.Empirical evaluations indicate that the inductive bias introduced by the Lie point symmetries of the PDEs greatly boosts the sample efficiency of PINNs.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks learn solutions to partial differential equations by penalising violations of those equations during training. This paper asks whether they can also benefit from knowing the equation's symmetries. These Lie point symmetries describe transformations that preserve solutions, linking a learned solution to a family of nearby valid ones.

The authors introduce a symmetry loss alongside the usual equation-based training objective. It encodes the requirement that the symmetry group's infinitesimal generators preserve the equation's solutions. In plain terms, the network receives guidance about how a solution can change while remaining valid. This places information about relationships among solutions directly into the learning objective.

Empirical evaluations indicate that this additional inductive bias greatly improves sample efficiency. The result suggests that the network can make better use of training information when it learns both a solution and the neighbouring solutions generated by the equation's symmetries. The contribution is a loss-based route for bringing those mathematical relationships into physics-informed learning.
summary.tldr: A loss that encodes PDE symmetries helps physics-informed neural networks learn related solutions and empirically improves sample efficiency.

title: Lie Point Symmetry and Physics-Informed Networks

abstract: In this paper, we consider domain-adaptive imitation learning with visual observation, where an agent in a target domain learns to perform a task by observing expert demonstrations in a source domain. Domain adaptive imitation learning arises in practical scenarios where a robot, receiving visual sensory data, needs to mimic movements by visually observing other robots from different angles or observing robots of different shapes. To overcome the domain shift in cross-domain imitation learning with visual observation, we propose a novel framework for extracting domain-independent behavioral features from input observations that can be used to train the learner, based on dual feature extraction and image reconstruction. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach outperforms previous algorithms for imitation learning from visual observation with domain shift.

Domain adaptive imitation learning arises in practical scenarios where a robot, receiving visual sensory data, needs to mimic movements by visually observing other robots from different angles or observing robots of different shapes. To overcome the domain shift in cross-domain imitation learning with visual observation, we propose a novel framework for extracting domain-independent behavioral features from input observations that can be used to train the learner, based on dual feature extraction and image reconstruction. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach outperforms previous algorithms for imitation learning from visual observation with domain shift.

paragraphs: Learning a task by watching an expert becomes harder when the expert and learner look different. A robot may observe demonstrations from another viewpoint or from a robot with a different body shape. The paper studies this setting as domain-adaptive imitation learning from visual observations, with demonstrations in a source domain and a learner in a target domain.

The proposed framework extracts behavioral features intended to be independent of the domain. It combines dual feature extraction with image reconstruction, and uses the resulting features to train the learner. The central idea is to make the representation capture behavior that remains useful despite visual differences between the demonstrations and the learner's observations.

Empirical results show better performance than previous algorithms for visual imitation learning under domain shift. This supports the usefulness of learning transferable behavioral representations for the evaluated settings. The approach matters because the visual form of a demonstration and the behavior it conveys can differ in ways that complicate direct imitation.
summary.tldr: A feature extraction and reconstruction framework improves visual imitation across differences in viewpoint or robot appearance.

title: Domain Adaptive Imitation Learning with Visual Observation

abstract: The current trend of scaling language models involves increasing both parameter count and training dataset size. Extrapolating this trend suggests that training dataset size may soon be limited by the amount of text data available on the internet. Motivated by this limit, we investigate scaling language models in data-constrained regimes. Specifically, we run a large set of experiments varying the extent of data repetition and compute budget, ranging up to 900 billion training tokens and 9 billion parameter models. We find that with constrained data for a fixed compute budget, training with up to 4 epochs of repeated data yields negligible changes to loss compared to having unique data. However, with more repetition, the value of adding compute eventually decays to zero. We propose and empirically validate a scaling law for compute optimality that accounts for the decreasing value of repeated tokens and excess parameters. Finally, we experiment with approaches mitigating data scarcity, including augmenting the training dataset with code data or removing commonly used filters. Models and datasets from our 400 training runs are freely available at https://github.com/huggingface/datablations.

paragraphs: Language-model scaling usually increases both model size and the amount of training text. This paper studies what happens when the supply of distinct data is constrained. The researchers vary data repetition and computational budgets in experiments reaching nine billion parameters and 900 billion training tokens, examining how effectively repeated exposure substitutes for new data.

summary.tldr: Experiments and a scaling law characterize when repeated training data remains useful and when extra computation stops paying off.

title: Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models

abstract: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) provide a formalism to quantify and calibrate uncertainty in deep learning. Current inference approaches for BNNs often resort to few-sample estimation for scalability, which can harm predictive performance, while its alternatives tend to be computationally prohibitively expensive. We tackle this challenge by revealing a previously unseen connection between inference on BNNs and volume computation problems. With this observation, we introduce a novel collapsed inference scheme that performs Bayesian model averaging using collapsed samples. It improves over a Monte-Carlo sample by limiting sampling to a subset of the network weights while pairing it with some closed-form conditional distribution over the rest. A collapsed sample represents uncountably many models drawn from the approximate posterior and thus yields higher sample efficiency. Further, we show that the marginalization of a collapsed sample can be solved analytically and efficiently despite the non-linearity of neural networks by leveraging existing volume computation solvers. Our proposed use of collapsed samples achieves a balance between scalability and accuracy. On various regression and classification tasks, our collapsed Bayesian deep learning approach demonstrates significant improvements over existing methods and sets a new state of the art in terms of uncertainty estimation as well as predictive performance.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks represent uncertainty by considering multiple plausible settings of network weights. Approximating this averaging with only a few samples can hurt predictions, but using more expensive inference can undermine scalability. This paper introduces collapsed inference to obtain more information from each sample while keeping the computation manageable.

Instead of sampling every weight, a collapsed sample fixes only a subset and pairs it with a closed-form conditional distribution over the remaining weights. Each such sample therefore represents uncountably many models from the approximate posterior. The authors connect this averaging problem to volume computation and show that existing volume solvers can analytically and efficiently marginalize a collapsed sample despite the network's nonlinearity.

The approach aims to improve sample efficiency without paying the cost of separately evaluating all the models represented by a sample. Across regression and classification tasks, the authors report significant improvements over existing methods and state-of-the-art uncertainty estimation and predictive performance. The findings support collapsed samples as a useful way to balance accuracy with scalable Bayesian model averaging.
summary.tldr: Collapsed inference analytically averages over some neural-network weights to improve the efficiency and accuracy of Bayesian prediction.

title: Collapsed Inference for Bayesian Deep Learning

abstract: Recognizing and organizing text in correct reading order plays a crucial role in historical document analysis and preservation. While existing methods have shown promising performance, they often struggle with challenges such as diverse layouts, low image quality, style variations, and distortions. This is primarily due to the lack of consideration for these issues in the current benchmarks, which hinders the development and evaluation of historical document analysis and recognition (HDAR) methods in complex real-world scenarios. To address this gap, this paper introduces a complex multi-style Chinese historical document analysis benchmark, named M5HisDoc. The M5 indicates five properties of style, ie., Multiple layouts, Multiple document types, Multiple calligraphy styles, Multiple backgrounds, and Multiple challenges. The M5HisDoc dataset consists of two subsets, M5HisDoc-R (Regular) and M5HisDoc-H (Hard). The M5HisDoc-R subset comprises 4,000 historical document images. To ensure high-quality annotations, we meticulously perform manual annotation and triple-checking. To replicate real-world conditions for historical document analysis applications, we incorporate image rotation, distortion, and resolution reduction into M5HisDoc-R subset to form a new challenging subset named M5HisDoc-H, which contains the same number of images as M5HisDoc-R. The dataset exhibits diverse styles, significant scale variations, dense texts, and an extensive character set. We conduct benchmarking experiments on five tasks: text line detection, text line recognition, character detection, character recognition, and reading order prediction. We also conduct cross-validation with other benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that the M5HisDoc dataset can offer new challenges and great opportunities for future research in this field, thereby providing deep insights into the solution for HDAR. The dataset is available at https://github.com/HCIILAB/M5HisDoc.

paragraphs: M5HisDoc is a benchmark for reading and organizing Chinese historical documents under varied visual conditions. Recognizing individual characters is only part of the problem: systems must also detect text and determine its reading order. The authors argue that existing benchmarks insufficiently capture the diverse layouts, image degradation, writing styles, and distortions encountered in practice.

The dataset emphasizes five kinds of variation: layouts, document types, calligraphy styles, backgrounds, and challenges. Its regular subset contains 4,000 historical document images, manually annotated and checked three times. A hard subset contains another 4,000 images derived from the regular subset through rotation, distortion, and resolution reduction. This design adds controlled image difficulties to an already varied collection.

Benchmarking covers text-line detection and recognition, character detection and recognition, and reading-order prediction. The authors also conduct cross-validation with other benchmarks. Their results show that the collection presents new challenges for historical document analysis. Its contribution is a broader evaluation resource for studying both textual recognition and document organization across complex historical page appearances.
summary.tldr: M5HisDoc benchmarks Chinese historical document recognition and reading order across varied styles and deliberately degraded images.

title: M5HisDoc: A Large-scale Multi-style Chinese Historical Document Analysis Benchmark

abstract: We give an algorithm for Centroid-Linkage Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering (HAC), which computes a $c$-approximate clustering in roughly $n^{1+O(1/c^2)}$ time. We obtain our result by combining a new centroid-linkage HAC algorithm with a novel fully dynamic data structure for nearest neighbor search which works under adaptive updates.We also evaluate our algorithm empirically. By leveraging a state-of-the-art nearest-neighbor search library, we obtain a fast and accurate centroid-linkage HAC algorithm. Compared to an existing state-of-the-art exact baseline, our implementation maintains the clustering quality while delivering up to a $36\times$ speedup due to performing fewer distance comparisons.

We obtain our result by combining a new centroid-linkage HAC algorithm with a novel fully dynamic data structure for nearest neighbor search which works under adaptive updates.We also evaluate our algorithm empirically. By leveraging a state-of-the-art nearest-neighbor search library, we obtain a fast and accurate centroid-linkage HAC algorithm. Compared to an existing state-of-the-art exact baseline, our implementation maintains the clustering quality while delivering up to a $36\times$ speedup due to performing fewer distance comparisons.

paragraphs: Centroid-linkage hierarchical clustering builds a hierarchy by repeatedly combining clusters according to the distances between their centers. Maintaining the relevant nearest-neighbor relationships as clusters change can require many distance comparisons. This paper develops an approximate algorithm that addresses that computational burden while providing a formal approximation guarantee.

The theoretical algorithm computes a c-approximate clustering in roughly n raised to the power 1 + O(1/c²) time. This expresses a tradeoff between the approximation factor and the running-time exponent. The construction combines a new clustering algorithm with a fully dynamic nearest-neighbor data structure that supports adaptive updates, accommodating changes made as clustering proceeds.

The authors also evaluate an implementation built using a state-of-the-art nearest-neighbor search library. Against an existing exact baseline, it maintains clustering quality in the reported experiments and achieves speedups of up to 36 times. The reduction comes from performing fewer distance comparisons. The paper therefore offers both a theoretical route to faster approximate clustering and empirical evidence that nearest-neighbor search can make centroid linkage substantially more efficient.
summary.tldr: A new approximate centroid-linkage algorithm combines dynamic nearest-neighbor search with empirical speedups of up to 36 times while maintaining clustering quality.

title: Efficient Centroid-Linkage Clustering

abstract: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) have successfully handled various tasks. As one fundamental module in Transformers, position encoding encodes the positional information of tokens in a sequence. Specifically, rotary position embedding (RoPE), one of the most widely used techniques, encodes the positional information by dividing the query or key value with $d$ elements into $d/2$ pairs and rotating the 2d vectors corresponding to each pair of elements. Therefore, the direction of each pair and the position-related rotation jointly determine the attention score. In this paper, we show that the direction of the 2d pair is largely affected by the angle between the corresponding weight vector pair. We theoretically show that non-orthogonal weight vector pairs lead to great attention on tokens at a certain relative position and are less sensitive to the input which may correspond to basic syntactic information. Meanwhile, the orthogonal weight vector pairs are more flexible regarding the relative position, which may correspond to high-level syntactic information. Empirical evidence supports the hypothesis that shallow layers of LLMs focus more on local syntax and deep layers focus more on high-level semantics. Furthermore, we show that LLMs fine-tuning mainly changes the pairs of weight vectors that are nearly orthogonal, i.e., the weight corresponding to high-level semantics, which enables the reduction of the number of trainable parameters during fine-tuning without sacrificing performance. We propose a method namely Angle-based Weight Selection (AWS) to reduce the fine-tuning overhead and verify the effectiveness of the proposed method on widely used Alpaca fine-tuned Llama-2.

paragraphs: Rotary position embedding represents token position by rotating pairs of query and key components. Attention therefore depends on both those components' directions and the position-dependent rotations. This paper investigates how the angle between the corresponding learned weight vectors shapes that behavior and what it may reveal about the information being processed.

The theoretical analysis shows that non-orthogonal weight pairs strongly favor particular relative positions and respond less to input changes, behavior that may correspond to basic syntax. Orthogonal pairs allow more positional flexibility. Empirical results support a related hypothesis: shallow layers emphasize local syntax, while deeper layers emphasize higher-level semantics.

The authors also find that fine-tuning mainly changes nearly orthogonal weight pairs. They use this observation to develop Angle-based Weight Selection, which reduces the number of trainable parameters by selecting weights according to their angles. Tests on Alpaca-fine-tuned Llama-2 support reduced fine-tuning overhead without sacrificing performance. The method turns an analysis of positional attention geometry into a practical criterion for deciding which parameters to update.
summary.tldr: Analysis of rotary-position weight angles motivates selective fine-tuning that reduces trainable parameters while preserving performance in the reported tests.

title: What Rotary Position Embedding Can Tell Us: Identifying Query and Key Weights Corresponding to Basic Syntactic or High-level Semantic Information

abstract: We study online classification when the learner has access to predictions about future examples. We design an online learner whose expected regret is never worse than the worst-case regret, gracefully improves with the quality of the predictions, and can be significantly better than the worst-case regret when the predictions of future examples are accurate. As a corollary, we show that if the learner is always guaranteed to observe data where future examples are easily predictable, then online learning can be as easy as transductive online learning. Our results complement recent work in online algorithms with predictions and smoothed online classification, which go beyond a worse-case analysis by using machine-learned predictions and distributional assumptions respectively.

As a corollary, we show that if the learner is always guaranteed to observe data where future examples are easily predictable, then online learning can be as easy as transductive online learning. paragraphs: Online classification asks a learner to make classification decisions as examples arrive. This paper considers a learner that also receives predictions about future examples. Such forecasts offer information about what comes next, but their quality may vary. The central question is whether a learner can benefit from accurate forecasts while retaining a worst-case performance guarantee.

The authors design an online learner whose expected regret never exceeds the worst-case regret guarantee and improves gracefully as predictions become more accurate. Accurate forecasts can therefore lead to substantially better regret. The guarantee connects the usefulness of the extra information to its quality, allowing the analysis to describe more than the most difficult possible sequence.

A corollary shows that, if future examples are always guaranteed to be easily predictable, online learning can be as easy as transductive online learning. This conclusion depends on that predictability condition. The work complements approaches that move beyond worst-case analysis through machine-learned forecasts or distributional assumptions, establishing a direct theoretical role for predictions of future examples.
summary.tldr: An online classifier gains better expected regret from accurate forecasts of future examples while preserving its worst-case regret guarantee.

title: Online Classification with Predictions

abstract: Deep learning models like AlphaFold2 have revolutionized protein structure prediction, achieving unprecedented accuracy. However, the dependence on robust multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) continues to pose a challenge, especially for proteins that lack a wealth of homologous sequences. To overcome this limitation, we introduce MSA-Generator, a self-supervised generative protein language model. Trained on a sequence-to-sequence task using an automatically constructed dataset, MSA-Generator employs protein-specific attention mechanisms to harness large-scale protein databases, generating virtual MSAs that enrich existing ones and boost prediction accuracy. Our experiments on CASP14 and CASP15 benchmarks reveal significant improvements in LDDT scores, particularly for complex and challenging sequences, enhancing the performance of both AlphaFold2 and RoseTTAFold. The code is released at \url{https://github.com/lezhang7/MSAGen}.

paragraphs: Protein structure predictors such as AlphaFold2 depend on strong multiple sequence alignments, or MSAs, which organize related protein sequences together. This creates a challenge for proteins with few available homologous sequences. The paper addresses that bottleneck by generating additional sequence-alignment material to enrich what is already available.

MSA-Generator is a self-supervised protein language model trained on a sequence-to-sequence task using an automatically constructed dataset. It uses protein-specific attention mechanisms to draw on large protein databases and produce virtual MSAs. These generated alignments supplement existing ones, placing the contribution in the information supplied to structure predictors rather than in a replacement for those predictors.

Experiments on the CASP14 and CASP15 benchmarks report significant improvements in LDDT scores for both AlphaFold2 and RoseTTAFold. The gains are particularly notable for complex and challenging sequences. The findings support using a generative protein model to strengthen alignment inputs, with the practical benefit appearing in the accuracy of downstream structure prediction on the evaluated benchmarks.
summary.tldr: MSA-Generator creates virtual sequence alignments that improve reported AlphaFold2 and RoseTTAFold structure predictions.

title: MSA Generation with Seqs2Seqs Pretraining: Advancing Protein Structure Predictions

abstract: Exploring unknown environments efficiently is a fundamental challenge in unsupervised goal-conditioned reinforcement learning. While selecting exploratory goals at the frontier of previously explored states is an effective strategy, the policy during training may still have limited capability of reaching rare goals on the frontier, resulting in reduced exploratory behavior. We propose "Cluster Edge Exploration" (CE$^2$), a new goal-directed exploration algorithm that when choosing goals in sparsely explored areas of the state space gives priority to goal states that remain accessible to the agent. The key idea is clustering to group states that are easily reachable from one another by the current policy under training in a latent space, and traversing to states holding significant exploration potential on the boundary of these clusters before doing exploratory behavior. In challenging robotics environments including navigating a maze with a multi-legged ant robot, manipulating objects with a robot arm on a cluttered tabletop, and rotating objects in the palm of an anthropomorphic robotic hand, CE$^2$ demonstrates superior efficiency in exploration compared to baseline methods and ablations.

paragraphs: An agent exploring an unfamiliar environment can choose goals near the boundary of places it has already visited. However, a promising frontier goal may still be too difficult for its current policy to reach. Repeatedly choosing such goals can reduce useful exploration. This paper addresses that mismatch between where exploration would be valuable and where the agent can actually go.

Cluster Edge Exploration, abbreviated CE², groups states in a learned latent space according to how easily the current policy can move between them. It prioritizes accessible goals in sparsely explored regions. The agent first moves toward a cluster boundary with substantial exploration potential and then performs exploratory behavior from that location.

The authors evaluate the method on an ant robot navigating a maze, a robot arm manipulating objects on a cluttered table, and a robotic hand rotating objects. CE² explores more efficiently than the evaluated baselines and ablations. These results support making goal selection sensitive to current capabilities, so frontier exploration begins from states the agent is better positioned to reach.
summary.tldr: CE² improves exploration by choosing promising cluster-boundary goals that remain accessible to the agent's current policy.

title: Exploring the Edges of Latent State Clusters for Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) offers a promising solution to the data sparsity problem by enabling knowledge transfer across source and target domains. However, many recent CDR models overlook crucial issues such as privacy as well as the risk of negative transfer (which negatively impact model performance), especially in multi-domain settings. To address these challenges, we propose FedGCDR, a novel federated graph learning framework that securely and effectively leverages positive knowledge from multiple source domains. First, we design a positive knowledge transfer module that ensures privacy during inter-domain knowledge transmission. This module employs differential privacy-based knowledge extraction combined with a feature mapping mechanism, transforming source domain embeddings from federated graph attention networks into reliable domain knowledge. Second, we design a knowledge activation module to filter out potential harmful or conflicting knowledge from source domains, addressing the issues of negative transfer. This module enhances target domain training by expanding the graph of the target domain to generate reliable domain attentions and fine-tunes the target model for improved negative knowledge filtering and more accurate predictions. We conduct extensive experiments on 16 popular domains of the Amazon dataset, demonstrating that FedGCDR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Cross-domain recommendation uses information from other domains to improve recommendations where data are sparse. Sharing information introduces two problems addressed by FedGCDR: protecting privacy during transfer and avoiding negative transfer, where source-domain knowledge harms the target model. These concerns become especially relevant when several source domains contribute information.

FedGCDR combines federated graph attention networks with a positive knowledge transfer module. This module uses differential privacy-based extraction and feature mapping to turn source embeddings into transferable domain knowledge. A separate knowledge activation module filters information that may be harmful or conflict with the target domain.

The activation process expands the target-domain graph to produce domain attentions and fine-tunes the target model to improve filtering and prediction. Thus, knowledge transfer includes both a privacy-oriented extraction step and a relevance-oriented selection step. Experiments across 16 Amazon domains report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The findings support jointly addressing privacy and the quality of transferred information when using multiple domains to strengthen recommendation models.
summary.tldr: FedGCDR combines privacy-preserving knowledge transfer with harmful-knowledge filtering to improve cross-domain recommendations.

title: Federated Graph Learning for Cross-Domain Recommendation

abstract: In this paper, we propose a provably efficient natural policy gradient algorithm called Spectral Dynamic Embedding Policy Optimization (\SDEPO) for two-player zero-sum stochastic Markov games with continuous state space and finite action space. In the policy evaluation procedure of our algorithm, a novel kernel embedding method is employed to construct a finite-dimensional linear approximations to the state-action value function. We explicitly analyze the approximation error in policy evaluation, and show that \SDEPO\ achieves an $\tilde{O}(\frac{1}{(1-\gamma)^3\epsilon})$ last-iterate convergence to the $\epsilon-$optimal Nash equilibrium, which is independent of the cardinality of the state space. The complexity result matches the best-known results for global convergence of policy gradient algorithms for single agent setting. Moreover, we also propose a practical variant of \SDEPO\ to deal with continuous action space and empirical results demonstrate the practical superiority of the proposed method.

paragraphs: This paper develops SDEPO, a natural policy gradient algorithm for two-player zero-sum Markov games. The theoretical setting allows continuously varying states but finitely many actions. The goal is to learn strategies approaching a Nash equilibrium, with a convergence guarantee that does not depend on counting the states in that continuous space.

During policy evaluation, a kernel embedding constructs a finite-dimensional linear approximation of the state-action value function. The authors explicitly account for the error introduced by this approximation. They prove last-iterate convergence to an epsilon-optimal equilibrium with complexity of order 1/((1−gamma)^3 epsilon), up to logarithmic factors, where gamma is the discount factor.

The stated complexity matches the best-known global convergence results for policy gradient algorithms in the single-agent setting. The paper also introduces a practical variant for continuous actions and reports empirical superiority. These are distinct contributions: the finite-action analysis supplies the formal guarantee, while the continuous-action variant extends the method's practical scope through experimental evaluation.
summary.tldr: SDEPO uses finite-dimensional kernel embeddings to obtain state-cardinality-independent convergence guarantees for continuous-state, finite-action zero-sum games.

title: Solving Zero-Sum Markov Games with Continuous State via Spectral Dynamic Embedding

abstract: Fine-tuning Diffusion Models remains an underexplored frontier in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), especially when compared with the remarkable progress made in fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs). While cutting-edge diffusion models such as Stable Diffusion (SD) and SDXL rely on supervised fine-tuning, their performance inevitably plateaus after seeing a certain volume of data. Recently, reinforcement learning (RL) has been employed to fine-tune diffusion models with human preference data, but it requires at least two images (``winner'' and ``loser'' images) for each text prompt.In this paper, we introduce an innovative technique called self-play fine-tuning for diffusion models (SPIN-Diffusion), where the diffusion model engages in competition with its earlier versions, facilitating an iterative self-improvement process. Our approach offers an alternative to conventional supervised fine-tuning and RL strategies, significantly improving both model performance and alignment. Our experiments on the Pick-a-Pic dataset reveal that SPIN-Diffusion outperforms the existing supervised fine-tuning method in aspects of human preference alignment and visual appeal right from its first iteration. By the second iteration, it exceeds the performance of RLHF-based methods across all metrics, achieving these results with less data. Codes are available at \url{https://github.com/uclaml/SPIN-Diffusion/}.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to improve text-to-image diffusion models after initial training. It motivates the problem through diminishing returns from supervised fine-tuning and the paired winner-and-loser images required by the preference-based reinforcement-learning approaches it discusses. The proposed alternative, SPIN-Diffusion, organizes improvement around competition with earlier versions of the model.

Self-play creates an iterative fine-tuning process in which the model's previous versions participate in its improvement. The central contribution is applying this mechanism to diffusion models as an alternative to conventional supervised and reinforcement-learning strategies. The intended benefits concern both generated-image quality and alignment with human preferences.

On the Pick-a-Pic dataset, the first iteration outperforms the existing supervised fine-tuning method in human preference alignment and visual appeal. By the second iteration, the authors report performance above the compared RLHF-based methods across all evaluated metrics, using less data. These results support self-play as an effective fine-tuning approach in the reported experiments, rather than establishing an unlimited sequence of improvements from further iterations.
summary.tldr: SPIN-Diffusion fine-tunes image generators through competition with earlier versions, improving preference alignment and visual quality in reported experiments.

title: Self-Play Fine-tuning of Diffusion Models for Text-to-image Generation

abstract: Open-World Object Detection (OWOD) is a challenging task that requires the detector to identify unlabeled objects and continuously demands the detector to learn new knowledge based on existing ones. Existing methods primarily focus on recalling unknown objects, neglecting to explore the reasons behind them. This paper aims to understand the model's behavior in predicting the unknown category. First, we model the text attribute and the positive sample probability, obtaining their empirical probability, which can be seen as the detector's estimation of the likelihood of the target with certain known attributes being predicted as the foreground. Then, we jointly decide whether the current object should be categorized in the unknown category based on the empirical, the in-distribution, and the out-of-distribution probability. Finally, based on the decision-making process, we can infer the similarity of an unknown object to known classes and identify the attribute with the most significant impact on the decision-making process. This additional information can help us understand the behavior of the model's prediction in the unknown class. The evaluation results on the Real-World Object Detection (RWD) benchmark, which consists of five real-world application datasets, show that we surpassed the previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) with an absolute gain of 5.3 mAP for unknown classes, reaching 20.5 mAP. Our code is available at https://github.com/xxyzll/UMB.

paragraphs: Open-world object detection requires identifying objects outside the detector's known categories while continuing to learn new knowledge. This paper focuses on understanding why a detector assigns an object to the unknown category. It seeks to attach interpretable information to that decision while also improving unknown-object detection performance.

UMB models text attributes together with positive-sample probability to obtain an empirical probability. This represents the detector's estimated likelihood that a target with certain known attributes will be treated as foreground. The method combines this estimate with in-distribution and out-of-distribution probabilities to decide whether the object belongs in the unknown category.

The same decision process provides information about an unknown object's similarity to known classes and identifies the attribute with the greatest influence on the decision. On the Real-World Object Detection benchmark, comprising five application datasets, UMB reaches 20.5 mAP for unknown classes, an absolute improvement of 5.3 over the previous state of the art. The method thus connects improved detection with a more inspectable account of unknown-category predictions.
summary.tldr: UMB combines attribute-based and distributional probabilities to improve unknown-object detection and explain which known attributes influence its decisions.

title: UMB: Understanding Model Behavior for Open-World Object Detection

abstract: Homomorphic encryption (HE)-based deep neural network (DNN) inference protects data and model privacy but suffers from significant computation overhead. We observe transforming the DNN weights into circulant matrices converts general matrix-vector multiplications into HE-friendly 1-dimensional convolutions, drastically reducing the HE computation cost. Hence, in this paper, we propose PrivCirNet, a protocol/network co-optimization framework based on block circulant transformation. At the protocol level, PrivCirNet customizes the HE encoding algorithm that is fully compatible with the block circulant transformation and reduces the computation latency in proportion to the block size. At the network level, we propose a latency-aware formulation to search for the layer-wise block size assignment based on second-order information. PrivCirNet also leverages layer fusion to further reduce the inference cost. We compare PrivCirNet with the state-of-the-art HE-based framework Bolt (IEEE S\&P 2024) and HE-friendly pruning method SpENCNN (ICML 2023). For ResNet-18 and Vision Transformer (ViT) on Tiny ImageNet, PrivCirNet reduces latency by $5.0\times$ and $1.3\times$ with iso-accuracy over Bolt, respectively, and improves accuracy by $4.1$\% and $12$\% over SpENCNN, respectively. For MobileNetV2 on ImageNet, PrivCirNet achieves $1.7\times$ lower latency and $4.2$\% better accuracy over Bolt and SpENCNN, respectively. Our code and checkpoints are available on Git Hub.

Hence, in this paper, we propose PrivCirNet, a protocol/network co-optimization framework based on block circulant transformation. At the protocol level, PrivCirNet customizes the HE encoding algorithm that is fully compatible with the block circulant transformation and reduces the computation latency in proportion to the block size. At the network level, we propose a latency-aware formulation to search for the layer-wise block size assignment based on second-order information. PrivCirNet also leverages layer fusion to further reduce the inference cost. We compare PrivCirNet with the state-of-the-art HE-based framework Bolt (IEEE S\&P 2024) and HE-friendly pruning method SpENCNN (ICML 2023). For ResNet-18 and Vision Transformer (ViT) on Tiny ImageNet, PrivCirNet reduces latency by $5.0\times$ and $1.3\times$ with iso-accuracy over Bolt, respectively, and improves accuracy by $4.1$\% and $12$\% over SpENCNN, respectively. For MobileNetV2 on ImageNet, PrivCirNet achieves $1.7\times$ lower latency and $4.2$\% better accuracy over Bolt and SpENCNN, respectively. Our code and checkpoints are available on Git Hub.

paragraphs: Homomorphic encryption protects data and model privacy during neural-network inference, but computation is expensive. PrivCirNet reduces this cost by restructuring network weights into block-circulant matrices. This converts general matrix-vector operations into one-dimensional convolutions that are better suited to encrypted computation, linking the network’s structure to the encryption protocol’s efficiency.

The framework customizes the encryption encoding to match that structure, with latency reductions proportional to block size. It also searches for a block-size assignment for each layer using a latency-aware objective and second-order information. Layer fusion provides an additional reduction in inference cost. These components jointly address protocol operations and network design.

On Tiny ImageNet, reported latency reductions relative to Bolt are 5.0 times for ResNet-18 and 1.3 times for ViT at equal accuracy. Accuracy improvements over SpENCNN are 4.1% and 12%, respectively. For MobileNetV2 on ImageNet, the paper reports 1.7 times lower latency than Bolt and 4.2% better accuracy than SpENCNN. These comparisons demonstrate benefits across the evaluated architectures.
summary.tldr: PrivCirNet co-designs structured network weights and encryption operations to reduce private-inference latency while preserving or improving reported accuracy.

title: PrivCirNet: Efficient Private Inference via Block Circulant Transformation

abstract: While standard evaluation scores for generative models are mostly reference-based, a reference-dependent assessment of generative models could be generally difficult due to the unavailability of applicable reference datasets. Recently, the reference-free entropy scores, VENDI and RKE, have been proposed to evaluate the diversity of generated data. However, estimating these scores from data leads to significant computational costs for large-scale generative models. In this work, we leverage the random Fourier features framework to reduce the metrics' complexity and propose the *Fourier-based Kernel Entropy Approximation (FKEA)* method. We utilize FKEA's approximated eigenspectrum of the kernel matrix to efficiently estimate the mentioned entropy scores. Furthermore, we show the application of FKEA's proxy eigenvectors to reveal the method's identified modes in evaluating the diversity of produced samples. We provide a stochastic implementation of the FKEA assessment algorithm with a complexity $O(n)$ linearly growing with sample size $n$. We extensively evaluate FKEA's numerical performance in application to standard image, text, and video datasets. Our empirical results indicate the method's scalability and interpretability applied to large-scale generative models. The codebase is available at [https://github.com/aziksh-ospanov/FKEA](https://github.com/aziksh-ospanov/FKEA).

paragraphs: Evaluating generated data against a reference collection is difficult when a suitable reference dataset is unavailable. Reference-free entropy scores such as VENDI and RKE provide a way to measure diversity without that requirement. However, calculating these scores becomes computationally expensive as the number of generated samples grows.

The paper introduces Fourier-based Kernel Entropy Approximation, or FKEA, using random Fourier features to reduce this cost. It approximates the eigenspectrum of the kernel matrix, the spectral information needed to estimate the entropy scores. The method also provides proxy eigenvectors that can reveal the modes identified in the generated samples, giving an interpretable view of the measured diversity.

A stochastic version of the assessment algorithm has computational complexity that grows linearly with sample count. Evaluations on image, text, and video datasets support its numerical scalability and interpretability. The contribution is therefore both computational and explanatory: it makes these diversity measures more practical at scale while helping users inspect the modes underlying the assessment.
summary.tldr: FKEA approximates reference-free diversity scores with linear sample-size scaling and interpretable information about generated modes.

title: Towards a Scalable Reference-Free Evaluation of Generative Models

abstract: We introduce \textbf{N}on-\textbf{Euc}lidean-\textbf{MDS} (Neuc-MDS), which extends Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) to generate outputs that can be non-Euclidean and non-metric. The main idea is to generalize the inner product to other symmetric bilinear forms to utilize the negative eigenvalues of dissimiliarity Gram matrices. Neuc-MDS efficiently optimizes the choice of (both positive and negative) eigenvalues of the dissimilarity Gram matrix to reduce STRESS, the sum of squared pairwise error. We provide an in-depth error analysis and proofs of the optimality in minimizing lower bounds of STRESS. We demonstrate Neuc-MDS's ability to address limitations of classical MDS raised by prior research, and test it on various synthetic and real-world datasets in comparison with both linear and non-linear dimension reduction methods.

Neuc-MDS efficiently optimizes the choice of (both positive and negative) eigenvalues of the dissimilarity Gram matrix to reduce STRESS, the sum of squared pairwise error. We provide an in-depth error analysis and proofs of the optimality in minimizing lower bounds of STRESS. paragraphs: Multidimensional scaling represents objects using their pairwise dissimilarities. Neuc-MDS extends this approach so the resulting representation can be non-Euclidean and even non-metric. This flexibility matters when the supplied dissimilarities contain structure that a conventional Euclidean representation does not capture well. The paper changes the geometry available to the method rather than requiring the output to use ordinary distances.

Its central step replaces the usual inner product with more general symmetric bilinear forms. That allows the representation to use negative as well as positive eigenvalues of the dissimilarity Gram matrix. The algorithm efficiently chooses among both kinds of eigenvalues to reduce STRESS, a measure of the summed squared errors in reconstructed pairwise relationships.

The authors analyze reconstruction error and prove optimality for minimizing lower bounds on STRESS. This is a specific theoretical result about those bounds, rather than a stated guarantee of globally minimizing STRESS itself. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets compare Neuc-MDS with linear and nonlinear dimensionality-reduction methods and demonstrate its ability to address previously identified limitations of classical MDS.
summary.tldr: Neuc-MDS uses more general geometry and both positive and negative eigenvalues to better represent pairwise dissimilarities.

title: Neuc-MDS: Non-Euclidean Multidimensional Scaling Through Bilinear Forms

abstract: This paper introduces a novel prior called Diversified Block Sparse Prior to characterize the widespread block sparsity phenomenon in real-world data. By allowing diversification on intra-block variance and inter-block correlation matrices, we effectively address the sensitivity issue of existing block sparse learning methods to pre-defined block information, which enables adaptive block estimation while mitigating the risk of overfitting. Based on this, a diversified block sparse Bayesian learning method (DivSBL) is proposed, utilizing EM algorithm and dual ascent method for hyperparameter estimation. Moreover, we establish the global and local optimality theory of our model. Experiments validate the advantages of DivSBL over existing algorithms.

paragraphs: Block sparsity describes data whose sparse structure occurs in groups. Learning that structure can be difficult when a method depends strongly on block information supplied beforehand. This paper introduces a Bayesian prior designed to make block sparse learning more flexible, addressing sensitivity to those predefined blocks while also mitigating the risk of overfitting.

The Diversified Block Sparse Prior allows variation in within-block variance and between-block correlation matrices. That flexibility enables adaptive estimation of the blocks instead of relying as heavily on the original block specification. The resulting method, DivSBL, uses an expectation-maximization algorithm together with dual ascent to estimate its hyperparameters.

The authors establish global and local optimality theory for the model and report experimental advantages over existing algorithms. The theoretical and empirical contributions address different aspects of the proposal: how the model behaves as an optimization problem and how it performs in the evaluated cases. The central idea is to make the prior's treatment of block structure adaptable while retaining a Bayesian learning formulation.
summary.tldr: DivSBL uses a more flexible Bayesian prior to estimate block sparsity adaptively and reduce dependence on predefined block information.

title: Block Sparse Bayesian Learning: A Diversified Scheme

abstract: Current text-to-image models struggle to render the nuanced facial expressions required for compelling manga narratives, largely due to the ambiguity of language itself. To bridge this gap, we introduce an interactive system built on a novel, dual-hybrid pipeline. The first stage combines landmark-based auto-detection with a manual framing tool for robust, artist-centric face preparation. The second stage maps expressions using the LivePortrait engine, blending intuitive performative input from video for fine-grained control. Our case study analysis suggests that this integrated workflow can streamline the creative process and effectively translate narrative intent into visual expression. This work presents a practical model for human-AI co-creation, offering artists a more direct and intuitive means of "infusing souls" into their characters. Our primary contribution is not a new generative model, but a novel, interactive workflow that bridges the gap between artistic intent and AI execution.

paragraphs: Panel-by-Panel Souls addresses the difficulty of communicating nuanced manga facial expressions through words. A text description can leave the intended emotion ambiguous, making it hard for image generation systems to express a particular narrative moment. The paper introduces an interactive workflow that lets artists guide expressions through performance.

The first stage prepares the face by combining automatic landmark detection with a manual framing tool. This gives the artist a role in establishing the facial region used by the system. The second stage uses LivePortrait to map expressions from video, bringing performed facial movements into the process as a source of fine-grained control.

Case study analysis suggests that the combined workflow can streamline creation and translate narrative intent into visual expressions effectively. The contribution is the integration of tools and artist interaction, rather than a newly developed generative model. Its significance is a more direct connection between the expression an artist performs and the expression assigned to a character, reducing reliance on verbal descriptions alone.
summary.tldr: An interactive manga workflow combines face preparation with video-driven expression mapping to help artists convey nuanced narrative intent.

title: Panel-by-Panel Souls: A Performative Workflow for Expressive Faces in AI-Assisted Manga Creation

abstract: The Mamba-type neural networks have gained significant popularity recently. To effectively and efficiently establish model architectures of Mamba, it is natural to introduce Neural Architecture Search (NAS) methods into Mamba. However, existing NAS methods tailored for Mamba are training-based, leading to substantial time and computational resource expenditure. To address this issue, and considering that Mamba2 is an improved version of the original Mamba, we propose a training-free NAS method specifically designed for Mamba2. Based on rank collapse in stacked State Space Duality (SSD) blocks, we design a proxy that only requires the computation of the transformation matrix and its gradient between two tensors within the network. Additionally, we develop a corresponding search space and introduce a novel approach for determining adjustable hyperparameter ranges. Experimental results show that our method outperforms all existing training-free NAS approaches in terms of both ranking correlation and the performance of search results for Mamba2 architecture. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first training-free NAS method designed for Mamba-type architectures. Our codes are available at https://github.com/fanyi-plus/tf-nas.

paragraphs: TF-MAS searches for effective Mamba2 architectures without training candidate networks as part of the search. Training-based architecture search can require substantial computation because assessing alternatives involves learning their parameters. The paper develops a proxy tailored to Mamba2 so candidates can be ranked through a cheaper architectural evaluation.

The proxy is motivated by rank collapse in stacked State Space Duality blocks. It requires computing a transformation matrix and its gradient between two tensors within the network. The authors also define a corresponding architecture search space and propose a method for choosing the ranges of adjustable hyperparameters, making the proxy part of a complete search procedure.

Experiments report better ranking correlation and better resulting architectures than all existing training-free search approaches evaluated for Mamba2. Ranking correlation concerns how effectively the proxy orders candidates, while search-result performance concerns the quality of the architectures ultimately selected. Improvements in both support the value of using a Mamba2-specific signal. The authors describe TF-MAS as, to their knowledge, the first training-free search method designed for Mamba-type networks.
summary.tldr: TF-MAS uses a rank-collapse-inspired proxy to search Mamba2 architectures without training candidates during search.

title: TF-MAS: Training-free Mamba2 Architecture Search

abstract: Learning from multi-agent expert demonstrations, known as Multi-Agent Imitation Learning (MAIL), provides a promising approach to sequential decision-making. However, existing MAIL methods including Behavior Cloning (BC) and Adversarial Imitation Learning (AIL) face significant challenges: BC suffers from the compounding error issue, while the very nature of adversarial optimization makes AIL prone to instability. In this work, we propose \textbf{M}ulti-\textbf{A}gent imitation by learning and sampling from \textbf{F}actor\textbf{I}zed \textbf{S}oft Q-function (MAFIS), a novel method that addresses these limitations for both online and offline MAIL settings. Built upon the single-agent IQ-Learn framework, MAFIS introduces the value decomposition network to factorize the imitation objective at agent level, thus enabling scalable training for multi-agent systems. Moreover, we observe that the soft Q-function implicitly defines the optimal policy as an energy-based model, from which we can sample actions via stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics. This allows us to estimate the gradient of the factorized optimization objective for continuous control tasks, avoiding the adversarial optimization between the soft Q-function and the policy required by prior work. By doing so, we obtain a tractable and \emph{non-adversarial} objective for both discrete and continuous multi-agent control. Experiments on common benchmarks including the discrete control tasks StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge v2 (SMACv2), Gold Miner, and Multi Particle Environments (MPE), as well as the continuous control task Multi-Agent MuJoCo (MaMuJoCo), demonstrate that MAFIS achieves superior performance compared with baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/LAMDA-RL/MAFIS.

paragraphs: Learning coordinated behavior from expert demonstrations poses difficulties for multi-agent systems. Behavior cloning can accumulate errors over successive decisions, while adversarial imitation methods can be unstable to optimize. MAFIS introduces a non-adversarial approach for both online and offline imitation, covering systems with discrete or continuous actions.

Building on IQ-Learn, the method uses a value decomposition network to break the imitation objective into agent-level components. This factorization supports scalable training. The authors also use the soft Q-function as an implicit energy-based description of the optimal policy. Actions can then be sampled through stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, providing a way to estimate the objective's gradient for continuous control.

The results support combining agent-level factorization with direct sampling as a tractable route to multi-agent imitation.
summary.tldr: MAFIS learns coordinated behavior from demonstrations through factorized soft Q-functions and action sampling, avoiding adversarial policy optimization.

title: Multi-Agent Imitation by Learning and Sampling from Factorized Soft Q-Function

abstract: Gene regulatory network inference (GRNI) aims to discover how genes causally regulate each other from gene expression data. It is well-known that statistical dependencies in observed data do not necessarily imply causation, as spurious dependencies may arise from *latent confounders*, such as non-coding RNAs. Numerous GRNI methods have thus been proposed to address this confounding issue. However, dependencies may also result from *selection*—only cells satisfying certain survival or inclusion criteria are observed—while these selection-induced spurious dependencies are frequently overlooked in gene expression data analyses. In this work, we show that such selection is ubiquitous and, when ignored or conflated with true regulations, can lead to flawed causal interpretation and misguided intervention recommendations. To address this challenge, a fundamental question arises: can we distinguish dependencies due to regulation, confounding, and crucially, selection? We show that gene perturbations offer a simple yet effective answer: selection-induced dependencies are *symmetric* under perturbation, while those from regulation or confounding are not. Building on this motivation, we propose GISL (Gene regulatory network Inference in the presence of Selection bias and Latent confounders), a principled algorithm that leverages perturbation data to uncover both true gene regulatory relations and non-regulatory mechanisms of selection and confounding up to the equivalence class. Experiments on synthetic and real-world gene expression data demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Gene expression measurements can show two genes varying together without one regulating the other. Hidden factors can create these associations, but so can observing only cells that survive or meet inclusion criteria. This paper argues that the latter mechanism, selection bias, is widespread and often overlooked, potentially distorting inferred regulatory networks and recommendations for intervention.

The authors use gene perturbations to distinguish these mechanisms. Their key observation is that dependencies induced by selection behave symmetrically under perturbation, whereas dependencies arising from regulation or confounding do not. This difference supplies information that observational associations alone cannot provide and motivates a method that explicitly separates regulatory and non-regulatory explanations.

The resulting algorithm, GISL, uses perturbation data to recover gene regulatory relations together with mechanisms of selection and hidden confounding. Recovery is up to an equivalence class, meaning the method can leave multiple explanations indistinguishable rather than always identifying one unique network. Experiments on synthetic and real gene expression data support its effectiveness in handling these competing sources of dependence.
summary.tldr: GISL uses gene perturbations to distinguish regulation, hidden confounding, and selection effects, recovering their structure up to an equivalence class.

title: Gene Regulatory Network Inference in the Presence of Selection Bias and Latent Confounders

abstract: Recent advances have significantly improved our understanding of the generalization performance of gradient descent (GD) methods in deep neural networks. A natural and fundamental question is whether GD can achieve generalization rates comparable to the minimax optimal rates established in the kernel setting. Existing results either yield suboptimal rates of $O(1/\sqrt{n})$, or focus on networks with smooth activation functions, incurring exponential dependence on network depth $L$. In this work, we establish optimal generalization rates for GD with deep ReLU networks by carefully trading off optimization and generalization errors, achieving only polynomial dependence on depth. Specifically, under the assumption that the data are NTK separable from the margin $\gamma$, we prove an excess risk rate of $\widetilde{O}(L^4 (1 + \gamma L^2) / (n \gamma^2))$, which aligns with the optimal SVM-type rate $\widetilde{O}(1 / (n \gamma^2))$ up to depth-dependent factors. A key technical contribution is our novel control of activation patterns near a reference model, enabling a sharper Rademacher complexity bound for deep ReLU networks trained with gradient descent.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether gradient descent training of deep ReLU classifiers can achieve generalization rates comparable to optimal kernel methods. Earlier results described in the abstract either improve only at an inverse-square-root rate with sample size or treat smooth activations with an exponential dependence on network depth. The authors seek a stronger rate for ReLU networks without that exponential depth cost.

Their theorem assumes the data are separable in the neural tangent kernel sense with margin gamma. Under this condition, they bound excess risk by approximately L^4(1 + gamma L^2)/(n gamma^2), suppressing logarithmic factors. Here L is depth and n is sample size. The result matches the optimal SVM-type inverse-sample-size rate up to depth-dependent factors, with only polynomial dependence on depth.

The proof carefully balances optimization error against generalization error. Its key technical step controls activation patterns near a reference model, enabling a sharper Rademacher complexity bound. The significance is a conditional theoretical guarantee connecting gradient descent with strong statistical rates for deep ReLU classification, while explicitly retaining the effects of depth and separation margin.
summary.tldr: Under NTK separability, gradient descent for deep ReLU classifiers achieves optimal sample-size generalization rates up to polynomial depth factors.

title: Optimal Rates for Generalization of Gradient Descent for Deep ReLU Classification

abstract: Graph machine learning architectures are typically tailored to specific tasks on specific datasets, which hinders their broader applicability. This has led to a new quest in graph machine learning: \emph{how to build graph foundation models (GFMs)} capable of generalizing across arbitrary graphs and features? In this work, we present a recipe for designing GFMs for node-level tasks from first principles. The key ingredient underpinning our study is a systematic investigation of the symmetries that a graph foundation model must respect. In a nutshell, we argue that label permutation-equivariance alongside feature permutation-invariance are necessary in addition to the common node permutation-equivariance on each local neighborhood of the graph. To this end, we first characterize the space of linear transformations that are equivariant to permutations of nodes and labels, and invariant to permutations of features. We then prove that the resulting network is a universal approximator on multisets that respect the aforementioned symmetries. Our recipe uses such layers on the multiset of features induced by the local neighborhood of the graph to obtain a class of graph foundation models for node property prediction. We validate our approach through extensive experiments on 29 real-world node classification datasets, demonstrating both strong zero-shot empirical performance and consistent improvement as the number of training graphs increases.

paragraphs: This paper develops a design recipe for graph foundation models that predict properties of individual nodes. Such models must transfer across graphs whose features and labels may be organized differently. The authors approach this problem by asking which changes in ordering should leave predictions unchanged or transform them in a corresponding way.

They argue that respecting node permutations alone is insufficient for their setting. The model should also respond consistently to permutations of labels and remain invariant to permutations of features within local neighborhoods. They characterize linear transformations satisfying these requirements and prove a universal approximation result for multisets that obey the specified symmetries.

The resulting layers process collections of features drawn from each node’s neighborhood. Experiments on 29 real-world node-classification datasets demonstrate strong zero-shot performance and consistent gains as training includes more graphs. The theoretical result concerns functions with the stated symmetries, while the experiments support the practical value of those design choices for transfer across node-prediction datasets.
summary.tldr: A symmetry-based architecture recipe produces graph models with strong reported zero-shot node classification across diverse datasets.

title: Equivariance Everywhere All At Once: A Recipe for Graph Foundation Models

abstract: Recent models such as OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek-R1 have demonstrated strong performance on reasoning-intensive tasks by generating extended Chain-of-Thought (CoT) traces. While longer reasoning helps with thorough exploration of solution paths for complex problems, it also often leads to inefficient and redundant outputs—a phenomenon commonly described as $\textit{overthinking}$. In this paper, we propose $\texttt{ShorterBetter}$, a simple yet effective reinforcement learning method that enables reasoning models to learn their own optimal CoT lengths without manual supervision. We define the $\textit{Sample Optimal Length}$ (SOL) as the length of the shortest correct response among multiple generations, which serves as a dynamic reward signal to guide the model toward efficient reasoning. Applied to DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B as base models, $\texttt{ShorterBetter}$ achieves 50\%-80\% reduction in output lengths in both in-domain and out-of-domain reasoning tasks while maintaining accuracy. Our reasoning trace analysis shows that $\texttt{ShorterBetter}$ refines the structure of the reasoning traces by reducing unnecessary repetition, excessive self-verification, and over-exploration of alternatives.

In this paper, we propose $\texttt{ShorterBetter}$, a simple yet effective reinforcement learning method that enables reasoning models to learn their own optimal CoT lengths without manual supervision. We define the $\textit{Sample Optimal Length}$ (SOL) as the length of the shortest correct response among multiple generations, which serves as a dynamic reward signal to guide the model toward efficient reasoning.
