title: ShorterBetter: Guiding Reasoning Models to Find Optimal Inference Length for Efficient Reasoning

abstract: End-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving models have demonstrated strong performance in open-loop evaluations but often suffer from cascading errors and poor generalization in closed-loop settings. To address this gap, we propose Model-based Policy Adaptation (MPA), a general framework that enhances the robustness and safety of pretrained E2E driving agents during deployment. MPA first generates diverse counterfactual trajectories using a geometry-consistent simulation engine, exposing the agent to scenarios beyond the original dataset. Based on this generated data, MPA trains a diffusion-based policy adapter to refine the base policy’s predictions and a multi-step Q value model to evaluate long-term outcomes. At inference time, the adapter proposes multiple trajectory candidates, and the Q value model selects the one with the highest expected utility. Experiments on the nuScenes benchmark using a photorealistic closed-loop simulator demonstrate that MPA significantly improves performance across in-domain, out-of-domain, and safety-critical scenarios. We further investigate how the scale of counterfactual data and inference-time guidance strategies affect overall effectiveness.

paragraphs: Model-based Policy Adaptation addresses a gap between evaluating driving predictions in isolation and letting those predictions control a vehicle over time. In closed-loop driving, earlier decisions influence later situations, allowing errors to cascade. The framework adapts pretrained end-to-end driving agents to improve robustness and safety under that feedback.

These examples train two components: a diffusion-based adapter that refines the base policy's predictions, and a multi-step Q-value model that evaluates longer-term outcomes. Experiments use nuScenes with a photorealistic closed-loop simulator and report significant improvements across familiar, out-of-domain, and safety-critical scenarios. The authors also examine how counterfactual-data scale and inference-time guidance affect performance. The results support combining simulated alternatives with longer-horizon evaluation to improve deployed policy decisions within the tested simulation setting, where the consequences of actions feed back into subsequent inputs.
summary.tldr: MPA improves pretrained driving agents in closed-loop simulation by generating candidate trajectories and selecting them using predicted long-term outcomes.

title: Model-Based Policy Adaptation for Closed-Loop End-to-end Autonomous Driving

abstract: Generating high-quality and photorealistic 3D assets remains a longstanding challenge in 3D vision and computer graphics. Although state-of-the-art generative models, such as diffusion models, have made significant progress in 3D generation, they often fall short of human-designed content due to limited ability to follow instructions, align with human preferences, or produce realistic textures, geometries, and physical attributes. In this paper, we introduce Nabla-R2D3, a highly effective and sample-efficient reinforcement learning alignment framework for 3D-native diffusion models using 2D rewards. Built upon the recently proposed Nabla-GFlowNet method for reward finetuning, our Nabla-R2D3 enables effective adaptation of 3D diffusion models through pure 2D reward feedback. Extensive experiments show that, unlike naive finetuning baselines which either fail to converge or suffer from overfitting, Nabla-R2D3 consistently achieves higher rewards and reduced prior forgetting within few finetuning steps.

Built upon the recently proposed Nabla-GFlowNet method for reward finetuning, our Nabla-R2D3 enables effective adaptation of 3D diffusion models through pure 2D reward feedback. Extensive experiments show that, unlike naive finetuning baselines which either fail to converge or suffer from overfitting, Nabla-R2D3 consistently achieves higher rewards and reduced prior forgetting within few finetuning steps.

paragraphs: Generating a 3D asset involves more than producing a plausible overall shape. The paper highlights remaining gaps in instruction following, alignment with human preferences, realistic textures, geometry, and physical attributes. It investigates whether reward-based adaptation can improve models that generate directly in 3D using feedback supplied entirely through 2D rewards.

Its contribution is to enable effective adaptation of 3D-native diffusion models from that 2D feedback. This connects the space in which assets are generated with a different space in which the optimization feedback is provided.

The experiments report higher rewards and less forgetting of the model’s prior behavior within a small number of finetuning steps. In the same comparisons, naive finetuning baselines either fail to converge or overfit. These findings support the framework’s effectiveness and sample efficiency for the evaluated alignment tasks. They also emphasize preserving prior behavior during adaptation, so that improving the targeted reward involves less loss of what the model had already learned.
summary.tldr: Nabla-R2D3 adapts 3D diffusion models using only 2D rewards, achieving higher evaluated rewards with less prior forgetting in few finetuning steps.

title: Nabla-R2D3: Effective and Efficient 3D Diffusion Alignment with 2D Rewards

abstract: We introduce Toto, a time series forecasting foundation model with 151 million parameters. Toto uses a modern decoder-only architecture coupled with architectural innovations designed to account for specific challenges found in multivariate observability time series data. Toto's pre-training corpus is a mixture of observability data, open datasets, and synthetic data, and is 4-10$\times$ larger than those of leading time series foundation models. Additionally, we introduce BOOM, a large-scale benchmark consisting of 350 million observations across 2,807 real-world time series. For both Toto and BOOM, we source observability data exclusively from our own telemetry and internal observability metrics. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that Toto achieves state-of-the-art performance on both BOOM and on established general purpose time series forecasting benchmarks. Toto's model weights, inference code, and evaluation scripts, as well as BOOM's data and evaluation code, are all available as open source under the Apache 2.0 License.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Toto, a 151-million-parameter foundation model for time-series forecasting, with particular attention to multivariate observability data. Its decoder-only architecture includes adaptations for challenges in this setting. The training corpus combines observability measurements, open datasets, and synthetic data, and is four to ten times larger than those of leading time-series foundation models.

The authors also introduce BOOM, a benchmark containing 350 million observations across 2,807 real-world time series. Both the model’s observability training data and the benchmark’s observability data come exclusively from the authors’ own telemetry and internal metrics. BOOM therefore provides a substantial evaluation resource grounded in those operational measurements.

Evaluations report state-of-the-art forecasting performance on BOOM and on established general-purpose benchmarks, indicating that Toto’s reported strengths extend beyond the newly introduced benchmark. The release includes model weights, inference and evaluation code, and BOOM’s data under Apache 2.0. Together, the model and benchmark support further work on forecasting observability signals and comparing performance across broader time-series tasks.
summary.tldr: Toto pairs observability-focused forecasting adaptations with large-scale pretraining and achieves reported state-of-the-art results on BOOM and general forecasting benchmarks.

title: This Time is Different: An Observability Perspective on Time Series Foundation Models

abstract: AI spans from large language models to tiny models running on microcontrollers (MCUs). Extremely memory-efficient model architectures are decisive to fit within an MCU's tiny memory budget e.g., 128kB of RAM. However, inference latency must remain small to fit real-time constraints. An approach to tackle this is *patch-based fusion*, which aims to optimize data flows across neural network layers. In this paper, we introduce *msf-CNN*, a novel technique that efficiently finds optimal fusion settings for convolutional neural networks (CNNs) by walking through the fusion solution space represented as a directed acyclic graph. Compared to previous work on CNN fusion for MCUs, msf-CNN identifies a wider set of solutions. We published an implementation of msf-CNN running on various microcontrollers (ARM Cortex-M, RISC-V, ESP32). We show that msf-CNN can achieve inference using 50% less RAM compared to the prior art (MCUNetV2 and StreamNet). We thus demonstrate how msf-CNN offers additional flexibility for system designers.

paragraphs: Running neural networks on microcontrollers requires fitting inference into extremely small memory budgets, sometimes around 128 kB of RAM. At the same time, applications may require results quickly enough for real-time operation. The paper focuses on patch-based fusion, which optimizes how data moves through convolutional-network layers to address these competing demands.

msf-CNN represents possible fusion configurations as a directed acyclic graph and searches that space for optimal settings. Its formulation exposes a wider range of solutions than previous microcontroller CNN-fusion methods. The stated benefit is additional design flexibility: a broader fusion search can uncover useful execution arrangements that make better use of scarce memory while keeping inference latency an explicit concern.
summary.tldr: msf-CNN searches a broader space of layer-fusion settings and demonstrates microcontroller inference using 50% less RAM than prior approaches.

title: msf-CNN: Patch-based Multi-Stage Fusion with Convolutional Neural Networks for TinyML

abstract: We propose to scale RL to unverifiable data with a novel algorithm JEPO (Jensen's Evidence lower bound for Policy Optimization). While most prior effort on scaling RL for LLMs focuses on verifiable data where ground truth answers are typically short-form and can be matched easily, we investigate the case where such assumptions are less valid (e.g., when answers are long-form such as mathematical proofs). To scale RL training to unverifiable data with contemporary training constraints, we propose JEPO. JEPO applies Jensen's evidence lower bound, a pragmatic simplification of the evidence lower bound which views chain-of-thought as a latent variable in the generative process. We show that on verifiable datasets (math), JEPO is as effective as RL with verifiable reward; on semi-verifiable and unverifiable datasets (numina and numina-proof), JEPO improves on soft-match based evaluations compared to RL with verifiable reward which can only leverage a subset of the data source as well as test set likelihood evaluations.

While most prior effort on scaling RL for LLMs focuses on verifiable data where ground truth answers are typically short-form and can be matched easily, we investigate the case where such assumptions are less valid (e.g., when answers are long-form such as mathematical proofs). To scale RL training to unverifiable data with contemporary training constraints, we propose JEPO. JEPO applies Jensen's evidence lower bound, a pragmatic simplification of the evidence lower bound which views chain-of-thought as a latent variable in the generative process. paragraphs: Reinforcement learning for language models often depends on answers that can be checked easily against a short ground truth. That setup becomes less suitable for long responses such as mathematical proofs. This paper introduces JEPO to extend training to data where straightforward answer verification is less applicable.

JEPO treats the model’s chain of thought as a latent variable in the process that generates an answer. It uses a Jensen-based evidence lower bound, described as a practical simplification of the evidence lower bound, to construct its policy optimization approach. This formulation gives the method a route to use data beyond the subset that supports conventional verifiable rewards, while accounting for contemporary training constraints.

On verifiable mathematics datasets, JEPO performs as effectively as reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. On semi-verifiable and unverifiable numina datasets, it improves soft-match evaluations over that comparison method, which can use only part of the available data, and also improves test-set likelihood evaluations. These findings support the broader training approach under the reported evaluation criteria; they do not establish automatic verification of long-form proofs.
summary.tldr: JEPO extends language-model reinforcement learning to less easily verified answers by treating reasoning as a latent variable.

title: Beyond Verifiable Rewards: Scaling Reinforcement Learning in Language Models to Unverifiable Data

abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion models have driven rapid progress in video editing techniques. However, video object removal, a critical subtask of video editing, remains challenging due to issues such as hallucinated objects and visual artifacts. Furthermore, existing methods often rely on computationally expensive sampling procedures and classifier-free guidance (CFG), resulting in slow inference. To address these limitations, we propose **MiniMax-Remover**, a novel two-stage video object removal approach. Motivated by the observation that text condition is not best suited for this task, we simplify the pretrained video generation model by removing textual input and cross-attention layers. In this way, we obtain a more lightweight and efficient model architecture in the first stage. In the second stage, we proposed a minimax optimization strategy to further distill the remover with the successful videos produced by stage-1 model. Specifically, the inner maximization identifies adversarial input noise ("bad noise'') that leads to failure removals, while the outer minimization trains the model to generate high-quality removal results even under such challenging conditions. As a result, our method achieves a state-of-the-art video object removal results using as few as 6 sampling steps without CFG usage. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of MiniMax-Remover compared to existing methods. Codes and Videos are available at: **https://minimax-remover.github.io**.

paragraphs: MiniMax-Remover targets video object removal, where unwanted objects must disappear without introducing replacement objects or visual artifacts. Existing diffusion-based approaches can also require costly sampling and classifier-free guidance. The paper proposes a two-stage method that simplifies the underlying model and then trains it to withstand noise patterns associated with removal failures.

An inner maximization searches for adversarial input noise that causes failures, while an outer minimization trains the model to produce good removals under that challenging noise.

The resulting system achieves reported state-of-the-art removal results with as few as six sampling steps and without classifier-free guidance. Experiments support the effectiveness of both the approach and its performance against existing methods. The central finding is that explicitly training against failure-inducing noise can accompany a lighter architecture and shorter sampling process.
summary.tldr: MiniMax-Remover simplifies video diffusion and trains against failure-inducing noise to achieve strong object removal in as few as six steps.

title: MiniMax-Remover: Taming Bad Noise Helps Video Object Removal

abstract: Generating realistic 3D human-object interactions (HOIs) remains a challenging task due to the difficulty of modeling detailed interaction dynamics. Existing methods treat human and object motions independently, resulting in physically implausible and causally inconsistent behaviors. In this work, we present HOI-Dyn, a novel framework that formulates HOI generation as a driver-responder system, where human actions drive object responses. At the core of our method is a lightweight transformer-based interaction dynamics model that explicitly predicts how objects should react to human motion. To further enforce consistency, we introduce a residual-based dynamics loss that mitigates the impact of dynamics prediction errors and prevents misleading optimization signals. The dynamics model is used only during training, preserving inference efficiency. Through extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments, we demonstrate that our approach not only enhances the quality of HOI generation but also establishes a feasible metric for evaluating the quality of generated interactions. Project website: https://wulin97.github.io/hoi-dyn

paragraphs: HOI-Dyn addresses the generation of three-dimensional motion involving a person and an object. Generating their movements independently can produce interactions that are physically implausible or inconsistent about what causes what. The framework instead represents an interaction as a driver-responder system, with human movement driving the object's response.

A lightweight transformer learns to predict how an object should react to human motion. This supplies an explicit interaction model during training. Because that predictor can itself make errors, the authors introduce a residual-based dynamics loss to reduce the impact of those errors and avoid misleading training signals. The dynamics model is used only during training, preserving generation-time efficiency.

Qualitative and quantitative experiments report improvements in generated interaction quality. The authors also present their approach as a feasible basis for evaluating generated interactions. Its significance is the use of learned response dynamics to connect the two motion streams: training can assess whether object movement fits the human action, alongside producing the movements themselves, without requiring the auxiliary predictor at inference.
summary.tldr: HOI-Dyn improves generated human-object motion by teaching object responses to follow human actions through a training-only dynamics model.

title: HOI-Dyn: Learning Interaction Dynamics for Human-Object Motion Diffusion

abstract: We introduce Eagle2.5, a frontier vision-language model (VLM) for long-context multimodal learning. Our work addresses the challenges in long video comprehension and high-resolution image understanding, introducing a generalist framework for both tasks. The proposed training framework incorporates Automatic Degrade Sampling and Image Area Preservation, two techniques that preserve contextual integrity and visual details. The framework also includes numerous efficiency optimizations in the pipeline for long-context data training. Finally, we propose Eagle-Video-110K, a novel dataset that integrates both story-level and clip-level annotations, facilitating long-video understanding. Eagle2.5 demonstrates substantial improvements on long-context multimodal benchmarks, providing a robust solution to the limitations of existing VLMs. Notably, our best model Eagle2.5-8B achieves 72.4\% on Video-MME with 512 input frames, matching the results of top-tier commercial model such as GPT-4o and large-scale open-source models like Qwen2.5-VL-72B and InternVL2.5-78B.

paragraphs: Eagle 2.5 develops a shared training framework for two demanding visual tasks: understanding long videos and interpreting high-resolution images. Both require a vision-language model to handle substantial visual context while retaining the details needed for useful answers. The work addresses these demands through post-training methods, training-pipeline improvements, and a dedicated video dataset.

The framework introduces Automatic Degrade Sampling and Image Area Preservation to retain contextual integrity and visual detail. It also includes efficiency optimizations for training with long inputs. Its Eagle-Video-110K dataset combines annotations describing an overall story with annotations describing individual clips, providing supervision at both broad and local levels of video understanding.

The authors report substantial improvements on long-context multimodal benchmarks. Their best eight-billion-parameter model scores 72.4% on Video-MME when given 512 frames, matching reported results for GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-VL-72B, and InternVL2.5-78B. This comparison shows the effectiveness of the combined framework on that evaluation, demonstrating that the reported benchmark performance is achievable with a considerably smaller model than those named open-source comparators.
summary.tldr: Eagle 2.5 combines long-context training improvements and video annotations to strengthen long-video and high-resolution image understanding.

title: Eagle 2.5: Boosting Long-Context Post-Training for Frontier Vision-Language Models

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various tasks but require substantial computational resources, limiting their deployment in resource-constrained environments. While one-shot pruning methods can reduce model size without expensive retraining, they typically optimize for single objectives, ignoring LLMs' multi-faceted applications. We introduce Multi-Objective One-Shot Pruning (MOSP), which formulates LLM pruning as a multi-objective optimization problem. MOSP efficiently generates a Pareto set of pruned models representing different capability trade-offs, allowing users to select solutions aligned with their preferences. The proposed approach identifies share core support while enabling specialized support. Experiments across various LLMs and sparsity levels demonstrate MOSP's superior performance in navigating multi-objective trade-offs compared to baseline methods.

MOSP efficiently generates a Pareto set of pruned models representing different capability trade-offs, allowing users to select solutions aligned with their preferences. paragraphs: Pruning removes parts of a language model to reduce its resource requirements. One-shot approaches aim to do this without expensive retraining, but they commonly optimize a single objective. This paper starts from the observation that language models serve multiple purposes, so a pruning decision that favors one capability may create an undesirable trade-off for another.

Multi-Objective One-Shot Pruning, or MOSP, formulates compression as a problem with several objectives. It generates a Pareto set of pruned models representing different capability trade-offs, giving users alternatives aligned with their preferences. The approach identifies shared core support while also allowing specialized support, so the resulting choices can reflect both common and capability-specific requirements.

Experiments across multiple language models and sparsity levels show better handling of multi-objective trade-offs than the compared baselines. The contribution is therefore a way to produce useful compression options, rather than treating one pruned model as the preferred answer for every application. Users can select among models according to the combination of capabilities they want to preserve.
summary.tldr: MOSP produces a Pareto set of pruned language models so users can choose compression outcomes that match their capability preferences.

title: Multi-Objective One-Shot Pruning for Large Language Models

abstract: Aerial-Ground person re-identification (AG-ReID) is an emerging yet challenging task that aims to match pedestrian images captured from drastically different viewpoints, typically from unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and ground-based surveillance cameras. The task poses significant challenges due to extreme viewpoint discrepancies, occlusions, and domain gaps between aerial and ground imagery. While prior works have made progress by learning cross-view representations, they remain limited in handling severe pose variations and spatial misalignment. To address these issues, we propose a Geometric and Semantic Alignment Network (GSAlign) tailored for AG-ReID. GSAlign introduces two key components to jointly tackle geometric distortion and semantic misalignment in aerial-ground matching: a Learnable Thin Plate Spline (LTPS) Transformation Module and a Dynamic Alignment Module (DAM). The LTPS module adaptively warps pedestrian features based on a set of learned keypoints, effectively compensating for geometric variations caused by extreme viewpoint changes. In parallel, the DAM estimates visibility-aware representation masks that highlight visible body regions at the semantic level, thereby alleviating the negative impact of occlusions and partial observations in cross-view correspondence. Extensive experiments on the challenging CARGO benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of GSAlign, achieving significant improvements of +18.8\% in mAP and +16.8\% in Rank-1 accuracy over previous state-of-the-art methods.

GSAlign introduces two key components to jointly tackle geometric distortion and semantic misalignment in aerial-ground matching: a Learnable Thin Plate Spline (LTPS) Transformation Module and a Dynamic Alignment Module (DAM). The LTPS module adaptively warps pedestrian features based on a set of learned keypoints, effectively compensating for geometric variations caused by extreme viewpoint changes. In parallel, the DAM estimates visibility-aware representation masks that highlight visible body regions at the semantic level, thereby alleviating the negative impact of occlusions and partial observations in cross-view correspondence. Extensive experiments on the challenging CARGO benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of GSAlign, achieving significant improvements of +18.8\% in mAP and +16.8\% in Rank-1 accuracy over previous state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Matching a person seen by an aerial camera with the same person seen from the ground is difficult because the views can show different poses, proportions, and visible body regions. Earlier cross-view representations remain limited when these differences are severe. GSAlign addresses both the geometric distortion and the mismatch in which body information is available.

Its Learnable Thin Plate Spline module uses learned keypoints to adaptively warp pedestrian features, compensating for changes in apparent geometry. Alongside this, a Dynamic Alignment Module estimates masks that emphasize visible body regions at the semantic level. Together, the modules seek to align comparable information while reducing the influence of occlusion and partial observations.

On the CARGO benchmark, the authors report improvements of +18.8% in mean average precision and +16.8% in Rank-1 accuracy over previous state-of-the-art methods. These results support the value of addressing geometric alignment and visibility together for aerial-ground matching. The evidence concerns this challenging benchmark and shows that explicitly handling viewpoint distortion can materially improve learned cross-view representations.
summary.tldr: GSAlign improves aerial-ground person matching by jointly correcting feature geometry and emphasizing visible body regions.

title: GSAlign: Geometric and Semantic Alignment Network for Aerial-Ground Person Re-Identification

abstract: Vehicle aerodynamics optimization has become critical for automotive electrification, where drag reduction directly determines electric vehicle range and energy efficiency. Traditional approaches face an intractable trade-off: computationally expensive Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations requiring weeks per design iteration, or simplified models that sacrifice production-grade accuracy. While machine learning offers transformative potential, existing datasets exhibit fundamental limitations -- inadequate mesh resolution, missing vehicle components, and validation errors exceeding 5% -- preventing deployment in industrial workflows. We present DrivAerStar, comprising 12,000 industrial-grade automotive CFD simulations generated using STAR-CCM+${}^{\textregistered}$ software. The dataset systematically explores three vehicle configurations through 20 Computer Aided Design (CAD) parameters via Free Form Deformation (FFD) algorithms, including complete engine compartments and cooling systems with realistic internal airflow. DrivAerStar achieves wind tunnel validation accuracy below 1.04% -- a five-fold improvement over existing datasets -- through refined mesh strategies with strict wall $y^+$ control. Benchmarks demonstrate that models trained on this data achieve production-ready accuracy while reducing computational costs from weeks to minutes. This represents the first dataset bridging academic machine learning research and industrial CFD practice, establishing a new standard for data-driven aerodynamic optimization in automotive development. Beyond automotive applications, DrivAerStar demonstrates a paradigm for integrating high-fidelity physics simulations with Artificial Intelligence (AI) across engineering disciplines where computational constraints currently limit innovation.

abstract: Designing algorithms for solving high-dimensional Bayesian inverse problems directly in infinite‑dimensional function spaces – where such problems are naturally formulated – is crucial to ensure stability and convergence as the discretization of the underlying problem is refined. In this paper, we contribute to this line of work by analyzing a widely used sampler for linear inverse problems: Langevin dynamics driven by score‑based generative models (SGMs) acting as priors, formulated directly in function space. Building on the theoretical framework for SGMs in Hilbert spaces, we give a rigorous definition of this sampler in the infinite-dimensional setting and derive, for the first time, error estimates that explicitly depend on the approximation error of the score. As a consequence, we obtain sufficient conditions for global convergence in Kullback–Leibler divergence on the underlying function space. Preventing numerical instabilities requires preconditioning of the Langevin algorithm and we prove the existence and form of an optimal preconditioner. The preconditioner depends on both the score error and the forward operator and guarantees a uniform convergence rate across all posterior modes. Our analysis applies to both Gaussian and a general class of non‑Gaussian priors. Finally, we present examples that illustrate and validate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Some Bayesian inverse problems naturally ask for an unknown function rather than a finite list of numbers. Algorithms should remain stable as numerical representations of that function become finer. This paper studies Langevin sampling for linear inverse problems directly in function space, using a score-based generative model to supply the prior.

The authors rigorously define the sampler in an infinite-dimensional setting and derive error estimates that explicitly account for inaccuracies in the learned score. These estimates yield sufficient conditions for global convergence measured by Kullback–Leibler divergence. The result connects the quality of the score approximation to the behavior of the sampler within the underlying function space.

The analysis also establishes the existence and form of an optimal preconditioner, which adjusts the dynamics to prevent numerical instability. It depends on both score error and the forward operator describing the measurements, and guarantees a uniform convergence rate across posterior modes within the analysis. The theory covers Gaussian priors and a general class of non-Gaussian priors, with examples illustrating and validating the findings.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes function-space convergence conditions and an optimal preconditioner for Langevin inverse-problem sampling with approximate learned scores.

title: Preconditioned Langevin Dynamics with Score-based Generative Models for Infinite-Dimensional Linear Bayesian Inverse Problems

abstract: Pseudo-label-based Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) often suffers from classifier bias, particularly under class imbalance, as inaccurate pseudo-labels tend to exacerbate existing biases towards majority classes. Existing methods, such as \textit{CDMAD}\cite{cdmad}, utilize simplistic reference inputs—typically uniform or blank-colored images—to estimate and correct this bias. However, such simplistic references fundamentally ignore realistic statistical information inherent to real datasets, specifically typical color distributions, texture details, and frequency characteristics. This lack of \emph{statistical representativeness} can lead the model to inaccurately estimate its inherent bias, limiting the effectiveness of bias correction, particularly under severe class imbalance or substantial distribution mismatches between labeled and unlabeled datasets. To overcome these limitations, we introduce the \textbf{FARAD} (Fourier-Adapted Reference for Accurate Debiasing) System. This system utilizes random-phase images, constructed by preserving the amplitude spectrum of real data while randomizing the phase spectrum. This strategy ensures two critical properties: (1) \textbf{Semantic Irrelevance}, as randomizing phase removes any structural or recognizable semantic cues, and (2) \textbf{Statistical Representativeness}, as preserving the amplitude spectrum maintains realistic textures, color distributions, and frequency characteristics. Grounded theoretically in classical Fourier analysis, the FARAD System provides a robust, accurate estimation of per-class biases. Furthermore, computational efficiency is enhanced through optimized real-to-complex (R2C) batched Fast Fourier Transforms (FFTs). Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our approach, significantly improves minority-class accuracy and overall SSL performance, particularly under challenging imbalance scenarios, compared with existing reference-based bias correction methods.

Some bias-correction methods probe the classifier using blank or uniformly colored images. The paper argues that these references poorly reflect real data statistics, which can make the estimated bias inaccurate.

The intended combination is realistic statistical characteristics without recognizable semantic content. Preserved amplitudes retain relevant texture, color, and frequency information, while phase randomization removes structural cues. The classifier's responses to these references are then used to estimate per-class biases.

The approach is grounded in Fourier analysis, and an optimized batched real-to-complex FFT implementation improves computational efficiency. Experiments report significant gains in minority-class accuracy and overall semi-supervised performance relative to existing reference-based correction methods, especially under difficult imbalance conditions. The findings support the importance of choosing statistically representative reference inputs when estimating and correcting classifier bias.
summary.tldr: FARAD uses Fourier-based reference images to estimate classifier bias and improve imbalanced semi-supervised learning.

title: Fourier Clouds: Fast Bias Correction for Imbalanced Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: Diffusion and flow matching models have significantly advanced media generation, yet their design space is well-explored, somewhat limiting further improvements. Concurrently, autoregressive (AR) models, particularly those generating continuous tokens, have emerged as a promising direction for unifying text and media generation, showing improved performance at scale. This paper introduces Transition Matching (TM), a novel discrete-time, continuous-state generative paradigm that unifies and advances both diffusion/flow models and continuous AR generation. TM decomposes complex generation tasks into simpler Markov transitions, allowing for expressive non-deterministic probability transition kernels and arbitrary non-continuous supervision processes, thereby unlocking new flexible design avenues. We explore these choices through three TM variants: (i) Difference Transition Matching (DTM), which generalizes flow matching to discrete-time by directly learning transition probabilities, yielding state-of-the-art image quality and text adherence. (ii) Autoregressive Transition Matching (ARTM) and (iii) Full History Transition Matching (FHTM) are partially and fully causal models, respectively, that generalize continuous AR methods. They achieve continuous causal AR generation quality comparable to non-causal approaches and potentially enable seamless integration with existing AR text generation techniques. Notably, FHTM is the first fully causal model to match or surpass the performance of flow-based methods on text-to-image task in continuous domains. We demonstrate these contributions through a rigorous large-scale comparison of TM variants and relevant baselines, maintaining a fixed architecture, training data, and hyperparameters.

paragraphs: Transition Matching offers a shared framework for diffusion, flow matching, and continuous autoregressive generation. It represents generation as a sequence of transitions between continuous states at discrete steps. Each transition can be probabilistic, and supervision need not follow a continuous process, expanding the choices available for designing a generative model.

The paper explores three variants. Difference Transition Matching generalizes flow matching by learning transition probabilities in discrete time. Autoregressive Transition Matching and Full History Transition Matching extend continuous autoregressive methods with partially and fully causal structures, respectively. These variants examine how different transition and information-access choices affect generation within the same overall framework.

The authors report state-of-the-art image quality and text adherence for Difference Transition Matching, while Full History Transition Matching matches or surpasses flow-based text-to-image performance in continuous domains. The causal variants also reach quality comparable to non-causal approaches. Integration with existing autoregressive text generation is presented as a potential benefit, rather than an already demonstrated outcome.
summary.tldr: Transition Matching unifies continuous generative approaches through discrete probabilistic transitions, with strong reported results for both causal and non-causal image generation.

title: Transition Matching: Scalable and Flexible Generative Modeling

abstract: We study the problem of creating strong, yet narrow, AI systems. While recent AI progress has been driven by the training of large general-purpose foundation models, the creation of smaller models specialized for narrow domains could be valuable for both efficiency and safety. In this work, we explore two challenges involved in creating such systems, having to do with basic properties of how neural networks learn and structure their representations. The first challenge regards when it is possible to train narrow models from scratch. Through experiments on a synthetic task, we find that it is sometimes necessary to train networks on a wide distribution of data to learn certain narrow skills within that distribution. This effect arises when skills depend on each other hierarchically, and training on a broad distribution introduces a curriculum which substantially accelerates learning. The second challenge regards how to transfer particular skills from large general models into small specialized models. We find that model skills are often not perfectly localized to a particular set of prunable components. However, we find that methods based on pruning can still outperform distillation. We investigate the use of a regularization objective to align desired skills with prunable components while unlearning unnecessary skills.

paragraphs: Building a small model for a narrow task sounds straightforward, but the paper identifies obstacles in how neural networks acquire and organize skills. It examines both learning a specialized model from scratch and extracting a desired skill from a larger general model. These routes encounter different aspects of the network’s internal representation.

In synthetic-task experiments, learning certain narrow skills sometimes requires training on a broader data distribution. The effect appears when skills depend on one another hierarchically. Broad training supplies a curriculum that substantially accelerates learning, meaning that examples outside the final narrow target can contribute to acquiring the capabilities that target depends on.

For skill transfer, the authors find that capabilities are often not perfectly confined to components that can simply be retained or pruned. Even so, pruning-based approaches can outperform distillation in their study. They also investigate regularization that aligns desired skills with prunable components while unlearning unnecessary ones. The results identify both hierarchical learning dependencies and distributed skill storage as challenges for creating strong specialized models.
summary.tldr: Synthetic experiments show how skill dependencies and distributed representations can complicate training or extracting narrowly specialized models.

title: On the creation of narrow AI: hierarchy and nonlocality of neural network skills

abstract: While deep learning methods have achieved strong performance in time series prediction, their black-box nature and inability to explicitly model underlying stochastic processes often limit their robustness handling non-stationary data, especially in the presence of abrupt changes. In this work, we introduce Neural MJD, a neural network based non-stationary Merton jump diffusion (MJD) model. Our model explicitly formulates forecasting as a stochastic differential equation (SDE) simulation problem, combining a time-inhomogeneous Itô diffusion to capture non-stationary stochastic dynamics with a time-inhomogeneous compound Poisson process to model abrupt jumps. To enable tractable learning, we introduce a likelihood truncation mechanism that caps the number of jumps within small time intervals and provide a theoretical error bound for this approximation. Additionally, we propose an Euler-Maruyama with restart solver, which achieves a provably lower error bound in estimating expected states and reduced variance compared to the standard solver. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that Neural MJD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art deep learning and statistical learning methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/DSL-Lab/neural-MJD.

paragraphs: Neural MJD forecasts time series by explicitly representing both evolving random variation and abrupt jumps. The motivation is that non-stationary data can change its behavior over time, while sudden changes pose an additional challenge. The model formulates prediction as simulation of a stochastic differential equation learned with neural networks.

Its continuous component is a time-dependent Itô diffusion, while a time-dependent compound Poisson process represents jumps. To make learning tractable, the authors cap the number of jumps considered within short intervals when computing the likelihood. They provide a theoretical bound on the error introduced by this approximation, connecting computational simplification to a quantified approximation cost.

The paper also introduces an Euler–Maruyama solver with restart. Relative to the standard solver, it has a provably lower error bound for estimating expected states and reduced variance. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art deep learning and statistical methods. The contribution combines an explicit model of changing stochastic behavior with learning and simulation procedures designed to make that model usable for forecasting.
summary.tldr: Neural MJD combines time-varying diffusion and jump processes with tractable learning and an improved solver for time-series forecasting.

title: Neural MJD: Neural Non-Stationary Merton Jump Diffusion for Time Series Prediction

abstract: Early-Exit Deep Neural Networks enable adaptive inference by allowing prediction at intermediary layers, significantly reducing computational costs and latency. Most of the early exit strategies greedily exit a sample at an intermediary layer if the confidence in class prediction exceeds a predefined threshold that is set using a static validation set. This is problematic as the model might be overconfident in a wrong class. Also, they are not robust to distribution shifts encountered in deployment, which can undermine model trustworthiness and accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose UAT that adapts the threshold for exit decisions using a Multi-Armed Bandit framework, enabling online, unsupervised adjustment of exit decisions. UAT makes decisions based on a new reward function that assesses predictive certainty and its reliability to balance computational efficiency and prediction quality while penalizing unnecessary late exits. We provide guarantees on risk achieved by UAT and validate its performance on diverse tasks spanning vision-language understanding, text generation, and classification. Our framework demonstrates consistent improvements in speedup $(1.70-2.10\times)$ with a minimal performance drop $(<2)$\% as compared to full model performance.

paragraphs: Early-exit networks can make predictions at intermediate layers, saving computation when further processing is unnecessary. A common rule stops whenever confidence exceeds a fixed threshold chosen on validation data. The paper addresses two weaknesses of this rule: a model can confidently predict the wrong class, and deployment data can differ from the data used to set the threshold.

The proposed method, UAT, adjusts exit thresholds online through a multi-armed bandit framework. Its adjustments are unsupervised, allowing the exit policy to adapt without labeled deployment examples. A new reward evaluates predictive certainty together with its reliability, balancing prediction quality against computation and penalizing exits that occur unnecessarily late.

They report speedups of 1.70–2.10 times with a performance reduction below 2% relative to the full model. These results support adapting exit decisions during use instead of relying entirely on a threshold fixed before deployment.
summary.tldr: UAT adapts early-exit thresholds online to balance reliable predictions with computational savings.

title: Beyond Greedy Exits: Improved Early Exit Decisions for Risk Control and Reliability

abstract: This paper presents **Pixel-Perfect Depth**, a monocular depth estimation model based on pixel-space diffusion generation that produces high-quality, flying-pixel-free point clouds from estimated depth maps. Current generative depth estimation models fine-tune Stable Diffusion and achieve impressive performance. However, they require a VAE to compress depth maps into the latent space, which inevitably introduces flying pixels at edges and details. Our model addresses this challenge by directly performing diffusion generation in the pixel space, avoiding VAE-induced artifacts. To overcome the high complexity associated with pixel-space generation, we introduce two novel designs: 1) **Semantics-Prompted Diffusion Transformers** (**SP-DiT**), which incorporate semantic representations from vision foundation models into DiT to prompt the diffusion process, thereby preserving global semantic consistency while enhancing fine-grained visual details; and 2) **Cascade DiT Design** that progressively increases the number of tokens to further enhance efficiency and accuracy. Our model achieves the best performance among all published generative models across five benchmarks, and significantly outperforms all other models in edge-aware point cloud evaluation. Project page: https://pixel-perfect-depth.github.io/.

paragraphs: Estimating depth from a single image can produce a depth map that looks plausible yet creates stray points around edges when converted into a point cloud. This paper attributes such flying-pixel artifacts in existing generative approaches to compressing depth maps through a variational autoencoder. Pixel-Perfect Depth instead performs diffusion directly in pixel space.

Direct generation avoids the identified compression artifacts but increases computational complexity. The model addresses this with two designs. Semantics-Prompted Diffusion Transformers use representations from vision foundation models to guide generation, maintaining global semantic consistency while improving fine details. A cascaded transformer design progressively increases the token count to improve efficiency and accuracy.

The authors report the best performance among published generative models across five benchmarks and significant gains over all other models in edge-aware point-cloud evaluation. The model also produces point clouds described as free of flying pixels. These findings connect the choice of generation space to the geometry of the output: preserving depth boundaries matters when an estimated map becomes a three-dimensional collection of points.
summary.tldr: Pixel-space diffusion guided by semantic features improves monocular depth estimation and avoids the VAE-induced flying pixels described in the paper.

title: Pixel-Perfect Depth with Semantics-Prompted Diffusion Transformers

abstract: We study pool-based active learning of half-spaces. We revisit the aggressive approach for active learning in the realizable case, and show that it can be made efficient and practical, while also having theoretical guarantees under reasonable assumptions. We further show, both theoretically and experimentally, that it can be preferable to mellow approaches. Our efficient aggressive active learner of half-spaces has formal approximation guarantees that hold when the pool is separable with a margin. While our analysis is focused on the realizable setting, we show that a simple heuristic allows using the same algorithm successfully for pools with low error as well. We further compare the aggressive approach to the mellow approach, and prove that there are cases in which the aggressive approach results in significantly better label complexity compared to the mellow approach. We demonstrate experimentally that substantial improvements in label complexity can be achieved using the aggressive approach, for both realizable and low-error settings.

paragraphs: Pool-based active learning chooses which examples in an available collection should receive labels. This paper studies that problem for halfspaces, classifiers defined by a linear separating boundary. It revisits an aggressive approach and asks whether it can be both computationally practical and supported by theoretical guarantees.

The main analysis concerns the realizable setting, where a suitable classifier can separate the pool correctly. Formal approximation guarantees apply when that separation has a margin. The authors also establish that there are cases in which the aggressive approach needs significantly fewer labels than a mellow approach, giving a theoretical reason to prefer it in some settings.

For pools with a small amount of unavoidable error, the paper introduces a simple heuristic for using the same algorithm. Experiments show substantial label-complexity improvements in both realizable and low-error settings. The distinction between these findings matters: the formal margin-based guarantees concern the realizable analysis, while successful use on low-error pools is supported through the heuristic and experiments.
summary.tldr: An efficient aggressive active learner can reduce label requirements for halfspaces, with margin-based guarantees and encouraging low-error experiments.

title: Efficient Active Learning of Halfspaces: an Aggressive Approach

abstract: We consider large-scale Markov decision processes (MDPs) with parameter uncertainty, under the robust MDP paradigm. Previous studies showed that robust MDPs, based on a minimax approach to handling uncertainty, can be solved using dynamic programming for small to medium sized problems. However, due to the "curse of dimensionality", MDPs that model real-life problems are typically prohibitively large for such approaches. In this work we employ a reinforcement learning approach to tackle this planning problem: we develop a robust approximate dynamic programming method based on a projected fixed point equation to approximately solve large scale robust MDPs. We show that the proposed method provably succeeds under certain technical conditions, and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulation of an option pricing problem. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to scale up the robust MDP paradigm.

paragraphs: Robust Markov decision processes handle uncertainty about model parameters through a minimax planning approach. Dynamic programming can solve smaller instances, but the number of states and decisions in realistic problems can make direct computation prohibitive. The paper tackles this scaling problem while retaining the robust treatment of uncertainty.

The authors develop an approximate dynamic programming method using ideas from reinforcement learning and function approximation. Its mathematical basis is a projected fixed-point equation. A simulation involving option pricing demonstrates its effectiveness in the application studied. summary.tldr: Function approximation extends robust MDP planning to larger problems, with conditional theoretical guarantees and an option-pricing simulation.

title: Scaling Up Robust MDPs using Function Approximation

abstract: Semi-NMF is a matrix factorization technique that learns a low-dimensional representation of a dataset that lends itself to a clustering interpretation. It is possible that the mapping between this new representation and our original features contains rather complex hierarchical information with implicit lower-level hidden attributes, that classical one level clustering methodologies can not interpret. In this work we propose a novel model, Deep Semi-NMF, that is able to learn such hidden representations that allow themselves to an interpretation of clustering according to different, unknown attributes of a given dataset. We show that by doing so, our model is able to learn low-dimensional representations that are better suited for clustering, outperforming Semi-NMF, but also other NMF variants.

paragraphs: Semi-NMF compresses data into a lower-dimensional representation that can be interpreted in terms of clusters. The paper starts from the possibility that the relationship between those clusters and the original measurements contains several levels of hidden structure. A single clustering layer may not make these underlying attributes understandable.

Deep Semi-NMF introduces a layered model for learning such representations. Its purpose is to capture hidden attributes at different levels, allowing the resulting representations to be interpreted as groupings according to different, initially unknown properties of the data. The contribution therefore concerns both how data is compressed and what the compressed representation can express.

The authors report that the learned low-dimensional representations are better suited to clustering than those produced by Semi-NMF and other NMF variants. The stated finding supports using a hierarchy of representations when a single grouping does not capture the structure of interest. It connects the model’s ability to express hidden attributes with improved clustering performance.
summary.tldr: Deep Semi-NMF learns layered representations that capture hidden clustering attributes and improve clustering over the compared factorization methods.

title: A Deep Semi-NMF Model for Learning Hidden Representations

abstract: Can we learn the influence of a set of people in a social network from cascades of information diffusion? This question is often addressed by a two-stage approach: first learn a diffusion model, and then calculate the influence based on the learned model. Thus, the success of this approach relies heavily on the correctness of the diffusion model which is hard to verify for real world data. In this paper, we exploit the insight that the influence functions in many diffusion models are coverage functions, and propose a novel parameterization of such functions using a convex combination of random basis functions. Moreover, we propose an efficient maximum likelihood based algorithm to learn such functions directly from cascade data, and hence bypass the need to specify a particular diffusion model in advance. We provide both theoretical and empirical analysis for our approach, showing that the proposed approach can provably learn the influence function with low sample complexity, be robust to the unknown diffusion models, and significantly outperform existing approaches in both synthetic and real world data.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to learn the influence of a group of people from observed information cascades in a social network. A common strategy first estimates a model of how information spreads and then calculates influence from that model. This makes influence estimates depend strongly on whether the chosen spreading model describes the real data correctly.

The authors instead learn the influence function directly. Their starting observation is that influence functions in many diffusion models have the structure of coverage functions. They represent such functions through convex combinations of random basis functions and fit this representation using an efficient maximum-likelihood algorithm applied to cascade data.

This approach avoids specifying a particular diffusion model beforehand while retaining a mathematical structure that supports analysis. The paper provides theoretical results showing learnability with low sample complexity and robustness to unknown diffusion models. It also reports significant improvements over existing approaches on synthetic and real-world data. The contribution is therefore both a direct estimation strategy and evidence that it can reduce dependence on an uncertain intermediate model.
summary.tldr: The paper learns social influence directly from cascades using coverage-function structure, avoiding the need to choose a diffusion model first.

title: Influence Function Learning in Information Diffusion Networks

abstract: Functional data, where samples are random functions, are increasingly common and important in a variety of applications, such as health care and traffic analysis. They are naturally high dimensional and lie along complex manifolds. These properties warrant use of the subspace assumption, but most state-of-the-art subspace learning algorithms are limited to linear or other simple settings. To address these challenges, we propose a new framework called Functional Subspace Clustering (FSC). FSC assumes that functional samples lie in deformed linear subspaces and formulates the subspace learning problem as a sparse regression over operators. The resulting problem can be efficiently solved via greedy variable selection, given access to a fast deformation oracle. We provide theoretical guarantees for FSC and show how it can be applied to time series with warped alignments. Experimental results on both synthetic data and real clinical time series show that FSC outperforms both standard time series clustering and state-of-the-art subspace clustering.

paragraphs: Functional observations are entire functions, such as time series, rather than simple fixed collections of measurements. They can be high-dimensional and follow complex geometric structure. Functional Subspace Clustering, or FSC, addresses this setting by assuming that samples lie in deformed linear subspaces, allowing the representation to account for transformations beyond an ordinary linear subspace.

The framework expresses subspace learning as sparse regression over operators. This places the transformations into the learning formulation, so clustering can reflect functional structure despite deformation. The resulting problem is solved through greedy variable selection, with efficient computation depending on access to a fast deformation oracle. That requirement is part of the stated computational setting.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees and applies FSC to time series with warped alignments, where corresponding patterns need not occur at matching time positions. Experiments on synthetic data and real clinical time series show better performance than standard time-series clustering and existing subspace-clustering methods. These findings support the value of explicitly modeling deformation for the evaluated functional clustering problems.
summary.tldr: FSC clusters functional data using deformed linear subspaces, with theoretical guarantees and empirical gains on synthetic and clinical time series.

title: Functional Subspace Clustering with Application to Time Series

abstract: Multi-task feature selection methods often make the hypothesis that learning tasks share relevant and irrelevant features. However, this hypothesis may be too restrictive in practice. For example, there may be a few tasks with specific relevant and irrelevant features (outlier tasks). Similarly, a few of the features may be relevant for only some of the tasks (outlier features). To account for this, we propose a model for multi-task feature selection based on a robust prior distribution that introduces a set of binary latent variables to identify outlier tasks and outlier features. Expectation propagation can be used for efficient approximate inference under the proposed prior. Several experiments show that a model based on the new robust prior provides better predictive performance than other benchmark methods.

paragraphs: Multi-task feature selection learns which inputs matter across several related prediction tasks. A common assumption is that the tasks agree about which features are useful and which are irrelevant. This paper addresses exceptions to that assumption: an individual task may need a different feature set, or a particular feature may matter to only some tasks.

The authors introduce a probabilistic model with a robust prior that explicitly represents both types of exception. Binary latent variables identify outlier tasks and outlier features. These hidden indicators let the model account for departures from shared relevance instead of requiring every task and feature to follow the same pattern.

The paper uses expectation propagation for efficient approximate inference under this prior. Several experiments show better predictive performance than the benchmark methods considered. The stated result supports allowing selective exceptions to shared feature structure: related tasks can still be modeled together while accommodating differences that a stricter sharing assumption would overlook.
summary.tldr: A robust probabilistic prior improves multi-task feature selection by explicitly modeling tasks and features that depart from shared relevance patterns.

title: A Probabilistic Model for Dirty Multi-task Feature Selection

abstract: We propose the contextual combinatorial cascading bandits, a combinatorial online learning game, where at each time step a learning agent is given a set of contextual information, then selects a list of items, and observes stochastic outcomes of a prefix in the selected items by some stopping criterion. In online recommendation, the stopping criterion might be the first item a user selects; in network routing, the stopping criterion might be the first edge blocked in a path. We consider position discounts in the list order, so that the agent’s reward is discounted depending on the position where the stopping criterion is met. We design a UCB-type algorithm, C^3-UCB, for this problem, prove an n-step regret bound \tildeO(\sqrtn) in the general setting, and give finer analysis for two special cases. Our work generalizes existing studies in several directions, including contextual information, position discounts, and a more general cascading bandit model. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the advantage of involving contextual information and position discounts.

paragraphs: This paper studies online decisions in which an agent chooses an ordered list but observes outcomes only until a stopping event. A recommendation list may stop yielding feedback at the first selected item; a route may reveal outcomes only as far as the first blocked edge. The agent also receives contextual information before choosing the list.

The model incorporates position discounts, so the reward depends on where the stopping event occurs. Ordering therefore affects more than which items are presented: it also affects how their outcomes contribute to reward. The authors combine contextual information, list selection, partial feedback, and position-dependent rewards in a broader cascading bandit formulation.

They propose C³-UCB, an algorithm based on upper confidence bounds, and prove a general regret bound growing as the square root of the number of steps, up to logarithmic factors. They also provide finer analyses for two special cases. Synthetic and real-data experiments demonstrate advantages from including context and position discounts, supporting the value of representing both in the learning problem.
summary.tldr: C³-UCB learns ordered lists using context, position-dependent rewards, and feedback that stops partway through the list.

title: Contextual Combinatorial Cascading Bandits

abstract: We investigate the performance of the standard Greedy algorithm for cardinality constrained maximization of non-submodular nondecreasing set functions. While there are strong theoretical guarantees on the performance of Greedy for maximizing submodular functions, there are few guarantees for non-submodular ones. However, Greedy enjoys strong empirical performance for many important non-submodular functions, e.g., the Bayesian A-optimality objective in experimental design. We prove theoretical guarantees supporting the empirical performance. Our guarantees are characterized by a combination of the (generalized) curvature $\alpha$ and the submodularity ratio $\gamma$. In particular, we prove that Greedy enjoys a tight approximation guarantee of $\frac{1}{\alpha}(1- e^{-\gamma\alpha})$ for cardinality constrained maximization. In addition, we bound the submodularity ratio and curvature for several important real-world objectives, including the Bayesian A-optimality objective, the determinantal function of a square submatrix and certain linear programs with combinatorial constraints. We experimentally validate our theoretical findings for both synthetic and real-world applications.

paragraphs: Greedy selection builds a set by repeatedly choosing an attractive next addition. It has strong guarantees for submodular objectives, which exhibit a diminishing-returns structure, but often also works well when that structure is absent. This paper develops guarantees for nondecreasing, non-submodular objectives when the number of selected items is constrained.

The analysis describes performance using two quantities: generalized curvature, alpha, and the submodularity ratio, gamma. Together they yield a tight approximation guarantee of (1 − exp(−gamma × alpha)) / alpha. This connects the strength of the greedy solution to measurable properties of the objective, providing a theoretical explanation for performance beyond the usual submodular setting.

The authors bound these quantities for several objectives, including Bayesian A-optimal experimental design, determinants of square submatrices, and certain linear programs with combinatorial constraints. Experiments on synthetic and real-world applications support the theoretical findings. The contribution gives objective-specific ways to assess greedy selection, with the guarantee depending on the curvature and submodularity ratio.
summary.tldr: A tight guarantee explains greedy maximization for non-submodular objectives through their curvature and submodularity ratio.

title: Guarantees for Greedy Maximization of Non-submodular Functions with Applications

abstract: We propose a new approach to the problem of neural network expressivity, which seeks to characterize how structural properties of a neural network family affect the functions it is able to compute. Our approach is based on an interrelated set of measures of expressivity, unified by the novel notion of trajectory length, which measures how the output of a network changes as the input sweeps along a one-dimensional path. Our findings show that: (1) The complexity of the computed function grows exponentially with depth (2) All weights are not equal: trained networks are more sensitive to their lower (initial) layer weights (3) Trajectory regularization is a simpler alternative to batch normalization, with the same performance.

Our approach is based on an interrelated set of measures of expressivity, unified by the novel notion of trajectory length, which measures how the output of a network changes as the input sweeps along a one-dimensional path. Our findings show that: (1) The complexity of the computed function grows exponentially with depth (2) All weights are not equal: trained networks are more sensitive to their lower (initial) layer weights (3) Trajectory regularization is a simpler alternative to batch normalization, with the same performance.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how network structure influences the functions a neural network can compute. It introduces a collection of related expressivity measures organized around trajectory length. The idea is to move the input along a one-dimensional path and measure how much the network's output changes during that movement.

This perspective provides a way to connect architecture to the complexity of the computed function. The authors report exponential growth in complexity with network depth through their approach. They also find that trained networks are more sensitive to weights in their initial layers, showing that weight changes at different depths do not have equivalent effects.

The paper then connects trajectory-based analysis to training through trajectory regularization. The authors report that it provides a simpler alternative to batch normalization with the same performance. Taken together, the findings use one organizing notion to study depth, differences between layers, and a training method. The complexity result concerns expressivity, while the regularization result concerns the reported performance of the proposed training alternative.
summary.tldr: Trajectory length links network expressivity to depth, reveals greater sensitivity to early-layer weights, and motivates a regularization alternative to batch normalization.

title: On the Expressive Power of Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Feature selection is an important challenge in machine learning. It plays a crucial role in the explainability of machine-driven decisions that are rapidly permeating throughout modern society. Unfortunately, the explosion in the size and dimensionality of real-world datasets poses a severe challenge to standard feature selection algorithms. Today, it is not uncommon for datasets to have billions of dimensions. At such scale, even storing the feature vector is impossible, causing most existing feature selection methods to fail. Workarounds like feature hashing, a standard approach to large-scale machine learning, helps with the computational feasibility, but at the cost of losing the interpretability of features. In this paper, we present MISSION, a novel framework for ultra large-scale feature selection that performs stochastic gradient descent while maintaining an efficient representation of the features in memory using a Count-Sketch data structure. MISSION retains the simplicity of feature hashing without sacrificing the interpretability of the features while using only O(log^2(p)) working memory. We demonstrate that MISSION accurately and efficiently performs feature selection on real-world, large-scale datasets with billions of dimensions.

paragraphs: Feature selection becomes difficult when datasets have billions of dimensions, because even storing a full feature vector can be infeasible. Feature hashing helps make computation manageable, but loses the interpretability of individual features. This paper addresses the need to select useful, identifiable features under severe memory constraints.

MISSION combines stochastic gradient descent with a Count-Sketch data structure that maintains an efficient representation of features in memory. The framework retains the simplicity associated with hashing while preserving feature interpretability. Its stated working-memory requirement is O(log²(p)), where p is the number of dimensions, allowing memory to grow slowly as dimensionality increases.

Experiments demonstrate accurate and efficient feature selection on real-world datasets with billions of dimensions. The result matters because the memory representation is part of what makes selection possible at this scale, rather than merely speeding up an already feasible full-vector method. The framework links large-scale learning with the ability to retain meaningful feature identities for understanding the selected inputs.
summary.tldr: MISSION uses Count-Sketches during stochastic gradient descent to select interpretable features from billion-dimensional data with very small working memory.

title: MISSION: Ultra Large-Scale Feature Selection using Count-Sketches

abstract: We establish geometric and topological properties of the space of value functions in finite state-action Markov decision processes. Our main contribution is the characterization of the nature of its shape: a general polytope (Aigner et al., 2010). To demonstrate this result, we exhibit several properties of the structural relationship between policies and value functions including the line theorem, which shows that the value functions of policies constrained on all but one state describe a line segment. Finally, we use this novel perspective and introduce visualizations to enhance the understanding of the dynamics of reinforcement learning algorithms.

To demonstrate this result, we exhibit several properties of the structural relationship between policies and value functions including the line theorem, which shows that the value functions of policies constrained on all but one state describe a line segment. Finally, we use this novel perspective and introduce visualizations to enhance the understanding of the dynamics of reinforcement learning algorithms.

paragraphs: A policy in reinforcement learning determines a value function describing expected returns from states. This paper studies the geometry of all value functions obtainable in a Markov decision process with finite state and action spaces. Its main result characterizes this space as a general polytope, giving the collection a concrete geometric structure.

The analysis develops structural relationships between policies and their values. One central result, the line theorem, fixes the policy at every state except one. As the remaining state's policy varies, the resulting value functions trace a line segment. This connects a restricted change in decision behavior to a simple shape in value-function space.

The authors use this geometric perspective to introduce visualizations of reinforcement learning dynamics. These visualizations aim to make the behavior of learning algorithms easier to understand by showing their relationship to the attainable value space. The contribution centers on the structure of that space and its explanatory uses, with the finite state-action setting defining the scope of the stated results.
summary.tldr: The attainable value functions of a finite Markov decision process form a general polytope, enabling geometric explanations of reinforcement learning.

title: The Value Function Polytope in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Many machine learning tasks such as multiple instance learning, 3D shape recognition, and few-shot image classification are defined on sets of instances. Since solutions to such problems do not depend on the order of elements of the set, models used to address them should be permutation invariant. We present an attention-based neural network module, the Set Transformer, specifically designed to model interactions among elements in the input set. The model consists of an encoder and a decoder, both of which rely on attention mechanisms. In an effort to reduce computational complexity, we introduce an attention scheme inspired by inducing point methods from sparse Gaussian process literature. It reduces the computation time of self-attention from quadratic to linear in the number of elements in the set. We show that our model is theoretically attractive and we evaluate it on a range of tasks, demonstrating the state-of-the-art performance compared to recent methods for set-structured data.
