paragraphs: Set Transformer addresses learning problems whose inputs are sets, where rearranging the elements should not change the answer. Examples in the abstract include multiple instance learning, 3D shape recognition, and few-shot image classification. The model is designed to capture interactions among set elements while respecting this requirement of permutation invariance.

Both its encoder and decoder use attention mechanisms. This makes relationships within the set part of the representation, allowing the model to account for how elements relate to one another. To reduce computational cost, the authors introduce an attention scheme inspired by inducing-point methods used in sparse Gaussian processes.

The proposed scheme reduces self-attention computation from quadratic to linear in the number of set elements. That change addresses the growing cost of processing larger sets while retaining an attention-based architecture. The authors report theoretical appeal and state-of-the-art performance against recent set-learning methods across a range of tasks, supporting the combination of interaction modeling, order invariance, and more efficient computation.
summary.tldr: Set Transformer models interactions in unordered inputs using attention, with a scheme that reduces self-attention cost to linear in set size.

title: Set Transformer: A Framework for Attention-based Permutation-Invariant Neural Networks

abstract: Solving for adversarial examples with projected gradient descent has been demonstrated to be highly effective in fooling the neural network based classifiers. However, in the black-box setting, the attacker is limited only to the query access to the network and solving for a successful adversarial example becomes much more difficult. To this end, recent methods aim at estimating the true gradient signal based on the input queries but at the cost of excessive queries. We propose an efficient discrete surrogate to the optimization problem which does not require estimating the gradient and consequently becomes free of the first order update hyperparameters to tune. Our experiments on Cifar-10 and ImageNet show the state of the art black-box attack performance with significant reduction in the required queries compared to a number of recently proposed methods. The source code is available at https://github.com/snu-mllab/parsimonious-blackbox-attack.

paragraphs: The paper studies adversarial examples when an attacker can query a classifier but cannot directly access its gradients. Gradient-based attacks can be effective when that information is available. In the black-box setting, estimating gradients through queries introduces a substantial cost, making the number of model queries a central practical concern.

The authors replace the original optimization problem with an efficient discrete surrogate. This changes the search procedure so that it does not need to estimate the gradient. As a consequence, it also avoids tuning the hyperparameters associated with first-order updates. The method’s contribution is therefore a different optimization formulation for finding adversarial examples under query-only access.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet report state-of-the-art black-box attack performance together with a significant reduction in required queries relative to several recently proposed methods. These findings support the discrete formulation as a query-efficient alternative in the tested settings. The reported gains concern both the effectiveness of the attack and the amount of classifier access needed to carry it out.
summary.tldr: A discrete optimization surrogate produces effective black-box adversarial attacks with fewer queries and no gradient estimation.

title: Parsimonious Black-Box Adversarial Attacks via Efficient Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: Making sense of Wasserstein distances between discrete measures in high-dimensional settings remains a challenge. Recent work has advocated a two-step approach to improve robustness and facilitate the computation of optimal transport, using for instance projections on random real lines, or a preliminary quantization of the measures to reduce the size of their support. We propose in this work a “max-min” robust variant of the Wasserstein distance by considering the maximal possible distance that can be realized between two measures, assuming they can be projected orthogonally on a lower k-dimensional subspace. Alternatively, we show that the corresponding “min-max” OT problem has a tight convex relaxation which can be cast as that of finding an optimal transport plan with a low transportation cost, where the cost is alternatively defined as the sum of the k largest eigenvalues of the second order moment matrix of the displacements (or matchings) corresponding to that plan (the usual OT definition only considers the trace of that matrix). We show that both quantities inherit several favorable properties from the OT geometry. We propose two algorithms to compute the latter formulation using entropic regularization, and illustrate the interest of this approach empirically.

We propose in this work a “max-min” robust variant of the Wasserstein distance by considering the maximal possible distance that can be realized between two measures, assuming they can be projected orthogonally on a lower k-dimensional subspace. Alternatively, we show that the corresponding “min-max” OT problem has a tight convex relaxation which can be cast as that of finding an optimal transport plan with a low transportation cost, where the cost is alternatively defined as the sum of the k largest eigenvalues of the second order moment matrix of the displacements (or matchings) corresponding to that plan (the usual OT definition only considers the trace of that matrix). We show that both quantities inherit several favorable properties from the OT geometry. We propose two algorithms to compute the latter formulation using entropic regularization, and illustrate the interest of this approach empirically.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to compare discrete probability distributions in high-dimensional spaces using optimal transport. Its first construction asks which lower-dimensional orthogonal projection makes two distributions as far apart as possible. The resulting max-min quantity seeks a subspace that preserves a strong distinction between the distributions.

The authors also study the corresponding min-max transport problem and establish a tight convex relaxation. In that formulation, a transport plan is scored using the sum of the largest k eigenvalues of a second-moment matrix built from its matching displacements. Ordinary transport instead uses the trace of that matrix, incorporating all its eigenvalues.

This gives the second formulation a cost based on the strongest k directions of displacement. Both quantities retain several favorable properties of optimal-transport geometry. The paper provides two algorithms using entropic regularization to compute the latter formulation and illustrates the approach empirically. Its contribution is a pair of subspace-oriented comparisons together with a tractable formulation and computational methods for the min-max version.
summary.tldr: Subspace-robust transport compares distributions through lower-dimensional projections and provides an eigenvalue-based convex formulation for the corresponding min-max problem.

title: Subspace Robust Wasserstein Distances

abstract: Nowadays, many problems require learning a model from data owned by different participants who are restricted to share their examples due to privacy concerns, which is referred to as multiparty learning in the literature. In conventional multiparty learning, a global model is usually trained from scratch via a communication protocol, ignoring the fact that each party may already have a local model trained on her own dataset. In this paper, we define a multiparty multiclass margin to measure the global behavior of a set of heterogeneous local models, and propose a general learning method called HMR (Heterogeneous Model Reuse) to optimize the margin. Our method reuses local models to approximate a global model, even when data are non-i.i.d distributed among parties, by exchanging few examples under predefined budget. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data covering different multiparty scenarios show the effectiveness of our proposal.

paragraphs: Multiparty learning combines information held by participants who face restrictions on sharing their data. Conventional approaches often train a global model from scratch through a communication protocol. This paper instead starts from the observation that participants may already have useful local models trained on their own datasets.

The proposed Heterogeneous Model Reuse method, or HMR, defines a multiparty multiclass margin to measure the collective behavior of those models. It then optimizes that margin to reuse the models in approximating a global predictor. The formulation accommodates heterogeneous local models and data that are not identically distributed across participants.

HMR exchanges a small number of examples within a predefined budget, so bounded example sharing is part of the method. Its contribution is to organize collaboration around existing models and a shared performance criterion. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data across different multiparty scenarios demonstrate effectiveness, supporting model reuse as a practical route to learning from distributed data.
summary.tldr: HMR combines heterogeneous existing local models through a multiparty margin objective and a predefined budget for sharing examples.

title: Heterogeneous Model Reuse via Optimizing Multiparty Multiclass Margin

abstract: In self-supervised visual representation learning, a feature extractor is trained on a "pretext task" for which labels can be generated cheaply, without human annotation. A central challenge in this approach is that the feature extractor quickly learns to exploit low-level visual features such as color aberrations or watermarks and then fails to learn useful semantic representations. Much work has gone into identifying such "shortcut" features and hand-designing schemes to reduce their effect. Here, we propose a general framework for mitigating the effect shortcut features. Our key assumption is that those features which are the first to be exploited for solving the pretext task may also be the most vulnerable to an adversary trained to make the task harder. We show that this assumption holds across common pretext tasks and datasets by training a "lens" network to make small image changes that maximally reduce performance in the pretext task. Representations learned with the modified images outperform those learned without in all tested cases. Additionally, the modifications made by the lens reveal how the choice of pretext task and dataset affects the features learned by self-supervision.

A problem arises when that task can be solved through superficial clues, such as watermarks or color aberrations. Success on the training task can then fail to produce representations that capture useful semantic information.

The paper proposes an automatic way to reduce these shortcuts. Its central assumption is that features exploited early in training may also be especially vulnerable to an adversary that makes the task harder. A separate lens network learns small image modifications chosen to maximally reduce performance on the pretext task. Training on the altered images therefore challenges the features supporting an easy solution.

Across the common pretext tasks and datasets tested, the authors find support for this assumption. Representations trained with lens-modified images outperform those trained without them in every tested case. The modifications also provide insight into which features different tasks and datasets encourage, making the lens both a training intervention and a way to inspect shortcut learning.
summary.tldr: An adversarial lens network makes small image changes that discourage shortcuts and improve self-supervised representations across the tested settings.

title: Automatic Shortcut Removal for Self-Supervised Representation Learning

abstract: Multi-step greedy policies have been extensively used in model-based reinforcement learning (RL), both when a model of the environment is available (e.g., in the game of Go) and when it is learned. In this paper, we explore their benefits in model-free RL, when employed using multi-step dynamic programming algorithms: $\kappa$-Policy Iteration ($\kappa$-PI) and $\kappa$-Value Iteration ($\kappa$-VI). These methods iteratively compute the next policy ($\kappa$-PI) and value function ($\kappa$-VI) by solving a surrogate decision problem with a shaped reward and a smaller discount factor. We derive model-free RL algorithms based on $\kappa$-PI and $\kappa$-VI in which the surrogate problem can be solved by any discrete or continuous action RL method, such as DQN and TRPO. We identify the importance of a hyper-parameter that controls the extent to which the surrogate problem is solved and suggest a way to set this parameter. When evaluated on a range of Atari and MuJoCo benchmark tasks, our results indicate that for the right range of $\kappa$, our algorithms outperform DQN and TRPO. This shows that our multi-step greedy algorithms are general enough to be applied over any existing RL algorithm and can significantly improve its performance.

paragraphs: Multi-step greedy policies have been widely used when reinforcement learning has access to an environment model. This paper brings their benefits into model-free learning through two dynamic programming methods: kappa-policy iteration and kappa-value iteration. They update policies or value functions by repeatedly solving an auxiliary decision problem.

That auxiliary problem uses a shaped reward and a smaller discount factor. Existing reinforcement learning methods can solve it, including methods for discrete and continuous actions such as DQN and TRPO. This makes the approach a general construction around an underlying learning algorithm. The authors also identify an important parameter controlling how thoroughly each auxiliary problem is solved and suggest how to choose it.

The findings support multi-step greedy updates as a way to improve existing learners, while making parameter choice part of the result. The reported gains depend on using a suitable range rather than holding uniformly across every setting.
summary.tldr: Multi-step greedy updates can improve model-free reinforcement learning by repeatedly solving shaped auxiliary problems with existing algorithms.

title: Multi-step Greedy Reinforcement Learning Algorithms

abstract: With a better understanding of the loss surfaces for multilayer networks, we can build more robust and accurate training procedures. Recently it was discovered that independently trained SGD solutions can be connected along one-dimensional paths of near-constant training loss. In this paper, we in fact demonstrate the existence of mode-connecting simplicial complexes that form multi-dimensional manifolds of low loss, connecting many independently trained models. Building on this discovery, we show how to efficiently construct simplicial complexes for fast ensembling, outperforming independently trained deep ensembles in accuracy, calibration, and robustness to dataset shift. Notably, our approach is easy to apply and only requires a few training epochs to discover a low-loss simplex.

paragraphs: Independently trained neural networks can reach different parameter settings with similarly low training loss. Earlier findings showed that pairs of such solutions can be connected by one-dimensional paths that keep loss nearly constant. This paper extends that picture by demonstrating multidimensional low-loss structures connecting many independently trained models.

The structures are simplicial complexes: collections of simple geometric pieces that form higher-dimensional regions in parameter space. Their existence means that useful connections among trained solutions can occupy more than a single curve. The authors use this observation to develop an efficient construction procedure aimed at fast ensembling.

The resulting ensembles outperform independently trained deep ensembles in accuracy, calibration, and robustness to dataset shift in the reported evaluation. The procedure needs only a few training epochs to discover a low-loss simplex. Together, these findings connect the geometry of the loss surface to a practical way of building ensembles with better predictive behavior and a short additional training procedure.
summary.tldr: Multidimensional low-loss connections between trained networks enable fast ensembles with improved accuracy, calibration, and robustness to dataset shift.

title: Loss Surface Simplexes for Mode Connecting Volumes and Fast Ensembling

abstract: Understanding the fundamental limits of robust supervised learning has emerged as a problem of immense interest, from both practical and theoretical standpoints. In particular, it is critical to determine classifier-agnostic bounds on the training loss to establish when learning is possible. In this paper, we determine optimal lower bounds on the cross-entropy loss in the presence of test-time adversaries, along with the corresponding optimal classification outputs. Our formulation of the bound as a solution to an optimization problem is general enough to encompass any loss function depending on soft classifier outputs. We also propose and provide a proof of correctness for a bespoke algorithm to compute this lower bound efficiently, allowing us to determine lower bounds for multiple practical datasets of interest. We use our lower bounds as a diagnostic tool to determine the effectiveness of current robust training methods and find a gap from optimality at larger budgets. Finally, we investigate the possibility of using of optimal classification outputs as soft labels to empirically improve robust training.

paragraphs: Evaluating adversarially robust learning requires knowing how well a classifier could perform under the same attack conditions. This paper derives optimal lower bounds on cross-entropy loss in the presence of test-time adversaries. Because the bounds do not depend on a particular classifier, they provide a reference for separating fundamental difficulty from shortcomings of a training method.

The authors formulate the bound as an optimization problem and identify the corresponding optimal classification outputs. The formulation also accommodates other losses that depend on soft classifier outputs, such as predicted probabilities. They develop a specialized algorithm for computing the lower bound efficiently and prove its correctness, making the theoretical benchmark usable on practical datasets.

Using these bounds diagnostically, the authors find that existing robust training methods remain above the optimum at larger adversarial budgets. This indicates room for improvement relative to the derived benchmark. They also investigate whether the optimal outputs can serve as soft training labels to improve robustness empirically, connecting the analysis of fundamental limits with a possible training intervention.
summary.tldr: Computable optimal loss bounds reveal gaps in robust training performance, especially at larger adversarial budgets.

title: Lower Bounds on Cross-Entropy Loss in the Presence of Test-time Adversaries

abstract: The pairwise interaction paradigm of graph machine learning has predominantly governed the modelling of relational systems. However, graphs alone cannot capture the multi-level interactions present in many complex systems and the expressive power of such schemes was proven to be limited. To overcome these limitations, we propose Message Passing Simplicial Networks (MPSNs), a class of models that perform message passing on simplicial complexes (SCs). To theoretically analyse the expressivity of our model we introduce a Simplicial Weisfeiler-Lehman (SWL) colouring procedure for distinguishing non-isomorphic SCs. We relate the power of SWL to the problem of distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs and show that SWL and MPSNs are strictly more powerful than the WL test and not less powerful than the 3-WL test. We deepen the analysis by comparing our model with traditional graph neural networks (GNNs) with ReLU activations in terms of the number of linear regions of the functions they can represent. We empirically support our theoretical claims by showing that MPSNs can distinguish challenging strongly regular graphs for which GNNs fail and, when equipped with orientation equivariant layers, they can improve classification accuracy in oriented SCs compared to a GNN baseline.

This paper introduces Message Passing Simplicial Networks, which operate on simplicial complexes to represent such structure. The aim is to extend both the relationships a model can handle and its ability to distinguish different structures.

The findings connect richer relational representations with formal distinguishing power and empirical benefits in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Message passing on simplicial complexes provides stronger structural expressivity than standard WL-based graph learning and supports improved empirical discrimination.

title: Weisfeiler and Lehman Go Topological: Message Passing Simplicial Networks

abstract: In this paper, we propose a natural notion of individual preference (IP) stability for clustering, which asks that every data point, on average, is closer to the points in its own cluster than to the points in any other cluster. Our notion can be motivated from several perspectives, including game theory and algorithmic fairness. We study several questions related to our proposed notion. We first show that deciding whether a given data set allows for an IP-stable clustering in general is NP-hard. As a result, we explore the design of efficient algorithms for finding IP-stable clusterings in some restricted metric spaces. We present a polytime algorithm to find a clustering satisfying exact IP-stability on the real line, and an efficient algorithm to find an IP-stable 2-clustering for a tree metric. We also consider relaxing the stability constraint, i.e., every data point should not be too far from its own cluster compared to any other cluster. For this case, we provide polytime algorithms with different guarantees. We evaluate some of our algorithms and several standard clustering approaches on real data sets.

paragraphs: This paper evaluates clustering from the perspective of each individual data point. Its proposed individual preference stability criterion requires a point to be closer, on average, to its own cluster than to any other cluster. This gives a concrete meaning to a point preferring its assigned group, with motivations from game theory and algorithmic fairness.

The authors first show that deciding whether an IP-stable clustering exists is NP-hard in general. They then identify settings where efficient exact algorithms are possible. One polynomial-time algorithm finds an exactly stable clustering for points on the real line. Another efficiently finds a stable division into two clusters when distances come from a tree metric.

The paper also studies relaxed stability, allowing a point’s average distance to its own cluster to be somewhat worse than its distance to another. It supplies polynomial-time algorithms with different guarantees for these relaxations and evaluates selected methods alongside standard clustering approaches on real datasets. The contribution connects an individually meaningful clustering requirement to its computational costs, showing where exact satisfaction or controlled relaxation can be achieved efficiently.
summary.tldr: Individual preference stability requires every point to favor its own cluster on average, with efficient algorithms available in restricted settings and for relaxations.

title: Individual Preference Stability for Clustering

abstract: The inaccessibility of the target domain data causes domain generalization (DG) methods prone to forget target discriminative features, and challenges the pervasive theme in existing literature in pursuing a single classifier with an ideal joint risk. In contrast, this paper investigates model misspecification and attempts to bridge DG with classifier ensemble theoretically and methodologically. By introducing a pruned Jensen-Shannon (PJS) loss, we show that the target square-root risk w.r.t. the PJS loss of the $\rho$-ensemble (the averaged classifier weighted by a quasi-posterior $\rho$) is bounded by the averaged source square-root risk of the Gibbs classifiers. We derive a tighter bound by enforcing a positive principled diversity measure of the classifiers. We give a PAC-Bayes upper bound on the target square-root risk of the $\rho$-ensemble. Methodologically, we propose a diversified neural averaging (DNA) method for DG, which optimizes the proposed PAC-Bayes bound approximately. The DNA method samples Gibbs classifiers transversely and longitudinally by simultaneously considering the dropout variational family and optimization trajectory. The $\rho$-ensemble is approximated by averaging the longitudinal weights in a single run with dropout shut down, ensuring a fast ensemble with low computational overhead. Empirically, the proposed DNA method achieves the state-of-the-art classification performance on standard DG benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Domain generalization trains on available source domains without access to the target domain. This makes it difficult to preserve features that will distinguish classes in the unseen setting. The paper studies classifier ensembles as a response to model misspecification and develops a theoretical connection between ensemble diversity and target-domain risk.

Using a pruned Jensen-Shannon loss, the authors bound an ensemble’s target square-root risk through averaged source square-root risks of sampled classifiers. They obtain a tighter bound by enforcing a particular positive diversity measure, then derive a PAC-Bayes upper bound. The relevance of diversity is therefore tied to a specified mathematical measure and risk formulation.

Their diversified neural averaging method approximately optimizes this bound. It draws classifier variation from both dropout and different points along the optimization trajectory. To keep prediction inexpensive, it approximates the ensemble by averaging weights across training with dropout disabled, using a single run. The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art classification performance on standard domain-generalization benchmarks, supporting the practical value of this theoretically motivated averaging approach.
summary.tldr: DNA uses a diversity-sensitive generalization bound to guide efficient neural averaging for unseen target domains.

title: DNA: Domain Generalization with Diversified Neural Averaging

abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with momentum is widely used for training modern deep learning architectures. While it is well-understood that using momentum can lead to faster convergence rate in various settings, it has also been observed that momentum yields higher generalization. Prior work argue that momentum stabilizes the SGD noise during training and this leads to higher generalization. In this paper, we adopt another perspective and first empirically show that gradient descent with momentum (GD+M) significantly improves generalization compared to gradient descent (GD) in some deep learning problems. From this observation, we formally study how momentum improves generalization. We devise a binary classification setting where a one-hidden layer (over-parameterized) convolutional neural network trained with GD+M provably generalizes better than the same network trained with GD, when both algorithms are similarly initialized. The key insight in our analysis is that momentum is beneficial in datasets where the examples share some feature but differ in their margin. Contrary to GD that memorizes the small margin data, GD+M still learns the feature in these data thanks to its historical gradients. Lastly, we empirically validate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Momentum is widely used to speed neural-network training, and it has also been associated with better generalization. Earlier explanations emphasized its effect on stochastic gradient noise. This paper examines another mechanism by showing empirically that momentum can improve generalization even with gradient descent, where the comparison does not depend on stochastic gradient sampling.

The authors construct a binary classification setting using an overparameterized convolutional network with one hidden layer. Under similar initialization, they prove that gradient descent with momentum generalizes better than gradient descent alone. The result is tied to this constructed setting and provides a concrete example in which optimization history changes what the network learns.

The key data property is a shared feature appearing in examples with different margins. In the analysis, ordinary gradient descent memorizes small-margin examples, while momentum continues to learn their shared feature by drawing on historical gradients. Empirical results validate the theoretical findings. This offers an explanation for momentum's generalization benefit based on feature learning, alongside previously proposed explanations involving noise stabilization.
summary.tldr: In a constructed classification setting, momentum improves generalization by using past gradients to learn shared features instead of memorizing small-margin examples.

title: Towards understanding how momentum improves generalization in deep learning

abstract: While reinforcement learning (RL) provides a framework for learning through trial and error, translating RL algorithms into the real world has remained challenging. A major hurdle to real-world application arises from the development of algorithms in an episodic setting where the environment is reset after every trial, in contrast with the continual and non-episodic nature of the real-world encountered by embodied agents such as humans and robots. Enabling agents to learn behaviors autonomously in such non-episodic environments requires that the agent to be able to conduct its own trials. Prior works have considered an alternating approach where a forward policy learns to solve the task and the backward policy learns to reset the environment, but what initial state distribution should the backward policy reset the agent to? Assuming access to a few demonstrations, we propose a new method, MEDAL, that trains the backward policy to match the state distribution in the provided demonstrations. This keeps the agent close to the task-relevant states, allowing for a mix of easy and difficult starting states for the forward policy. Our experiments show that MEDAL matches or outperforms prior methods on three sparse-reward continuous control tasks from the EARL benchmark, with 40% gains on the hardest task, while making fewer assumptions than prior works.

paragraphs: Many reinforcement learning systems practice in episodes, with the environment reset after each attempt. An embodied agent operating continuously must instead help create the conditions for its next trial. One approach alternates between a forward policy that attempts the task and a backward policy that resets the environment. This paper investigates which states that backward policy should aim to produce.

The proposed method, MEDAL, assumes access to a few demonstrations. It trains the backward policy to match the distribution of states appearing in those demonstrations. This keeps the agent near situations relevant to the task while supplying the forward policy with both easier and harder starting points. The demonstrations therefore guide the organization of continued practice through their state distribution.

Across three sparse-reward continuous control tasks from the EARL benchmark, MEDAL matches or exceeds the performance of prior methods. The abstract reports a 40% gain on the hardest task and fewer assumptions than earlier approaches. These findings support demonstration-based state matching as a useful way to organize autonomous trials in the evaluated non-episodic environments.
summary.tldr: MEDAL uses demonstration state distributions to train a reset policy that supports learning without externally reset episodes.

title: A State-Distribution Matching Approach to Non-Episodic Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The eXtreme Multi-label Classification (XMC) problem seeks to find relevant labels from an exceptionally large label space. Most of the existing XMC learners focus on the extraction of semantic features from input query text. However, conventional XMC studies usually neglect the side information of instances and labels, which can be of use in many real-world applications such as recommendation systems and e-commerce product search. We propose Predicted Instance Neighborhood Aggregation (PINA), a data augmentation method for the general XMC problem that leverages beneficial side information. Unlike most existing XMC frameworks that treat labels and input instances as featureless indicators and independent entries, PINA extracts information from the label metadata and the correlations among training instances. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the consistent gain of PINA on various XMC tasks compared to the state-of-the-art methods: PINA offers a gain in accuracy compared to standard XR-Transformers on five public benchmark datasets. Moreover, PINA achieves a $\sim 5$% gain in accuracy on the largest dataset LF-AmazonTitles-1.3M.
originalAbstract: The eXtreme Multi-label Classification (XMC) problem seeks to find relevant labels from an exceptionally large label space. Most of the existing XMC learners focus on the extraction of semantic features from input query text. However, conventional XMC studies usually neglect the side information of instances and labels, which can be of use in many real-world applications such as recommendation systems and e-commerce product search. We propose Predicted Instance Neighborhood Aggregation (PINA), a data augmentation method for the general XMC problem that leverages beneficial side information. Unlike most existing XMC frameworks that treat labels and input instances as featureless indicators and independent entries, PINA extracts information from the label metadata and the correlations among training instances. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the consistent gain of PINA on various XMC tasks compared to the state-of-the-art methods: PINA offers a gain in accuracy compared to standard XR-Transformers on five public benchmark datasets. Moreover, PINA achieves a $\sim 5$% gain in accuracy on the largest dataset LF-AmazonTitles-1.3M.

This paper argues that useful information also resides in label metadata and relationships among training instances, particularly in applications such as recommendations and product search.

PINA, or Predicted Instance Neighborhood Aggregation, is a data-augmentation method designed to use that side information. It extracts information from label descriptions or other metadata and from correlations between instances. This expands the evidence available to the classifier beyond treating each input and label as an isolated entry.

Experiments show consistent improvements across the evaluated extreme-classification tasks. PINA improves accuracy over standard XR-Transformers on five public benchmark datasets, including an approximately 5% gain on LF-AmazonTitles-1.3M, the largest dataset considered. The findings support incorporating relationships and metadata into the learning process. In this setting, improving prediction can come from making better use of the surrounding training information as well as the query text itself.
summary.tldr: PINA improves extreme multi-label classification by augmenting learning with label metadata and relationships among training instances.

title: PINA: Leveraging Side Information in eXtreme Multi-label Classification via Predicted Instance Neighborhood Aggregation

abstract: Solving large-scale multistage stochastic programming (MSP) problems poses a significant challenge as commonly used stagewise decomposition algorithms, including stochastic dual dynamic programming (SDDP), face growing time complexity as the subproblem size and problem count increase. Traditional approaches approximate the value functions as piecewise linear convex functions by incrementally accumulating subgradient cutting planes from the primal and dual solutions of stagewise subproblems. Recognizing these limitations, we introduce TranSDDP, a novel Transformer-based stagewise decomposition algorithm. This innovative approach leverages the structural advantages of the Transformer model, implementing a sequential method for integrating subgradient cutting planes to approximate the value function. Through our numerical experiments, we affirm TranSDDP’s effectiveness in addressing MSP problems. It efficiently generates a piecewise linear approximation for the value function, significantly reducing computation time while preserving solution quality, thus marking a promising progression in the treatment of large-scale multistage stochastic programming problems.

paragraphs: Multistage stochastic programming handles sequences of decisions under uncertainty. Common stagewise decomposition methods become increasingly expensive as subproblems grow or more problems must be solved. This paper introduces TranSDDP, a Transformer-based method intended to reduce the computational burden of constructing the value-function approximations used in that process.

These planes come from primal and dual solutions of stagewise subproblems. TranSDDP uses a Transformer to integrate cutting planes sequentially. It therefore applies learned sequence processing to the construction of the approximation while retaining a piecewise linear representation of the value function.

Numerical experiments show that TranSDDP efficiently generates these approximations and significantly reduces computation time while preserving solution quality. The result matters because the desired improvement is faster optimization with useful solutions, rather than speed alone. In the evaluated problems, the Transformer-based construction achieves that combination, supporting its potential for handling large multistage stochastic optimization problems.
summary.tldr: TranSDDP uses a Transformer to construct cutting-plane value approximations, reducing computation time while preserving solution quality in experiments.

title: Transformer-based Stagewise Decomposition for Large-Scale Multistage Stochastic Optimization

abstract: We introduce Neuro-Symbolic Continual Learning, where a model has to solve a sequence of neuro-symbolic tasks, that is, it has to map sub-symbolic inputs to high-level concepts and compute predictions by reasoning consistently with prior knowledge. Our key observation is that neuro-symbolic tasks, although different, often share concepts whose semantics remains stable over time. Traditional approaches fall short: existing continual strategies ignore knowledge altogether, while stock neuro-symbolic architectures suffer from catastrophic forgetting. We show that leveraging prior knowledge by combining neuro-symbolic architectures with continual strategies does help avoid catastrophic forgetting, but also that doing so can yield models affected by reasoning shortcuts. These undermine the semantics of the acquired concepts, even when detailed prior knowledge is provided upfront and inference is exact, and in turn continual performance. To overcome these issues, we introduce COOL, a COncept-level cOntinual Learning strategy tailored for neuro-symbolic continual problems that acquires high-quality concepts and remembers them over time. Our experiments on three novel benchmarks highlights how COOL attains sustained high performance on neuro-symbolic continual learning tasks in which other strategies fail.

paragraphs: This paper studies models that learn a sequence of tasks requiring both perception and symbolic reasoning. Each task maps low-level inputs to concepts and uses prior knowledge to produce predictions. A useful feature of this setting is that different tasks often share concepts whose meanings remain stable, even as the tasks themselves change.

Simply combining existing approaches does not fully solve the problem. Standard continual-learning strategies ignore knowledge, while ordinary neuro-symbolic models can forget earlier tasks. Combining the two helps with forgetting but can introduce reasoning shortcuts: predictions may fit the reasoning structure while the learned concepts acquire the wrong meanings. The authors show that detailed prior knowledge and exact inference do not by themselves prevent this failure.

The proposed strategy, COOL, focuses continual learning at the concept level so that useful concept meanings are acquired and retained. On three new benchmarks, it sustains high performance on tasks where other strategies fail. The findings make concept quality a central part of continual learning: preserving predictive behavior alone can leave the underlying concepts unsuitable for later tasks.
summary.tldr: COOL preserves concept meanings across neuro-symbolic tasks, addressing both forgetting and reasoning shortcuts that can survive exact inference.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Continual Learning: Knowledge, Reasoning Shortcuts and Concept Rehearsal

abstract: We address the challenge of exploration in reinforcement learning (RL) when the agent operates in an unknown environment with sparse or no rewards. In this work, we study the maximum entropy exploration problem of two different types. The first type is visitation entropy maximization previously considered by Hazan et al. (2019) in the discounted setting. For this type of exploration, we propose a game-theoretic algorithm that has $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(H^3S^2A/\varepsilon^2)$ sample complexity thus improving the $\varepsilon$-dependence upon existing results, where $S$ is a number of states, $A$ is a number of actions, $H$ is an episode length, and $\varepsilon$ is a desired accuracy. The second type of entropy we study is the trajectory entropy. This objective function is closely related to the entropy-regularized MDPs, and we propose a simple algorithm that has a sample complexity of order $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\mathrm{poly}(S,A,H)/\varepsilon)$. Interestingly, it is the first theoretical result in RL literature that establishes the potential statistical advantage of regularized MDPs for exploration. Finally, we apply developed regularization techniques to reduce sample complexity of visitation entropy maximization to $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(H^2SA/\varepsilon^2)$, yielding a statistical separation between maximum entropy exploration and reward-free exploration.

paragraphs: An agent with little or no reward feedback still needs a principled way to explore an unknown environment. This paper studies two entropy objectives: encouraging diverse visitation and encouraging diverse complete trajectories. Distinguishing these objectives matters because their statistical costs can have different dependence on the desired accuracy.

For visitation entropy, the authors first propose a game-theoretic algorithm whose sample complexity scales as H³S²A/ε², up to logarithmic factors. Here H is episode length, S and A count states and actions, and ε is the target error. For trajectory entropy, they exploit its connection to entropy-regularized decision processes to obtain a bound polynomial in S, A, and H, with inverse-linear dependence on ε.

The authors then apply regularization techniques to visitation entropy, improving its bound to H²SA/ε² up to logarithmic factors. They interpret the trajectory result as establishing a potential statistical advantage of regularization for exploration. The improved visitation result also establishes a statistical separation between maximizing exploration entropy and reward-free exploration, showing that these exploration goals need not demand the same amount of data.
summary.tldr: New entropy-exploration algorithms improve sample-complexity guarantees and establish potential statistical benefits from regularization.

title: Fast Rates for Maximum Entropy Exploration

abstract: We study efficient mechanisms for differentially private kernel density estimation (DP-KDE). Prior work for the Gaussian kernel described algorithms that run in time exponential in the number of dimensions $d$. This paper breaks the exponential barrier, and shows how the KDE can privately be approximated in time linear in $d$, making it feasible for high-dimensional data. We also present improved bounds for low-dimensional data. Our results are obtained through a general framework, which we term Locality Sensitive Quantization (LSQ), for constructing private KDE mechanisms where existing KDE approximation techniques can be applied. It lets us leverage several efficient non-private KDE methods—like Random Fourier Features, the Fast Gauss Transform, and Locality Sensitive Hashing—and “privatize” them in a black-box manner. Our experiments demonstrate that our resulting DP-KDE mechanisms are fast and accurate on large datasets in both high and low dimensions.

This paper develops private approximations whose running time depends linearly on dimension, addressing a major obstacle for high-dimensional data.

It allows existing techniques for approximating kernel densities to be converted into private mechanisms through a black-box construction. The authors apply this framework to Random Fourier Features, the Fast Gauss Transform, and Locality Sensitive Hashing, connecting private estimation to several established computational approaches.

The paper also improves theoretical bounds for low-dimensional data, so the contribution extends beyond changing the high-dimensional dependence. Experiments report fast and accurate private density estimates on large datasets in both dimensional regimes. Together, the results show how a reusable conversion framework can preserve useful computational advantages of non-private approximation methods while supplying differential privacy.
summary.tldr: Locality Sensitive Quantization converts existing density approximation methods into private mechanisms with linear rather than exponential dependence on dimension.

title: Fast Private Kernel Density Estimation via Locality Sensitive Quantization

abstract: Pedestrian trajectory prediction aims to predict future trajectories based on observed trajectories. Current state-of-the-art methods often assume that the observed sequences of agents are complete, which is a strong assumption that overlooks inherent uncertainties. Understanding pedestrian behavior when dealing with missing values in the observed sequence is crucial for enhancing the performance of predictive models. In this work, we propose the MultiScale hypergraph for Trajectory Imputation and Prediction (MS-TIP), a novel approach that simultaneously addresses the imputation of missing observations and the prediction of future trajectories. Specifically, we leverage transformers with diagonal masked self-attention to impute incomplete observations. Further, our approach promotes complex interaction modeling through multi-scale hypergraphs, optimizing our trajectory prediction module to capture different types of interactions. With the inclusion of scenic attention, we learn contextual scene information, instead of sole reliance on coordinates. Additionally, our approach utilizes an intermediate control point and refinement module to infer future trajectories accurately. Extensive experiments validate the efficacy of MS-TIP in precisely predicting pedestrian future trajectories. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Pranav-chib/MS-TIP.

paragraphs: Pedestrian trajectory prediction uses observed movement to estimate where people will go next. Many existing methods assume that the observation sequence is complete, even though missing positions create uncertainty about past behavior. MS-TIP addresses this issue by combining the reconstruction of missing observations with prediction of future trajectories.

The method uses transformers with diagonally masked self-attention to fill gaps in the observed sequence. Multi-scale hypergraphs then model different kinds of interactions, allowing prediction to account for complex relationships among pedestrians. A scenic-attention component learns contextual information from the scene, so the model's input goes beyond movement coordinates alone.

MS-TIP also uses an intermediate control point and a refinement module to infer future paths. The authors report extensive experiments supporting accurate trajectory prediction. The contribution brings several sources of information into a coordinated approach: incomplete movement history, interactions at different scales, and scene context. Treating observation repair as part of the prediction problem directly addresses the completeness assumption highlighted by the paper.
summary.tldr: MS-TIP jointly fills missing pedestrian observations and predicts future paths using interaction modeling and scene context.

title: MS-TIP: Imputation Aware Pedestrian Trajectory Prediction

abstract: We consider multiple senders with informational advantage signaling to convince a single self-interested actor to take certain actions. Generalizing the seminal Bayesian Persuasion framework, such settings are ubiquitous in computational economics, multi-agent learning, and machine learning with multiple objectives. The core solution concept here is the Nash equilibrium of senders’ signaling policies. Theoretically, we prove that finding an equilibrium in general is PPAD-Hard; in fact, even computing a sender’s best response is NP-Hard. Given these intrinsic difficulties, we turn to finding local Nash equilibria. We propose a novel differentiable neural network to approximate this game’s non-linear and discontinuous utilities. Complementing this with the extra-gradient algorithm, we discover local equilibria that Pareto dominates full-revelation equilibria and those found by existing neural networks. Broadly, our theoretical and empirical contributions are of interest to a large class of economic problems.

paragraphs: This paper studies persuasion when several informed senders try to influence the actions of one self-interested receiver. Each sender chooses a signaling policy, and those policies interact strategically. The central question is how to find a Nash equilibrium, where no sender benefits from unilaterally changing its policy.

The authors establish serious computational obstacles: finding an equilibrium in general is PPAD-hard, and even calculating one sender’s best response is NP-hard. These results motivate a shift toward finding local equilibria. The proposed method uses a differentiable neural network to approximate utilities that are nonlinear and discontinuous, and combines it with an extra-gradient optimization algorithm.

In the reported experiments, the method finds local equilibria that Pareto-dominate full-revelation equilibria and equilibria obtained using existing neural networks. Such comparisons indicate improved utilities without making another party worse off in the relevant comparison. The contribution pairs general computational hardness results with an empirical approach to finding beneficial local solutions, rather than claiming to efficiently solve every instance of the full equilibrium problem.
summary.tldr: After proving multi-sender persuasion is computationally hard, the paper uses neural utility approximation and extra-gradient optimization to find improved local equilibria.

title: Multi-Sender Persuasion: A Computational Perspective

abstract: Contrary to traditional deterministic notions of algorithmic fairness, this paper argues that fairly allocating scarce resources using machine learning often requires randomness. We address why, when, and how to randomize by offering a set of stochastic procedures that more adequately account for all of the claims individuals have to allocations of social goods or opportunities and effectively balances their interests.

paragraphs: This position paper considers fairness when machine learning helps distribute scarce social goods or opportunities. Scarcity means that allocation must balance competing individual claims. The authors argue that doing so fairly often requires randomness, challenging traditional approaches that treat a deterministic allocation rule as the basis for algorithmic fairness.

Their proposal is to make randomization part of the allocation procedure itself. The paper addresses three connected questions: why randomness can be appropriate, when it should be used, and how to incorporate it. It offers stochastic procedures intended to account more adequately for the claims individuals have on the available resources while balancing their interests.

The contribution is a position on what fair allocation should involve, together with procedures for putting that position into practice. It shifts attention toward how the allocation process treats competing claims, including through the chances it assigns. The argument is qualified: randomness is described as often required, rather than as a universal requirement for every allocation. Its focus is specifically on scarce-resource decisions that rely on machine learning.
summary.tldr: This position paper argues that fair machine-learning-assisted allocation of scarce resources often requires deliberate randomization to balance individual claims.

title: Position: Scarce Resource Allocations That Rely On Machine Learning Should Be Randomized

abstract: A large body of work has investigated the properties of graph neural networks and identified several limitations, particularly pertaining to their expressive power. Their inability to count certain patterns (e.g., cycles) in a graph lies at the heart of such limitations, since many functions to be learned rely on the ability of counting such patterns. Two prominent paradigms aim to address this limitation by enriching the graph features with subgraph or homomorphism pattern counts. In this work, we show that both of these approaches are sub-optimal in a certain sense and argue for a more fine-grained approach, which incorporates the homomorphism counts of all structures in the “basis” of the target pattern. This yields strictly more expressive architectures without incurring any additional overhead in terms of computational complexity compared to existing approaches. We prove a series of theoretical results on node-level and graph-level motif parameters and empirically validate them on standard benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can struggle to count structural patterns such as cycles, limiting the functions they can learn. One response is to add pattern counts to graph features. Existing approaches use either subgraph counts or homomorphism counts, which encode structural information through different kinds of pattern relationships.

This paper argues that both approaches are suboptimal in a particular sense when they do not use the full collection of relevant basis structures. The proposed alternative incorporates homomorphism counts for every structure in the target pattern’s basis. The key idea is that a richer set of related counts can expose distinctions that a coarser pattern description misses.

The authors prove that this construction yields strictly more expressive architectures without increasing computational complexity relative to existing approaches. They develop results for motif quantities defined at both node and whole-graph levels, then validate the theory on standard benchmarks. The result links a more careful choice of structural features to stronger representational power, while preserving the stated complexity level.
summary.tldr: Using homomorphism counts for all structures in a target pattern’s basis strengthens graph-network expressiveness without increasing the stated computational complexity.

title: Homomorphism Counts for Graph Neural Networks: All About That Basis

abstract: This paper addresses a policy optimization task with the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) objective. We introduce the predictive CVaR policy gradient, a novel approach that seamlessly integrates risk-neutral policy gradient algorithms with minimal modifications. Our method incorporates a reweighting strategy in gradient calculation – individual cost terms are reweighted in proportion to their predicted contribution to the objective. These weights can be easily estimated through a separate learning procedure. We provide theoretical and empirical analyses, demonstrating the validity and effectiveness of our proposed method.
originalAbstract: This paper addresses a policy optimization task with the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) objective. We introduce the predictive CVaR policy gradient, a novel approach that seamlessly integrates risk-neutral policy gradient algorithms with minimal modifications. Our method incorporates a reweighting strategy in gradient calculation – individual cost terms are reweighted in proportion to their predicted contribution to the objective. These weights can be easily estimated through a separate learning procedure. We provide theoretical and empirical analyses, demonstrating the validity and effectiveness of our proposed method.

paragraphs: Policy optimization trains a decision-making strategy by adjusting it according to an objective. This paper studies an objective based on conditional value-at-risk, or CVaR, which emphasizes costly outcomes in the adverse tail. The challenge is to incorporate that risk-sensitive objective into policy-gradient methods ordinarily used for risk-neutral optimization.

The proposed predictive CVaR policy gradient changes how individual cost terms contribute to the gradient. Each term receives a weight proportional to its predicted contribution to the CVaR objective. A separate learning procedure estimates these weights. The prediction therefore influences how strongly a cost term shapes the update to the policy.

This reweighting is designed to integrate with existing risk-neutral policy-gradient algorithms using only small modifications. The authors provide both theoretical and empirical analyses supporting the method’s validity and effectiveness. Its significance lies in connecting a risk-sensitive objective to an established optimization workflow: the gradient is redirected through learned contribution weights, providing a route to CVaR-focused learning without requiring a wholly separate policy-optimization framework.
summary.tldr: Predictive CVaR policy gradients adapt existing policy-gradient algorithms by weighting costs according to their predicted contribution to risk.

title: Risk-Sensitive Policy Optimization via Predictive CVaR Policy Gradient

abstract: Similar to natural language models, pre-trained genome language models are proposed to capture the underlying intricacies within genomes with unsupervised sequence modeling. They have become essential tools for researchers and practitioners in biology. However, the hand-crafted tokenization policies used in these models may not encode the most discriminative patterns from the limited vocabulary of genomic data. In this paper, we introduce VQDNA, a general-purpose framework that renovates genome tokenization from the perspective of genome vocabulary learning. By leveraging vector-quantized codebook as learnable vocabulary, VQDNA can adaptively tokenize genomes into pattern-aware embeddings in an end-to-end manner. To further push its limits, we propose Hierarchical Residual Quantization (HRQ), where varying scales of codebooks are designed in a hierarchy to enrich the genome vocabulary in a coarse-to-fine manner. Extensive experiments on 32 genome datasets demonstrate VQDNA’s superiority and favorable parameter efficiency compared to existing genome language models. Notably, empirical analysis of SARS-CoV-2 mutations reveals the fine-grained pattern awareness and biological significance of learned HRQ vocabulary, highlighting its untapped potential for broader applications in genomics.

paragraphs: Genome language models learn sequence structure without supervision, but their handcrafted tokenization rules may fail to capture the most discriminative genomic patterns. VQDNA treats tokenization itself as something to learn. Its aim is to build a vocabulary that adapts to genomic data, allowing the representation of sequences to reflect useful patterns rather than only predetermined token boundaries.

The framework uses a vector-quantized codebook as its learnable vocabulary and trains tokenization end to end. It also introduces Hierarchical Residual Quantization, or HRQ, which organizes codebooks of varying scales into a hierarchy. This enriches the vocabulary from coarse patterns to finer ones, giving the representation multiple levels of detail.

An empirical analysis of SARS-CoV-2 mutations also finds fine-grained pattern awareness and biological significance in the learned HRQ vocabulary. These results support learned genomic vocabularies as useful representations, while the paper presents broader applications in genomics as potential to explore.
summary.tldr: VQDNA learns genomic token vocabularies through vector quantization, using a coarse-to-fine hierarchy to capture biologically meaningful sequence patterns.

title: VQDNA: Unleashing the Power of Vector Quantization for Multi-Species Genomic Sequence Modeling

abstract: Robust Markov Decision Processes (RMDPs) have recently been recognized as a valuable and promising approach to discovering a policy with creditable performance, particularly in the presence of a dynamic environment and estimation errors in the transition matrix due to limited data. Despite extensive exploration of dynamic programming algorithms for solving RMDPs, there has been a notable upswing in interest in developing efficient algorithms using the policy gradient method. In this paper, we propose the first single-loop robust policy gradient (SRPG) method with the global optimality guarantee for solving RMDPs through its minimax formulation. Moreover, we complement the convergence analysis of the nonconvex-nonconcave min-max optimization problem with the objective function’s gradient dominance property, which is not explored in the prior literature. Numerical experiments validate the efficacy of SRPG, demonstrating its faster and more robust convergence behavior compared to its nested-loop counterpart.

paragraphs: Robust Markov decision processes seek policies that perform reliably when an environment’s dynamics are uncertain. This uncertainty can arise because the environment changes or because limited data produces inaccurate transition estimates. The paper studies how to solve these problems by directly improving the policy through gradient updates.

The proposed Single-loop Robust Policy Gradient method, or SRPG, works with a minimax formulation: policy optimization accounts for unfavorable dynamics within the robust problem. Its distinguishing feature is a single optimization loop, together with a global optimality guarantee. The analysis addresses a nonconvex, nonconcave optimization problem and uses a gradient dominance property of the objective to establish convergence results.

Numerical experiments report faster and more robust convergence than a nested-loop counterpart. The contribution therefore combines an algorithmic simplification with theoretical support for reaching a globally optimal solution in the studied formulation. Its practical significance is that robust policy optimization can avoid a nested-loop organization while retaining a global guarantee.
summary.tldr: SRPG uses a single optimization loop to solve robust policy problems with a global optimality guarantee and improved convergence in numerical experiments.

title: A Single-Loop Robust Policy Gradient Method for Robust Markov Decision Processes

abstract: The consistency of a learning method is usually established under the assumption that the observations are a realization of an independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) or mixing process. Yet, kernel methods such as support vector machines (SVMs), Gaussian processes, or conditional kernel mean embeddings (CKMEs) all give excellent performance under sampling schemes that are obviously non-i.i.d., such as when data comes from a dynamical system. We propose the new notion of empirical weak convergence (EWC) as a general assumption explaining such phenomena for kernel methods. It assumes the existence of a random asymptotic data distribution and is a strict weakening of previous assumptions in the field. Our main results then establish consistency of SVMs, kernel mean embeddings, and general Hilbert-space valued empirical expectations with EWC data. Our analysis holds for both finite- and infinite-dimensional outputs, as we extend classical results of statistical learning to the latter case. In particular, it is also applicable to CKMEs. Overall, our results open new classes of processes to statistical learning and can serve as a foundation for a theory of learning beyond i.i.d. and mixing.

The guarantees still rely on empirical weak convergence, providing a specified route beyond independent or mixing observations rather than a claim about arbitrary dependence.
summary.tldr: Empirical weak convergence provides a weaker assumption under which several kernel methods remain consistent with dependent observations.

title: On the Consistency of Kernel Methods with Dependent Observations

abstract: In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), agents collaborate to achieve common goals, such as defeating enemies and scoring a goal. However, learning goal-reaching paths toward such a semantic goal takes a considerable amount of time in complex tasks and the trained model often fails to find such paths. To address this, we present LAtent Goal-guided Multi-Agent reinforcement learning (LAGMA), which generates a goal-reaching trajectory in latent space and provides a latent goal-guided incentive to transitions toward this reference trajectory. LAGMA consists of three major components: (a) quantized latent space constructed via a modified VQ-VAE for efficient sample utilization, (b) goal-reaching trajectory generation via extended VQ codebook, and (c) latent goal-guided intrinsic reward generation to encourage transitions towards the sampled goal-reaching path. The proposed method is evaluated by StarCraft II with both dense and sparse reward settings and Google Research Football. Empirical results show further performance improvement over state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Cooperating reinforcement learning agents may share a clear objective while struggling to discover a sequence of actions that reaches it. In complex tasks, learning these paths can take considerable time, and trained agents may still fail to find them. LAGMA addresses this difficulty by giving learning agents a reference path toward the goal.

The reference path is constructed in a learned latent space, a compact representation of the task. A modified vector-quantized variational autoencoder builds a quantized space to support efficient use of samples. An extended codebook then generates goal-reaching trajectories within that space. Finally, an intrinsic reward encourages transitions toward a sampled trajectory, providing an additional training incentive linked to progress along the reference path.

The authors evaluate LAGMA in StarCraft II with both dense and sparse rewards, as well as Google Research Football. They report improved performance over state-of-the-art baselines in these experiments. The findings support combining a compact learned representation, goal-path generation, and internal reward guidance to help teams learn how to reach shared objectives.
summary.tldr: LAGMA guides cooperating agents with goal-reaching paths in a learned latent space and rewards progress toward those paths.

title: LAGMA: LAtent Goal-guided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The discovery of new catalysts is essential for the design of new and more efficient chemical processes in order to transition to a sustainable future. We introduce an AI-guided computational screening framework unifying linguistic reasoning with quantum-chemistry based feedback from 3D atomistic representations. Our approach formulates catalyst discovery as an uncertain environment where an agent actively searches for highly effective catalysts via the iterative combination of large language model (LLM)-derived hypotheses and atomistic graph neural network (GNN)-derived feedback. Identified catalysts in intermediate search steps undergo structural evaluation based on spatial orientation, reaction pathways, and stability. Scoring functions based on adsorption energies and reaction energy barriers steer the exploration in the LLM’s knowledge space toward energetically favorable, high-efficiency catalysts. We introduce planning methods that automatically guide the exploration without human input, providing competitive performance against expert-enumerated chemical descriptor-based implementations. By integrating language-guided reasoning with computational chemistry feedback, our work pioneers AI-accelerated, trustworthy catalyst discovery.

paragraphs: CHEMREASONER approaches catalyst discovery as an iterative computational search. This connects reasoning expressed in language with evaluations grounded in three-dimensional atomic structures, giving the search a way to revise its direction as evidence accumulates.

Candidates encountered during the search undergo structural evaluation that considers spatial orientation, reaction pathways, and stability. Scores based on adsorption energies and reaction energy barriers then guide further exploration. These quantities connect candidate selection to the energetics of the chemical process, so the language model’s suggestions are assessed using more than their linguistic plausibility.

The paper also introduces planning methods that guide exploration automatically, without human input during that exploration. The authors report competitive performance against implementations built around chemical descriptors enumerated by experts. The contribution is a computational screening framework that combines proposal generation, structural evaluation, and energy-based feedback to search for promising catalysts.
summary.tldr: CHEMREASONER combines language-model hypotheses with atomistic chemical feedback to automatically search for promising catalysts.

title: CHEMREASONER: Heuristic Search over a Large Language Model’s Knowledge Space using Quantum-Chemical Feedback

abstract: In cross-domain few-shot classification, nearest centroid classifier (NCC) aims to learn representations to construct a metric space where few-shot classification can be performed by measuring the similarities between samples and the prototype of each class. An intuition behind NCC is that each sample is pulled closer to the class centroid it belongs to while pushed away from those of other classes. However, in this paper, we find that there exist high similarities between NCC-learned representations of two samples from different classes. In order to address this problem, we propose a bi-level optimization framework, maximizing optimized kernel dependence (MOKD) to learn a set of class-specific representations that match the cluster structures indicated by labeled data of the given task. Specifically, MOKD first optimizes the kernel adopted in Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion (HSIC) to obtain the optimized kernel HSIC (opt-HSIC) that can capture the dependence more precisely. Then, an optimization problem regarding the opt-HSIC is addressed to simultaneously maximize the dependence between representations and labels and minimize the dependence among all samples. Extensive experiments on Meta-Dataset demonstrate that MOKD can not only achieve better generalization performance on unseen domains in most cases but also learn better data representation clusters. The project repository of MOKD is available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/MOKD.

paragraphs: In cross-domain few-shot classification, a model must adapt to a task using few labeled examples. A nearest-centroid classifier compares representations with a prototype for each class. The paper finds that representations learned this way can still make examples from different classes highly similar, despite the intended separation around class centers.

MOKD addresses this with a two-level optimization framework built around the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion, a measure of statistical dependence. First, it optimizes the kernel used by that criterion to measure dependence more precisely. It then uses the optimized criterion to increase dependence between representations and labels while decreasing dependence among samples.

The intended result is a representation whose clusters better reflect the class structure shown by the task’s labeled examples. Experiments on Meta-Dataset find better generalization to unseen domains in most cases, along with improved representation clusters. The qualification matters: the reported gains are not universal across every domain. The approach focuses adaptation on the relationship between labels, samples, and cluster structure, going beyond similarity to a class prototype alone.
summary.tldr: MOKD optimizes a kernel-based dependence objective to improve few-shot representation clusters and generalization to unseen domains in most evaluated cases.

title: MOKD: Cross-domain Finetuning for Few-shot Classification via Maximizing Optimized Kernel Dependence

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL), which seeks to learn an optimal policy using offline data, has garnered significant interest due to its potential in critical applications where online data collection is infeasible or expensive. This work explores the benefit of federated learning for offline RL, aiming at collaboratively leveraging offline datasets at multiple agents. Focusing on finite-horizon episodic tabular Markov decision processes (MDPs), we design FedLCB-Q, a variant of the popular model-free Q-learning algorithm tailored for federated offline RL. FedLCB-Q updates local Q-functions at agents with novel learning rate schedules and aggregates them at a central server using importance averaging and a carefully designed pessimistic penalty term. Our sample complexity analysis reveals that, with appropriately chosen parameters and synchronization schedules, FedLCB-Q achieves linear speedup in terms of the number of agents without requiring high-quality datasets at individual agents, as long as the local datasets collectively cover the state-action space visited by the optimal policy, highlighting the power of collaboration in the federated setting. In fact, the sample complexity almost matches that of the single-agent counterpart, as if all the data are stored at a central location, up to polynomial factors of the horizon length. Furthermore, FedLCB-Q is communication-efficient, where the number of communication rounds is only linear with respect to the horizon length up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: This paper asks when multiple agents can jointly learn a policy from existing datasets without gathering new interactions. It studies federated offline reinforcement learning in finite-horizon, episodic, tabular Markov decision processes. The key issue is whether collaboration can compensate for datasets that are individually inadequate for learning the optimal policy.

The proposed FedLCB-Q algorithm updates local Q-functions using tailored learning-rate schedules. A central server combines them through importance averaging and a pessimistic penalty. With appropriate parameters and synchronization, the analysis establishes linear speedup with the number of agents. The coverage requirement is collective: together, the datasets must cover the state–action pairs visited by the optimal policy.

This is a sufficient condition that does not require each agent to possess a high-quality dataset. The sample complexity nearly matches learning with centrally pooled data, up to polynomial factors in horizon length. Communication rounds also grow only linearly with the horizon, apart from logarithmic factors. The result quantifies how complementary offline data can support effective collaboration under the stated setting and conditions.
summary.tldr: Under collective optimal-policy coverage and suitable settings, FedLCB-Q achieves linear agent-count speedup with efficient communication.

title: Federated Offline Reinforcement Learning: Collaborative Single-Policy Coverage Suffices

abstract: Continuous-time generative models, such as Flow Matching (FM), construct probability paths to transport between one distribution and another through the simulation-free learning of the neural ordinary differential equations (ODEs). During inference, however, the learned model often requires multiple neural network evaluations to accurately integrate the flow, resulting in a slow sampling speed. We attribute the reason to the inherent (joint) heterogeneity of source and/or target distributions, namely the singularity problem, which poses challenges for training the neural ODEs effectively. To address this issue, we propose a more general framework, termed Switched FM (SFM), that eliminates singularities via switching ODEs, as opposed to using a uniform ODE in FM. Importantly, we theoretically show that FM cannot transport between two simple distributions due to the existence and uniqueness of initial value problems of ODEs, while these limitations can be well tackled by SFM. From an orthogonal perspective, our framework can seamlessly integrate with the existing advanced techniques, such as minibatch optimal transport, to further enhance the straightness of the flow, yielding a more efficient sampling process with reduced costs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the newly proposed SFM through several numerical examples.

paragraphs: Flow Matching learns a continuous transformation between probability distributions using a neural ordinary differential equation. Switched Flow Matching replaces a uniform ODE with switching ODEs to eliminate these singularities.
