paragraphs: Point-process observations consist of events that provide sparse, noisy evidence about an underlying intensity function. The paper focuses on recovering that function over time. A continuous estimate can be easier to analyze than the events themselves because it describes the intensity driving the process across the temporal domain.

Gaussian processes provide the inference framework, but a naive implementation has demanding memory and runtime requirements. The authors identify this computational burden as a barrier to using the approach on reasonably sized problems. Their work therefore targets the calculation needed to obtain the intensity estimate, making the inference procedure more practical.

For a class of renewal processes, the authors develop methods that exploit the particular problem structure. They report eliminating the memory burden and reducing solution time by orders of magnitude. The stated scope matters: these are specialized methods for the identified class of processes. Their significance is that problem-specific computation can make Gaussian-process intensity estimation accessible where a straightforward implementation would be computationally infeasible.
summary.tldr: Specialized Gaussian-process methods dramatically reduce the computational burden of intensity estimation for a class of renewal processes.

title: Fast Gaussian process methods for point process intensity estimation

abstract: In the ordinal classification with monotonicity constraints, it is assumed that the class label should increase with increasing values on the attributes. In this paper we aim at formalizing the approach to learning with monotonicity constraints from statistical point of view, which results in the algorithm for learning rule ensembles. The algorithm first "monotonizes" the data using a nonparametric classification procedure and then generates rule ensemble consistent with the training set. The procedure is justified by a theoretical analysis and verified in a computational experiment.
originalAbstract: In the ordinal classification with monotonicity constraints, it is assumed that the class label should increase with increasing values on the attributes. In this paper we aim at formalizing the approach to learning with monotonicity constraints from statistical point of view, which results in the algorithm for learning rule ensembles. The algorithm first "monotonizes" the data using a nonparametric classification procedure and then generates rule ensemble consistent with the training set. The procedure is justified by a theoretical analysis and verified in a computational experiment.

paragraphs: This paper considers ordinal classification, where class labels have an order, under a monotonicity assumption. Increasing the relevant attribute values is expected to move the class label upward rather than downward. The learning problem therefore involves both predicting ordered categories and respecting a specified direction of change between attributes and labels.

The authors formalize learning under these constraints from a statistical perspective and derive a rule-ensemble algorithm. Its first stage uses a nonparametric classification procedure to monotonize the data. Its second stage generates an ensemble of rules consistent with the resulting training set. This separates enforcing the ordered relationship in the data from constructing the rule-based predictor.

The procedure is supported by theoretical analysis and checked in a computational experiment. The contribution gives monotonic rule learning a statistical foundation as well as an explicit construction process. Its relevance depends on the stated modeling assumption: the attribute-to-label relationship should be monotone in the intended direction. Within that setting, the rules reflect the order structure built into the learning task.
summary.tldr: A statistically motivated algorithm first monotonizes ordinal data and then builds a consistent rule ensemble.

title: Rule learning with monotonicity constraints

abstract: We propose a method that detects the true direction of time series, by fitting an autoregressive moving average model to the data. Whenever the noise is independent of the previous samples for one ordering of the observations, but dependent for the opposite ordering, we infer the former direction to be the true one. We prove that our method works in the population case as long as the noise of the process is not normally distributed (for the latter case, the direction is not identifiable). A new and important implication of our result is that it confirms a fundamental conjecture in causal reasoning --- if after regression the noise is independent of signal for one direction and dependent for the other, then the former represents the true causal direction --- in the case of time series. We test our approach on two types of data: simulated data sets conforming to our modeling assumptions, and real world EEG time series. Our method makes a decision for a significant fraction of both data sets, and these decisions are mostly correct. For real world data, our approach outperforms alternative solutions to the problem of time direction recovery.

We prove that our method works in the population case as long as the noise of the process is not normally distributed (for the latter case, the direction is not identifiable). A new and important implication of our result is that it confirms a fundamental conjecture in causal reasoning --- if after regression the noise is independent of signal for one direction and dependent for the other, then the former represents the true causal direction --- in the case of time series. We test our approach on two types of data: simulated data sets conforming to our modeling assumptions, and real world EEG time series. Our method makes a decision for a significant fraction of both data sets, and these decisions are mostly correct. paragraphs: This paper asks whether the true direction of a time series can be recovered from its observations. The method fits an autoregressive moving average model and examines the relationship between noise and earlier samples. If noise is independent of previous samples in one ordering but dependent in the reverse ordering, it chooses the former.

The authors prove that the method works at the population level under their process model when the noise is not normally distributed. With normally distributed noise, the direction is not identifiable. This result supports a causal reasoning principle in the time-series setting: an asymmetry in noise independence after regression can distinguish the true direction from its reverse.

Experiments use simulated data conforming to the modeling assumptions and real EEG recordings. The method makes decisions for a significant fraction of both collections, and those decisions are mostly correct. On the real data it outperforms alternative time-direction recovery methods. The empirical claim thus concerns the decisions actually made, alongside a theoretical guarantee with explicit distributional conditions.
summary.tldr: Noise-independence asymmetry can recover time-series direction, with a population guarantee for non-normal noise and mostly correct decisions in reported experiments.

title: Detecting the direction of causal time series

abstract: Inverse optimal control, also known as inverse reinforcement learning, is the problem of recovering an unknown reward function in a Markov decision process from expert demonstrations of the optimal policy. We introduce a probabilistic inverse optimal control algorithm that scales gracefully with task dimensionality, and is suitable for large, continuous domains where even computing a full policy is impractical. By using a local approximation of the reward function, our method can also drop the assumption that the demonstrations are globally optimal, requiring only local optimality. This allows it to learn from examples that are unsuitable for prior methods.
originalAbstract: Inverse optimal control, also known as inverse reinforcement learning, is the problem of recovering an unknown reward function in a Markov decision process from expert demonstrations of the optimal policy. We introduce a probabilistic inverse optimal control algorithm that scales gracefully with task dimensionality, and is suitable for large, continuous domains where even computing a full policy is impractical. By using a local approximation of the reward function, our method can also drop the assumption that the demonstrations are globally optimal, requiring only local optimality. This allows it to learn from examples that are unsuitable for prior methods.

paragraphs: Inverse optimal control seeks to infer the reward function behind an expert's demonstrated behavior. The reward describes what makes some actions or outcomes preferable to others. In large continuous decision problems, this inference is challenging because even calculating a complete policy can be impractical. The paper develops a probabilistic approach aimed at such settings.

The key idea is to use a local approximation of the reward function. This changes the requirement placed on demonstrations: they need only be locally optimal, rather than globally optimal. Local optimality concerns behavior that cannot be improved through nearby alternatives, while global optimality requires comparison with the full range of possibilities.

The authors state that their algorithm scales gracefully with task dimensionality and is suitable for large continuous domains. Relaxing the demonstration requirement also lets it learn from examples that earlier methods cannot use. The contribution connects computational tractability with a weaker assumption about expert behavior: reward inference can proceed from locally optimal examples without requiring the demonstrations to solve the entire decision problem globally.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic inverse control method uses local reward approximations to learn in large continuous domains from locally optimal demonstrations.

title: Continuous Inverse Optimal Control with Locally Optimal Examples
